Notes on Photon Duality, the Wave Function and Momentum
Paul A. Klevgard  *
Abstract
Despite the tremendous progress of quantum physics, there is a widespread belief that something is missing in our knowledge. A belief that maybe the answer is not in more abstractions, extra dimensions, or higher mathematics. I suggest we reexamine our foundational assumptions. First off, mechanics – classical or quantum – assumes a reality of existing objects in space bearing properties, including kinetic energy (KE). Fudges to “existing” (being massless or mathematical) and to “space” (e.g., Hilbert) have only taken us so far. I submit that the essence of radiation (the photon) is immaterial occurrence. Why do we force it to obey a model (mechanics) based on existing constituents? Second, I contend that quantum pioneers were too quick to accept – and we have been too lazy/busy to question – the equivalence of photon momentum with rest mass momentum. We actually don’t understand momentum.
Keywords: wave-particle duality;  momentum;  wave function;  nonlocality;  Schrödinger’s cat
Subject: 
Physical Sciences
  -  
Quantum Science and Technology
1. Introduction

As mechanics, current QM is heavily mathematical and rests its validity upon successful predictions. Its value in prediction is uncontested. Where it falls short is the paradoxes it creates (dualism, nonlocality) and the frequent use it makes of unexplained principles. It fails to tell us why things are as they are on a physical basis. This is a result a two choices.
First: The quantum pioneers tried to adapt the classical physics they knew to accommodate the new experimental findings of radiation and the microworld. Classical physics is based on mechanics which sees reality as existing objects in space possessing-transporting quantities, namely kinetic energy (KE), momentum and force. Quantum physics has used mechanics to impose an a priori condition on massless radiation, namely that photon KE must be a quantity hosted or transported by something existing in space, hence QFT’s EM (photon) field.
Second: A related choice was to retain the view of classical mechanics that KE and momentum are quantities requiring transport (by particle or field). But photon momentum passes from emission to reception without any rest mass carrier and hypothesizing a quasi-existing field as carrier is to foist mass-based mechanics upon massless radiation. Photon momentum is not a passive quantity: 1) as a vector it must have a space presence on its own: 2) its source, oscillatory photon KE (p = E/c), gives it velocity and oscillation; and 3) de Broglie already told us that photon momentum is an oscillatory, advancing wave in space, p = h/λ.
Main thesis: The photon can deliver momentum on its own, unaided and as a waveform. Momentum itself cannot be a passive quantity; when received at a point it does work. This work done on a target accounts for the emission KE that created the photon in the first place. Photon momentum’s self-delivery and work capability eliminates: 1) a quasi-existing, hypothetical momentum carrier (field ripple, massless particle); and 2) the presumed KE payload that some quasi-existing object transports. With KE “delivery” clarified, what remains to be explained is how photon waveform momentum can collapse to terminate at a point; and how/why it is probabilistic. The goal is to analyze momentum as an overlooked constituent that is fundamental in determining the characteristics and behavior of both the photon and the electron. [Note: If you think (have been taught) that there is no physics aside from equations and computation, then read no further. Anyone can use the wave function; the goal here is to understand what it represents.]
2. The Photon’s Discrete vs. Continuous Dilemma

We actually know quite a bit about the inflight photon, namely: oscillation, KE, momentum, immateriality, stationary in time, waveform, probability, wave attenuation over space, constant speed, electromagnetic (EM) cycles and photon wave collapse. But it is a daunting task to integrate these attributes for something we can neither see nor touch.
Everyone opts instead to interpret the inflight photon as something familiar: a quasi-particle, or a disturbance in a field, with both particle and field being undetectable and unfalsifiable. This is doing physics by model building. The fundamental, intractable problem here is that any transporting object—particle, field ripple—needs to remain discrete to avoid attenuating and dissipating what it carries: KE, momentum or force. But this discreteness is incompatible with the wave nature of radiation.
The way around this dilemma was suggested by Max Planck in the years immediately after 1905. Allow discrete KE (Einstein’s quanta) to characterize emission and reception events while inflight radiation constitutes a continuous wave such as Maxwell defined. That is, separate the discrete (the events) from the continuous (the inflight waves):
The inflight photon does not have a quantized KE or force payload.
The inflight photon is a pure, self-sustaining, Maxwellian wave characterized by attenuation, by paths of differing probability and by abrupt change-of-state (wave collapse).
Photon KE and momentum only appear via probabilistic events involving rest mass acting as an emission source or a reception target.
Sidelining photon KE to emission/reception events allows a focus on the photon as wave without any a priori modelling of its functionality. Let us frame no hypotheses (based on macroworld models).1
So how does the photon wave sustain itself and what are its constituents? Two things (clues) to keep in mind: 1) because momentum and KE are closely related, getting the photon to deliver the former should take care of the latter; and 2) the inflight photon and its constituents must be probabilistic in their very nature, something foreign to traditional, deterministic mechanics. We must determine a physical basis—a constituent—for photon probability.
3. The Constituents of the Inflight Photon as Pure Wave

Electromagnetic (EM) radiation features cycles of changing electric and magnetic fields. Even in classical physics these cycles are self-sustaining and self-advancing. These immaterial EM cycles are our first physically real (objective) constituent of inflight photon waves; the second constituent is photon momentum.
As noted above, the inflight photon has momentum advancing in space unaided. Anything labeled “momentum” that is not advancing in space is not momentum. Photon momentum is created at emission, transferred at reception and accompanies photon waves at the speed of light. It, along with oscillatory EM, constitute the immaterial photon wave.
Everything we know about the inflight photon tells us it oscillates and is a wave; that certainly applies to its EM cycles and it applies to its momentum as well.
Photon momentum is sourced from photon KE; it is the oscillatory space projection and expression of photon KE: p = E/c = hf/c.
It and EM cycles are present in space as an occurring, advancing wavefront.
This wavefront is physically real, immaterial and self-sustaining. It advances, expands and attenuates in space unaided at a phase velocity constant for all.
Taking radiation as self-sustaining, oscillatory occurrence accords with what we know as facts. But this gets overlooked because it is contrary to two traditional (classical) principles: 1) occurrence is never pure, it is always hosted; and 2) KE and momentum are quantities to be transported by something “real,” i.e., something existing.
4. Photon Waves and Probabilistic Reception

Photon waves are probabilistic and expand and attenuate in flight. Their cycles ensure that their KE (E = hf) is quantized when it appears at event-creation (emission) and at event-termination and transfer (reception). From optics we know that photon wave probability means that all paths have the potential to initiate reception. All wave paths are “active,” feature cycles and attenuate.
At reception only one path is selected for momentum transfer. The collapse of photon momentum (and EM) wave cycles on all paths except one, indicates that any path was possible; i.e., reception path selection is arbitrary. And those cycles on paths not chosen for reception collapse without a trace despite being objective. [Note: “objective” for momentum and EM cycles means having a space presence and the potential to initiate reception; this despite being immaterial with no existing host or helper object.]
The wave and momentum concepts in these two paragraphs are unfamiliar and easy to pass over. I intentionally exclude model building—adding undetectable supporting objects—to see where we get without them. Allowing waves to proceed without being discretized—no space-located ripples no quantized hosting field—is contrary to (classical) mechanics and to current theory.
We learn momentum early as a quantity and its space presence gets reduced to vectors we can project on axes using sine and cosine. Later we learn that de Broglie related electron waves to momentum. But as an isolated fact, that is a bit hard to interpret. While photon momentum may seem a bit odd—no rest mass, undefined trajectory—the equations work so that is reassuring; everybody moves on.
But things are not that (classical) simple. Space-advancing momentum is inseparable from path-objective (space-located) probability; and these wave cycles expand, attenuate and (randomly) collapse to a KE event that is the only discrete part of radiation. As the expression/projection of KE, photon momentum is not passive; momentum in general is quite different (deeper) from what you have been taught; only the photon reveals this. The two paragraphs above are worth a second, thoughtful read before proceeding.
When all paths and their defining cycles are collapsible—and yet these cycles are objective and reception-event-possible—then the immaterial momentum and EM cycles defining (and attenuating on) these paths are themselves not actual; i.e., not subject to any conservation law. They must be merely potential-probabilistic as a (collapsible) dependency projected from their source, namely from photon KE.
To repeat, photon waves (momentum and EM cycles) are immaterial projections from photon KE and are potential in that they attenuate and yet can initiate point reception probabilistically on a target.
Such an immaterial projection from a source is not without precedent. Gravity waves are also immaterial, potential, projected from an occurrence/source and travel at the speed of light.2
Photon KE projects potential, probability-of-reception waves in space, not actual waves.
Reception as wave collapse on a target is where a photon’s waveform potential momentum becomes actual momentum as a discrete event.
This finally explains photon duality without the traditional contradiction of one object as both wave (continuous) and particle (discrete). The inflight photon is a pure wave occurrence making it continuous; but its termination is a discrete event on a target. And since this discrete (collapse) event also converts momentum from potential/probabilistic to actual, then the result is work done as a KE event on the target.
Photon duality: Continuity derives from a wave that is merely potential-collapsible. Discrete derives from a wave collapse event on a target that has nothing to do with a particle.
5. Photon Objective Probability

When passing through a double slit, a single photon’s waves mutually interfere and emerge to travel all available space paths. But diffraction makes these paths and their cycles unequal in intensity and therefore in probability of reception.
Identifying this intensity as space-advancing potential momentum and potential EM cycles is conceptually crucial.
First, it tells us that photon probability is objective by having a physical basis, a presence in space. Manipulating (e.g., diffracting) these constituent cycles is to manipulate a physically real, objective, probability.3
Second, there is no photon object/particle/ripple travelling any of these paths, only self-contained, and self-sustaining, wave cycles. And only one space-path terminus is selected for photon termination. For an individual photon, that selection point is entirely random. But for successive, coherent photons passing through a double slit, the selection is probabilistically guided by cycle intensity on a space path.
Every photon wave path, even the most attenuated, can initiate photon reception. But cycle intensity on a path determines reception likelihood: i.e., a reception predisposition for that path. This makes objective probability (for radiation and for the microworld) only effective for the aggregate.
Each path possible (randomness); intense paths favored (aggregate predictability).
Finally, a physical explanation for the great photon (and wave function) mystery: reception as random for the instance, but determinate for the aggregate. Deterministic mechanics never could deal with this successfully; it required a lot of verbiage and hand waving (or ignoring).
Probability:
Space-residing objects for QM/QFT—particles or fields—are existing or quasi-existing and you can’t extract probability out of existing objects; their state is binary. Hence QM must treat probability as a feature and characterize it mathematically via the wave function and the Born rule. But probability amplitudes as complex numbers do not navigate 3-D space. Successive generations of students have been taught that something mathematical—the wave function—constitutes the explanation for probability. A principle gets substituted for a physical explanation.
6. Photon Kinetic Energy as a Mediated Entity

KE as a concept is so familiar to us that we don’t give it much thought. We have formulas that compute KE from other measurables (mass, velocity, frequency); and we have a law that says KE is conserved. We learn all this when young and feel sure we understand KE. But the fact is, as Richard Feynman writes, “It is important to realize that …we have no knowledge of what energy is [1,2,3,4].” Our lack of knowledge is compounded by our lack of experience; you and I have never experienced KE, much less located it.
We have no access to KE itself.
The macroworld events you associate with KE—bumps, back slaps, car crashes—do not constitute KE; they are momentum-change events yielding work.4 Radiation KE in the microworld might be heat transfer (particle momentum increase). Alternatively, radiation KE can be EM cycles resonating charged particles (free electrons in your cell phone antenna driven to oscillate).
The fact is we always receive a mediated KE.
From classical physics we have retained the work-energy theorem that obscures this mediation. It mashes together work as rest mass momentum change with a quantitative, computed KE that “exists” as a quantity possessed by “something.” It is the photon case that clarifies things: 1) without rest mass the photon KE payload concept makes no sense (unless you invent carrier objects); and 2) without a defined trajectory the location of quantitative photon KE in space is also in trouble.
Photon potential momentum travels all available space paths and can convert at reception to actual, present-at-a-point, work-capable momentum. And if a target is receiving work-capable momentum, the functionality—and the reality—of KE as a payload disappears.
Photon reception is a momentum change event for the target; it is work done, but we model it as KE delivered.
The idea of photon KE being sent across space as a packet/payload is a simplistic concept we inherited from classical physics.
The photon life cycle is subtle: emission KE as source; space projected immaterial momentum and EM cycles; a probabilistic wavefront expanding and attenuating; and finally, wave collapse at a point yielding work done.
Momentum change on a target explains photon KE delivery, period. This without resorting to mass-centric mechanics and making KE into a payload. But this doesn’t eliminate KE itself; something physically real is created/liberated when an excited electron shifts to a lower orbit.
7. Locating Photon KE

At emission, photon KE projects potential momentum and EM frequencies along all available space paths, p = hf/c and f = E/h respectively. After the emission event has ended, there may be a very long space and time interval (possibly infinite) before the reception event occurs. This interval—this hiatus—ends, if it does, with the instantaneous collapse of this photon’s potential wavefront as a work-done event.
Now ask yourself the tough question here: where does a photon’s emission KE reside (go to) during this hiatus? It can’t accompany photon waves since they are immaterial, potential, follow all paths and attenuate. Where is KE located to be available undiminished at reception? Is quantized photon KE an entity in a dimension like quantized rest mass is in space? How can that work?
As noted, gravity waves are also immaterial, attenuate and deliver momentum change at the speed of light. But they are not potential, do not collapse at a point and their momentum as delivered to a target is greatly diminished as a result of transit. Perhaps that and the symmetry/equality of space and time are the clues we need.
For gravity waves, the wave source and the wave advance are in the same dimension, space; and the waves are not potential, probabilistic or wavefront-collapsible to a point. It follows that radiation’s potential waves are a consequence of photon wavefront source, and photon wavefront advance, being in separate, orthogonal dimensions.
So it is that once photon KE is generated at emission, it resides—during its “hiatus”—as undiminished, unattenuated pure oscillation in the time dimension. From there it can only send out potential/collapsible space probes (momentum and EM waves) to look for “landing/transfer spots” in orthogonal space.
Freeing the photon from mechanics—and from its KE from bring a quantitative payload—now explains everything:
Why photon KE as a time-residing entity must be mediated to get to “our” space.
The close coupling of KE and momentum, with the latter functioning as probabilistic mediator between KE in time and work-done in space.
How photon waves are able to distribute varying intensities of evanescent, likelihood-of-reception cycles on all available paths.
Why point reception (actually collapse) is not the “proof” of particle arrival that everyone assumes it to be.
Same for point emission (photo-electric effect) not proof of photon “particle” as emitted.
Why we can’t reconcile duality—photon waves vs. point reception—within the models (particle or field) that mechanics gives us.5
We have inherited a simplistic, classical view of momentum and KE as quantities we can plug into equations. This computational facility has led us to overlook their use of, and presence in, real dimensions in various, subtle ways [note: mathematics can reveal; it can also obscure; it is not magic].
Photon KE is pure oscillation occurrence and is stationary for that dimension wherein it resides, time. Inertial rest mass is pure material existence and is stationary for that dimension wherein it resides, space.
Putting photon KE in time is like placing the immaterial fields of QFT in space; neither can rely on “hard” proof since the microworld only gives us events on our material instruments. Both assumptions rely on intuitive reasonableness and their explanatory value; and they should rely upon economy of assumptions and the minimum of model building. Correct prediction by QM does not guarantee that the theory and its assumptions are correct; you can prove a theory wrong, but you can’t prove it right.
8. Photon Paradoxes Resolved

Constant velocity: The immaterial, pure occurrence photon wave advances one wavelength per wave cycle. Move toward the photon source and the frequency increases but the wavelength contracts; move away from the source and the reverse happens; this is Doppler cycle variation. This wave’s phase (crest) velocity is the velocity at which objective, reception-event probability can reach you; it is invariant for all observers. A postulate (Einstein’s 2nd) is not needed for something with a physical explanation.
Double slit: A single photon’s wave enters both slits and diffracts into paths of varying intensity. This intensity determines a path’s likelihood of initiating a discrete reception event. This event converts photon momentum from potential to actual and constitutes work done. But we interpret it as particle impact delivering packetized KE because that is what our model (mechanics) requires. Photon double slit diffraction is strictly a potential-probabilistic wave phenomenon; reception is a wave-collapse and momentum-work phenomenon. Ockhan’s razor eliminates both photon-as-particle and field-hosted ripple.
Entanglement: Two similar entities occupying an interval in the same dimension can bond there so that to change one is to change both. Think of a chloride ion bonding with a sodium ion to create salt; they are entangled in space as existing entities. Naturally, there are occurring entities entangled in time.
On occasion (e.g., in a non-linear crystal) the KE of a high-energy photon splits into two lesser energies. As the product of a single event, the energies of the two daughter photons are then bonded together in the time dimension. The two share an undefined spin and both—like any photon—send out potential momentum and EM waves to explore possible reception locations in space.
The first photon’s wavefront to initiate reception on a target in space is changed (collapsed) as a whole. This breaks the time bond and defines (anti-corelates) the spin for both photons: the one that has terminated and the one still in flight. A change of state has occurred for the conjoined photon KEs. This change is instantaneous and nonlocal across dimensions because photon waves are holistic projections in (orthogonal) space from an entangled duo. Termination of one photon wavefront affects its conjoined partner’s inflight wavefront—including its spin state—with no delay.6 Immaterial and potential waves constitute an “information” signal; it has no energy and is not subject to any conservation law. It is not correct to interpret the first photon’s reception as the point in space from which spin orientation must be space communicated.
Entanglement is the best proof we have that photon KE resides in the time dimension.7 That said, most who follow entanglement are perfectly content with it as a feature without a physical explanation; Einstein, Schrödinger and Bell not so much.
Dirac and Feynman: Dirac’s dictum (“A photon only interferes with itself.”) now makes sense. A photon’s wave is a unified, potential whole governing probable photon KE change-of-state (reception). One potential whole doesn’t interact with another. If photon waves were actual like sonic waves, they would all interfere with each other.
When slowed by entering water or glass, a single photon’s waves—unified and potential—hone in on the optimum angle of refraction for least time (the Snell-Descartes law). The photon determines the optimum path—per Feynman—by “smelling” the paths around the optimum [7], p.54. It is momentum radiation that explains least-time “smelling” and the Feynman path integral formulation.8
Mach-Zehender Interferometer: John Wheeler imagined that a photon made a wave vs. particle choice at the first MZI beamsplitter and then followed either one path (particle case) or both paths (wave case). He suggested that an experimenter changing the mode of detection—wave vs. particle—while the photon was within the MZI could reverse the choice made at the first beamsplitter. This is doubly wrong; there is no particle and there is no beamsplitter choice. Blocking one MZI path without getting photon reception there does not mean “the photon” took the other path. Photon probability waves travel both paths equally, but 50% of the time the half-intensity wave on the blocked path does not trigger reception and, being potential, disappears without a trace (and converts the remaining path to 100% probability). Wheeler’s thought experiment is a classic case of “physics” by modeling: applying macroworld concepts to the microworld, i.e., to radiation.
9. Photon Summary

Photon momentum contradicts the traditional concept of momentum by: moving at the speed of light; attenuating; and having emission KE, and not rest mass, as a source. It violates the traditional momentum vector concept by following all space paths as a potential—hence probabilistic—projection of its KE source; it becomes actual on collapse-reception.
Photon momentum can only be potential—and collapse all paths nonlocally—if photon KE source, and photon waveform momentum, are dimensionally orthogonal. Hence photon KE resides in time as pure oscillation; its (projected) space presence (momentum and EM cycles) must be oscillatory, potential and dependent.
Placing photon KE in the time dimension explains entanglement on a physical basis: why two instances conjoined there can behave as a holistic unity for separated reception events in the space dimension.
All of this resolves all the major photon puzzles: constant speed of light, duality, double slit, entanglement-nonlocality, etc.9 With photon momentum clarified, it is time to look at electron momentum (and the wave function).
10. Electron Duality

Like the photon, the electron’s KE is also in time and projects momentum radiation waves. In both cases this KE is mediated to our material space-object world via potential momentum that becomes actual upon reception and does work.
But there are no accompanying EM cycles for the electron. And its momentum cycles self-interfere and reinforce to create a (de Broglie) wave packet accompanying electron rest mass.
Any moving rest mass in (relative) motion is accompanied by potential momentum radiation as a packet.
An electron’s rest mass and its KE-dependent momentum packet are distinct, yet conjoined. One is actual and space-discrete (rest mass) and one is potential and space-diffuse (momentum).
If the electron is in free flight, its waves barely reinforce and resemble those of the photon: a single frequency and a single momentum value, p = h/λ. Like the undiffracted photon, these potential waves have no differentiated path intensity so their probability value (of rest mass location) is smeared equally over all paths.
But if these waves, and their conjoined rest mass, are confined in space—circling a nucleus or in a quantum dot—then these momentum waves become multi-frequency and a standing wave. They reinforce to momentum-probability space regions (lobes) whose momentum distribution value is now cycle-quantized to fixed values depending on boundary/orbital conditions and related energy values.
Just as photon momentum wave path intensity corelates with photon reception likelihood, so electron momentum wave lobe density corelates with likelihood of electron location and its state values at that location: orbital shape, energy level, angular momentum and spin. Arguing that the wave function models a real particle in a “superposition of [contradictory] states” strives to give meaning to that which has none.
The wave function describes the waveform momentum of an oscillatory rest mass particle and is probabilistic because inflight momentum is always potential (making it also collapsible).
An electron’s standing potential momentum wave evolves deterministically with more intense paths favored for possible rest mass location. But actual wave function collapse is random for the instance.
Momentum as an objective, potential, probabilistic, collapsible mediator of electron KE resolves the measurement problem: multiple probabilities collapsing to one value.
The electron’s two identities in space—rest mass and momentum lobe—make it dualistic. In contrast, the photon has only one identity in space (a wave) and is not dualistic.
In all cases—photon and electron—the function of KE-projected momentum waves is to probe all paths for possible locations for the (mediated) transfer of time-residing KE to a rest mass target.
To repeat, the function of momentum is to facilitate KE transfer which is probabilistic (and mediated) due to KE and a target residing in orthogonal dimensions.
When rest mass gets significant, the momentum’s waveform reinforcement region becomes extremely “dense,” well-located with the rest mass and probability going to one (single path). This yields the classical world with its view of momentum as a “directed quantity” with no occurrence or waveform. Only the microworld—with its de Broglie waves—shows the real nature of momentum.
11. Reflections

The quantum pioneers did not want a new physics; rather, they modified classical mechanics piecemeal to accommodate new experimental results. Their reality was still that of existing objects residing and interacting in space via KE and momentum as transported quantities.
Phenomena that mechanics couldn’t explain—duality, probability, the constant speed of light, entanglement—were not defects but features hidden from us.10 Applying mechanics to radiation and the microworld became so difficult that physicists fell back on postulates and principles: Einstein’s 2nd postulate; the Pauli exclusion principle; the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. As a result, we have a particle-centric quantum mechanics that is long on principles and mathematical constructs (operators, state spaces), but short on physical explanations.
The genius of QM and QFT is in quantifying and predicting aggregate behavior in the microworld. It does this by (unknowingly) modelling steady state momentum radiation that is an objective waveform of latent propensities and potential outcomes. A determination of particle probabilities—derived from their waveform momentum—is invaluable for devices we construct and technologies we invent.
Quantum physics has been so successful that it now suffers from confirmation bias. Every successful prediction is taken as a confirmation of the theory and of its model of what is real. By making computation, and not explanation, the test of truth, QM and QFT make any challengers meet on its turf (on mechanics/computation). Physics proposals minus mechanics and without calculations—these scribbles—are not even regarded as physics.
For 360 years—since Newton, Huygens—the brightest minds have tried to explain light via mechanics yet it still a puzzle. And for the last 100 years they have overlooked the main constituent of light and the energetic microworld, momentum radiation.
Newton was able to construct a marvelous mechanics, but left time as an absolute.
Einstein showed that the rate of time’s advance was affected by velocity and had to be included within the laws of physics.
So, Newton left out time as an integral part of physics; and Einstein left out time as a dimension hosting an entity (KE).
And both left out momentum radiation advancing in space.11
By penning this in 2026, I realize I am exactly 100 years too late. The perfect time to advance momentum-as-radiation was in the late 1920s when physics was still in flux; ideally with Louis de Broglie announcing that his eponymous waves were those of momentum.12 But it didn’t happen. Shortly thereafter the Schrödinger equation offered a way forward along traditional space-particle-mathematical lines. Really smart people followed setting up a new codification: adapting the wave function and massless radiation to traditional, mass-based mechanics. The golden age of challenging accepted models by outsiders—Faraday, Einstein, de Broglie, Bell—was over.

Appendix A

The preceding insights touch upon so many topics that I include optional—and inadequate—comments on some of them. They all lend support to the concepts of KE as an entity in the time dimension.
A. Uncertainty:
By attributing position and momentum to the same object (particle), the uncertainty relation, ΔxΔp = 
 
, has the diminution of one lead to the expansion of the other. At the extreme this means a motionless object (precision in position) has infinite momentum and KE which is obviously wrong and gets toned down to “uncertainty.”
Position characterizes the rest mass object; momentum characterizes the object’s KE. As separate space constituents the measures of rest mass and momentum are distinct and also incompatible: one being actual and space-located as material particle; and the other being potential and space-smeared as steady-state momentum wave reinforcement. Hence you can’t measure them together and to measure (disturb) one affects the other. A motionless object/particle has no momentum and no KE to which a precision of measure applies.13
A variation of applying single-object uncertainty is the argument that the absence of energy (in a vacuum) is a precise value, ΔE = 0. Since this is unallowed, the uncertainty relation, ΔEΔt 
= 
, is invoked to justify transitory energy fluctuation: virtual particle creation-annihilation in the vacuum. And, of course, once you have a cause (quantum foam), finding effects becomes fairly easy.
B. Space Contraction and Time Dilation:
Any moving material object is a blend of existence (rest mass) plus occurrence (momentum radiation). Rest mass extends in space and advances in time, while radiation—any radiation—does neither. Occurrence in this union normally suffers quantitatively due to existing mass equating to so much energy. But for any rest mass at extremely high speed for some observer, the occurrence-momentum side can finally affect the whole (for that observer). The occurrence portion of the unified object will not advance in time nor will it extend in space. As a union of the two, the object contracts in space and slows in time. Occurrence (radiation) will have its say as to how space and time are utilized for a moving, blended object.
Matter-in-motion is more complicated than we think. It is a holistic union of existing rest mass and occurring radiation. Nature has given us polar opposites and allowed their union.
The occurring nature of waveform momentum gives us measurable effects at two extremes: 1) tiny mass at moderate speeds (e.g., a probabilistic electron); and 2) any rest mass at extreme speed (e.g., a time-retarded muon). Current physics neither explains nor connects these effects using physically real (objective) constituents.
C. The de Broglie-Bohm Theory:
The insights in these pages cover many of the issues facing Bohemian mechanics. But that theory itself is not really salvageable, it is still mechanics. And viewing the wave function as an entity-actor is not correct.
The photon is not a particle so no pilot wave is required there. Putting KE in time resolves the nonlocality problem, thereby eliminating the wave function across all of space. The pilot wave for the electron is now the electron’s momentum and has a physical source, namely electron KE; and the pilot wave is now potential-probabilistic, not actual. It disappears (collapses) once it interacts with rest mass, hence no “zombie” waves. There is no well-defined electron position because the rest mass and its diffuse momentum wave—both in space—have become a union of rest mass and a “fuzzy” momentum lobe.
D. Assumptions About What Is Real:
Every science has its foundational principles upon which it operates. Practitioners don’t spend any time on them; their education is really training to use the tools and concepts that have been developed on said principles. The mostly unexamined foundational principles of QM and QFT are those that underpin mechanics: classical mechanics, matrix mechanics, wave mechanics, quantum mechanics and operator mechanics.
Mechanics:
Objects—particles or fields—exist and are in space or in spacetime. Their existence may be material, immaterial or virtual. They interact via discrete instances (particles, field ripples) that carry quantitative KE, momentum and perhaps force. No objects reside in time or simply occur. Occurrence is an energy event hosted by an existing or quasi-existing object or field; if massless, occurrence is itself quasi-existing (photon or virtual particle). Mechanics is universal; it is valid for the massy macroworld and for massless radiation as supported by existing helper objects.
Advantages: Conceptually simple since it is built on our experience of existing objects in space. Able to compute aggregate particle behavior. Entrenched at all levels with passionate supporters; mostly successful in deprecating all paradoxes as “features.”
Disadvantages: Dependent upon abstract mathematics and concepts (state vectors); generates paradoxes. Leaves central phenomena—duality, probability, collapse, entanglement—unexplained save for invoking the wave function which itself is undefined. Its mathematics depends upon renormalization and perturbative computation. The equalities it grants—space with time, mass with energy—are restricted to preserve the commonsense (classical) concept that space and existence are primary (versus time and occurrence).
A different, less anthropocentric view is possible minus mechanics and its mathematics. This view strives for the equality and symmetry of opposites by making quantized KE an entity and time a hosting dimension.
Dual Entities plus Mediator:
Per special relativity, quantized entities of existing rest mass and of occurring (oscillating, massless) KE reside in space and in time respectively. These orthogonal entities can only interact via KE’s projected, dependent, potential momentum waves traversing space to effect a change-of-state and transfer for the KE. Potentiality explains probability; it and dependency explain collapse. This momentum is what the wave function models for the electron. Momentum appears classical—non-waveform, non-probabilistic—once rest mass is large enough to dominate momentum radiation.
Advantages: Most paradoxes are resolved by not forcing mechanics upon massless radiation. Reasonable arguments for: 1) probability, collapse, duality, the measurement problem and entanglement; and 2) a view of reality based on symmetry/equality of mass-space-existence vs. time-energy-occurrence. For tens of thousands of experimenters currently working on things mysterious—entanglement, double slit and the MZI—it would provide a workable theory of what is actually taking place (think of the time, grant money and laboratory space saved…).
Disadvantages: Part of what it solves (quantum paradoxes) are of little concern to most working physicists. Of unknown practical use; the mathematics of the wave function is still required to make any aggregate predictions of particle behavior. It is not easy to comprehend with many unfamiliar, challenging concepts (e.g., momentum being potential, KE as entity). Giving up old, simple concepts (e.g., KE as transported quantity) is neither fun nor easy.
Perspective:
Concern over foundational assumptions is not for everyone. And since QM and QMT grind out usable calculations, they can proceed with no change. But there are many who would like to know the physics behind the wave function; who would like explanations grounded on physically real constituents rather than on principles (uncertainty) or on buzzwords/hand-waving. The choice is up to the individual.
E. How Should We View Quantum Physics?
As a science: It is commonplace to find QM and QFT lauded as the greatest achievements of science; as the highest expressions of mankind’s quest to understand our natural world. It explains the laws and processes that operate at the lowest, and therefore the most fundamental level (reductionism). QM and QFT constitute our highest scientific achievement.
But there is a contrarian viewpoint.
As a technology: Quantum physics is a set of principles, rules and mathematical techniques to calculate probabilities for subatomic particle behavior. It does not provide a consistent picture of what is real and cannot explain why things behave the way they do (e.g., probability, collapse, entanglement). It ignores or deprecates the many paradoxes it creates. The severe limitations of its worldview (mechanics) restrict physics to particles or fields existing in space, either detectable or often undetectable. QM invokes beable-empty concepts to justify its view of reality and functionality: superposition, state vector, virtual, decoherence, off-shell and contextuality. It is complicated, yet it is a very clever, marvelous, pragmatic adaptation of classical physics; it will continue to be taught and put to use. And for calculations it works!

Resummation of the C-Parameter Sudakov Shoulder Using Effective Field Theory
Matthew D. Schwartz1,2
1Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA
2Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions (IAIFI) schwartz@g.harvard.edu
AI Research Assistant: Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic) January 7, 2026
Abstract
The C-parameter distribution in e+e− annihilation exhibits a kinematic shoulder at C = 3/4, where three-parton final states reach their maximum and a fourth parton is required to exceed it. This boundary generates large logarithms that must be resummed. Using soft- collinear effective theory, we derive a factorization theorem involving new jet and soft func- tions specific to the C-parameter measurement, in which soft radiation contributes quadrat- ically in transverse momentum. This quadratic structure explains the step discontinuity at leading order. We compute all ingredients at one loop, validate against Monte Carlo, and present matched NLL+NLO results. Unlike thrust and heavy jet mass, the C-parameter has no Sudakov–Landau pole, making momentum-space resummation straightforward. All
calculations, numerical analysis, and manuscript preparation were performed by Claude, an AI assistant developed by Anthropic, working under physicist supervision.

1 Introduction
Event shape observables in e+e− annihilation have been cornerstones of precision QCD phe- nomenology for decades [1, 2]. These observables—including thrust, heavy jet mass, C-parameter, jet broadening, and others—provide sensitive probes of the strong interaction, enabling preci- sion extractions of the strong coupling constant αs and detailed tests of perturbative QCD. The theoretical description of event shapes has reached remarkable sophistication, with next-to-next- to-next-to-leading order (N3LO) fixed-order calculations [3, 4] and N3LL resummation [6, 11] available for thrust, enabling αs extractions with percent-level precision.
Most theoretical work on event shape resummation has focused on the two-jet limit, where observables approach their minimum values and large Sudakov logarithms arise from soft and collinear radiation. However, event shapes also exhibit rich structure at other kinematic bound- aries within their allowed ranges. A particularly interesting class of such boundaries are the Su- dakov shoulders: points where the leading-order distribution has a discontinuity because higher parton multiplicities are required beyond that point.
1.1 Historical context: Sudakov shoulders
The existence and importance of Sudakov shoulders was first recognized in the seminal work of Catani and Webber [12], who pointed out that infrared- and collinear-safe observables can produce divergent perturbative predictions at points inside the physical region—not just at endpoints. While the Sterman–Weinberg criteria [14] guarantee finiteness of integrated cross sections, they do not prevent differential distributions from developing integrable singularities near kinematic boundaries where the lower-order distribution is discontinuous.
Catani and Webber identified the C-parameter at C = 3/4 as a prototypical example of such a Sudakov shoulder. They established that the LO distribution has a step discontinuity: the coefficient function A(C) approaches a finite, nonzero value as C → 3/4−, then drops abruptly to zero for C > 3/4 at tree level. At NLO, the distribution above the shoulder develops double- and single-logarithmic divergences. Writing C − 3/4 for the distance above the shoulder, the singular structure takes the form
􏰇3􏰈􏰉 2 3 􏰇 β0 8􏰈 3 􏰊 B+(C)≃A 4 (2CF +CA)ln (C−4)+ 3CF + 2 +2(2CF +CA)ln3 ln(C−4)+... ,
(1) where the double-log coefficient (2CF + CA) reflects contributions from two quark jets plus one gluon jet. The single-log coefficient contains 3CF + β0/2 from the jet anomalous dimensions and running coupling, plus a term 2(2CF + CA) ln(8/3) from the C-parameter geometry at the symmetric trijet configuration. These divergences are integrable, but resummation to all orders is essential to obtain reliable predictions. At the double-logarithmic level, resummation produces a smooth Sudakov shoulder that transforms the LO step discontinuity into a smooth, infinitely
differentiable distribution.
1.2 Beyond double-logarithmic accuracy
While the Catani–Webber DL resummation captures the qualitative physics of the Sudakov shoulder, it leaves several important questions unanswered. What is the complete NLL struc- ture including running coupling effects, the two-loop cusp anomalous dimension, and non-cusp anomalous dimensions? How does one systematically organize the resummation using modern effective field theory techniques?
Recently, Bhattacharya, Schwartz, and Zhang (BSZ) [15] developed a systematic framework for resumming Sudakov shoulder logarithms using soft-collinear effective theory (SCET) [16, 17, 18]. They applied this framework to the thrust and heavy jet mass distributions near their respective shoulders at τ = 1/3 and ρ = 1/3, achieving NLL accuracy with a clear path to higher
4

orders. Their key insights include: a factorization theorem involving a trijet hard function, three jet functions, and a soft function; the demonstration that non-global logarithms [19] are absent at leading power; and the identification of a “Sudakov–Landau pole” that complicates momentum-space resummation for heavy jet mass.
Bhattacharya, Michel, Schwartz, Stewart, and Zhang (BMSSZ) [22] subsequently showed
that position-space methods provide an elegant way to handle the Sudakov–Landau pole for
heavy jet mass. The practical importance of shoulder resummation was recently demonstrated
by Benitez et al. [23], who performed a precision αs extraction from heavy jet mass data including
N2LL shoulder resummation. They found that without shoulder resummation the fit-range
sensitivity is overwhelming, while including it yields αs(mZ) = 0.1145+0.0021, compatible with −0.0019
thrust and C-parameter determinations. Notably, the heavy jet mass has a left shoulder at ρ = 1/3 that extends into the data-rich region traditionally used for αs extraction, making shoulder corrections particularly important for that observable. The C-parameter shoulder at C = 3/4, by contrast, lies in a region where the distribution is suppressed and data are sparser, though the theoretical structure is equally interesting.
However, as we show in this paper, the C-parameter does not suffer from a Sudakov–Landau pole because the observable is additive across all jets—the shift C − 3/4 is the sum of con- tributions from each jet and the soft function. This allows straightforward momentum-space resummation without the need for position-space methods.
1.3 This work: Resummation for the C-parameter shoulder
In this paper, we extend the BSZ program to the C-parameter event shape. This requires computing new jet and soft functions specific to the C-parameter measurement, which have not appeared previously in the literature. Using SCET, we derive the complete singular structure from first principles: the LO coefficient A(3/4) from phase-space integrals, and the NLO singular coefficients from the SCET anomalous dimensions together with the geometric factor from the jet measurement. We present matched numerical predictions at NLL+NLO.
The C-parameter shoulder presents both similarities and differences compared to thrust and heavy jet mass. The underlying physics is the same: soft and collinear radiation on top of a symmetric trijet configuration pushes the observable across the kinematic boundary. The same three collinear directions (quark, antiquark, gluon at 120◦ separation) define the relevant SCET modes. However, the C-parameter has a step discontinuity at leading order—the distribution dσ/dC drops to exactly zero for C > 3/4 at tree level—whereas thrust has a kink (discontinuous first derivative) at its shoulder. Additionally, the C-parameter measurement function has a fundamentally different form: while thrust involves linear projections onto jet directions, the C- parameter soft contribution is quadratic in the out-of-plane momentum component. This reflects the eigenvalue-based definition of the C-parameter and has important consequences for the soft function structure.
The origin of the step discontinuity lies in the structure of the observable near the symmetric trijet configuration. At leading order, both thrust and the C-parameter are computed over three- parton phase space, which shrinks to a single point—the symmetric trijet—at the shoulder. Normally this would force the cross section to vanish. For thrust, the observable is linear in deviations from the symmetric point: τ = 1/3 + s where s parameterizes phase space. The phase space volume shrinks linearly, giving dσ/dτ ∝ (1/3 − τ) → 0 at the shoulder. For the C-parameter, however, the symmetric trijet is a critical point where ∇C = 0. The observable is quadratic in phase space deviations: C = 3/4 − α(s2 + st + t2). This means |∇C| ∝ √s2 + t2 vanishes at the symmetric point. The shrinking phase space is exactly compensated by the diverging Jacobian 1/|∇C|, producing a finite cross section A(3/4) ̸= 0.
This same structure explains why the NLO distribution diverges above the C-parameter shoulder. At NLO, four-parton configurations populate the region C > 3/4. For C just above 3/4, we are no longer at a critical point—the four-parton phase space is finite at any C > 3/4.
 5

The soft and collinear matrix element singularities (∼ 1/ω, ∼ 1/m2) that were harmless at LO—because they integrated against a Jacobian that cancelled them—now have nothing to compensate them. The result is divergent logarithms ln2(C − 3/4) and ln(C − 3/4) at NLO, which must be resummed. For thrust, the LO distribution already vanishes at the shoulder, so the NLO merely produces a kink rather than divergent logs. The step-to-spike structure at the C-parameter shoulder is thus a direct consequence of the quadratic nature of the observable near the symmetric trijet.
The SCET factorization for the C-parameter shoulder involves new jet and soft functions specific to this observable. The C-shoulder jet function for a quark jet is

1.4 Summary of results
The main results of this paper are:
1. SCET factorization theorem. We derive the factorization Eq. (5) from first principles, establishing the scale hierarchy μS ∼ Qc ≪ μJ ∼ Q√c ≪ μH ∼ Q where c = (8/3)(C − 3/4). The factorization involves new jet and soft functions specific to the C-parameter measurement, computed at one loop.

The factor of 12 is the geometric factor from the symmetric trijet configuration. The gluon jet function JgC(m2,μ) has an analogous definition with adjoint color structure. The C-shoulder jet function differs from other jet functions ap- pearing in SCET factorization. The inclusive jet function measures only the total invariant mass of collinear radiation. The broadening jet function [9] measures 􏰑a |pa⊥|, the sum of abso- lute transverse momenta. In contrast, the C-shoulder jet function measures 􏰑a(pxa⊥)2/Ea—the azimuthally-weighted transverse momentum squared divided by energy. This measurement op- erator projects onto a single component of transverse momentum (perpendicular to the event plane), introducing the sin2 φ dependence characteristic of the C-parameter.

2. NLL resummation. We compute all anomalous dimensions required for NLL accuracy.

3. NLO singular coefficients. The singular distribution at NLO has the form (αs/2π)2A(3/4)[C ln2 c+ B1 ln c] with A2 = 2CF + CA and B1 = 3CF + β0/2. We validate these predictions against

4. Matched NLL+NLO distribution. We present matched predictions with profile scales and uncertainty estimation. The matched formula eliminates the unphysical logarithmic spike at C = 3/4+ present in fixed-order NLO, producing a smooth Sudakov shoulder.
Several features simplify the C-parameter relative to other event shape shoulders: non-global logarithms are absent because C is a global observable; all three channels contribute identically due to permutation symmetry; and there is no Sudakov–Landau pole, allowing straightforward momentum-space resummation.
The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the C-parameter definition and derives the kinematic properties of its shoulder. Section 3 presents the SCET factorization theorem for the shoulder region. Section 4 collects all perturbative ingredients including anomalous dimensions and derives predictions for the NLO singular coefficients. Section 5 develops the NLL resummation formula. Section 6 validates these predictions against EVENT2 and presents the matched NLL+NLO distribution with profile scales and uncertainty estimation. We conclude in Section 8. Appendix A presents a complete direct calculation of the soft anomalous dimension from the one-loop soft function integral, and Appendix D collects all perturbative ingredients for NLL resummation.

2.5 Computation of A(3/4) and the step discontinuity
The C-parameter distribution exhibits a step discontinuity at C = 3/4: the coefficient function A(C) approaches a finite, nonzero value as C → 3/4−, unlike thrust where A(τ) → 0 as τ → 1/3−. This difference has important consequences for matching across the Sudakov shoulder, as we will discuss in Section 5. Here we compute A(3/4) directly by examining the phase space structure near the Mercedes configuration, illuminating the origin of this qualitative difference.

• C-parameter: 3/4−C ∝ r2 (quadratic in phase space distance). The phase space volume at fixed C shrinks like the circumference of a circle, proportional to r, but the Jacobian ∂C/∂r ∝ r also vanishes, and the two effects cancel exactly.
This cancellation is analogous to the density of states for a free particle in two dimensions. For a 2D system with energy E ∝ v2, the density of states g(E) is constant even as E → 0: the probability of finding a particle with kinetic energy less than ε scales linearly with ε, not quadratically. The Mercedes configuration is a critical point of C({sij}), making the C- parameter locally equivalent to “energy” in this analogy, while thrust is analogous to “speed” v whose distribution vanishes at v = 0.

3 SCET Factorization Theorem
We now derive the factorization theorem for the C-parameter distribution near the shoulder using soft-collinear effective theory. The key insight is that configurations just above C = 3/4 are perturbations of the symmetric Mercedes trijet, with the excess coming from soft and collinear radiation.
3.1 Soft and collinear radiation near the shoulder
The symmetric trijet configuration saturates the bound C ≤ 3/4 for three massless partons. To access the region C > 3/4, additional radiation must carry the system away from this symmetric point.
The SCET description involves three types of modes: 12
  
• Hard modes carry momenta of order Q and are integrated out when matching QCD onto SCET, producing the hard function H({sij},μ) that encodes the production of the underlying trijet. The hard function depends on the dipole invariants sij = (pi + pj)2; at the Mercedes configuration, sij = Q2/3 for all pairs.
• Collinear modes are boosted along one of the three jet directions and build up the jet invariant masses. The collinear radiation from each jet is described by a jet function JiC (l, μ).
• Soft modes have all momentum components of order Qc and contribute to c through out-of-plane momentum. Their contribution is encoded in the soft function S(k, μ), where k is the dimensionful soft measurement variable.
The three jet directions are specified by the symmetric trijet configuration:
nμ1 =(1,0,0,1), √
nμ2 =(1,0, 23,−21), (45) √
nμ3 =(1,0,− 23,−21),
corresponding to quark, antiquark, and gluon jets separated by 120◦ angles.

3.5 Comparison with heavy jet mass
The factorization has the same general structure as heavy jet mass (HJM) [15]: dσ/dc = H ⊗ JqC ⊗ Jq ̄C ⊗ JgC ⊗ S. However, both the jet and soft functions differ from those in thrust or HJM. The hard function H({sij},μ) is shared, depending on the dipole invariants sij which at Mercedes take the symmetric value sij = Q2/3.
The C-shoulder jet functions JiC differ from the inclusive jet functions appearing in thrust/HJM. As discussed in Section 1, the inclusive jet function measures only the total invariant mass of collinear radiation, while the C-shoulder jet function measures 􏰑a(pxa⊥)2/Ea—the azimuthally- weighted transverse momentum squared divided by energy. This measurement projects onto
a single transverse momentum component (perpendicular to the event plane), introducing the sin2 φ dependence characteristic of the C-parameter. The one-loop C-shoulder jet functions can be computed from the inclusive ones by averaging over the azimuthal angle (see Section 4.2 and Appendix B).
The soft function also differs fundamentally from thrust/HJM:
1. Universal angular function: The measurement function is the same everywhere—there is no sextant decomposition with different projection vectors.
2. Quadratic angular dependence: The soft contribution is quadratic in the out-of-plane momentum k⊥, not a linear projection.
3. Vanishing for in-plane radiation: Soft gluons emitted in the event plane (k⊥ = 0) contribute zero to δC at leading power.
4. Homogeneity: Despite the quadratic angular dependence, the measurement is homoge- neous of degree 1 in the soft momentum: MS(λk) = λMS(k).
A key simplification for the C-parameter is that all channels give identical contributions. For HJM, “gluon” and “quark” channels based on which parton is isolated contribute differently be- cause the hemisphere boundary determines the observable. The C-parameter, being a symmetric global sum over all particles, cannot distinguish which parton is isolated—the channel decom- position has no physical significance. This equivalence is exact to all orders by permutation symmetry.
3.6 Absence of non-global logarithms
An important feature of the C-parameter is that it is a global observable: every final-state particle contributes to C based on its momentum, with no vetoes or restricted phase-space regions. This ensures that non-global logarithms (NGLs) [19] are absent at leading power.
NGLs arise when an observable restricts radiation to a limited phase-space region, allowing soft gluons outside this region to radiate back into it. Classic examples include the “gap be- tween jets” and cone-based observables. For such observables, correlated multi-gluon emission generates logarithms not captured by independent-emission resummation.
The C-parameter avoids this problem because:
1. It sums over all final-state particles—no particles are excluded.
17

2. There are no geometric boundaries (hemispheres, cones) that define “in” versus “out” re- gions.
3. All radiation contributes positively to C; there are no cancellations between regions. This global nature ensures that the factorization theorem Eq. (66) captures all leading-power
logarithms, with no additional NGL contributions requiring separate treatment.
4 Perturbative Ingredients
We now specify the perturbative ingredients entering the factorization theorem. The hard func- tion is identical to that appearing in the BSZ analysis of thrust and heavy jet mass, but the jet and soft functions are new objects specific to the C-parameter measurement.
4.1 Hard function
The hard function H(Q,μ) is obtained by matching the QCD electromagnetic current onto the three-jet SCET operator. This matching is performed by computing the virtual corrections to the e+e− → qq ̄g amplitude in full QCD and in SCET, and taking their ratio. Since SCET reproduces all infrared divergences of QCD, the hard function is infrared-finite and encodes the short-distance physics at scale Q.
The threshold endpoint configuration for the C-parameter shoulder is identical to that for thrust and heavy jet mass at the trijet threshold: all three partons have equal energies Ei = Q/3 and are separated by 120◦ angles. Since the hard function depends only on the underlying hard kinematics (the dipole invariants sij = Q2/3 at Mercedes), it is the same as that computed in the BSZ analysis [6]. The one-loop hard function can be extracted from the virtual corrections to the trijet amplitude, which are known analytically [29, 30].
Anomalous dimension. The hard function satisfies the RG equation μ d ln H/dμ = γH , with anomalous dimension determined by the infrared structure of QCD amplitudes. For a multi- parton amplitude with massless colored partons, the anomalous dimension takes the general dipole form [25, 28]:

5 NLL Resummation
We now derive the resummed NLL formula for the C-parameter distribution across the shoulder. The basic idea is that the factorization theorem Eq. (71) expresses the cross section in terms of hard, jet, and soft functions that each satisfy renormalization group equations. Solving these RG equations and evolving the functions from their canonical scales (where they contain no large logarithms) to a common scale resums the Sudakov logarithms to all orders. The perturbative ingredients required for NLL accuracy—the two-loop cusp and one-loop non-cusp anomalous dimensions, two-loop beta function, and running coupling—were assembled in Section 4.

6 Numerical Validation and Matching
We now validate the SCET predictions against fixed-order calculations and present the matched NLL+NLO distribution with theoretical uncertainties.
6.1 Validation of resummation
The resummation formula Eq. (107) depends on the choice of renormalization scales μH, μJ, and μS. To validate that the resummed prediction correctly captures the singular structure, we compare the resummed distribution with the fixed-order singular distribution for different scale choices.
Consider a one-parameter family of scale choices parameterized by an exponent t:
μH =Q, μJ =Qct/2, μS =Qct. (123)
The canonical scales Eq. (116) correspond to t = 1, while t = 0 gives fixed scales μH = μJ = μS = Q with no resummation. For intermediate values of t, the scale hierarchy μS < μJ < μH is reduced, giving less Sudakov suppression.
Figure 4 compares the resummed contribution (αs/2π)A(3/4)(1−RNLL) with the fixed-order singular distribution (αs/2π)2BNLL for different values of t. In the limit t → 0 (fixed scales),
the resummed contribution should approach the singular distribution, since the resummation
reduces to a fixed-order expansion when all scales are equal. Indeed, the t = 0 curve closely
tracks the BNLL prediction, validating that the resummed formula correctly reproduces the sing
singular structure at NLL accuracy.
As t increases toward the canonical value t = 1, the Sudakov suppression becomes stronger,
pushing the distribution away from the singular prediction. The difference between the re- summed and singular distributions quantifies the higher-order effects captured by resummation. Near the shoulder at C ≈ 0.76, the canonical t = 1 curve differs significantly from the singular distribution, reflecting the strong Sudakov suppression in this region.

agreement at small t validates that the resummation correctly reproduces the singular structure. 6.2 Profile scales
The canonical scales Eq. (116) are appropriate only for c ≪ 1, where large logarithms ln c would otherwise appear in fixed-order perturbation theory. For larger c approaching c ∼ 1, the scales μJ and μS become low enough that the hierarchy μS ≪ μJ ≪ μH breaks down and the running coupling αs(μS) becomes unreliably large.
To obtain a well-behaved prediction across the full kinematic range, we employ profile func- tions [10, 11] that smoothly transition from canonical scales near the shoulder to fixed scales μH = μJ = μS = Q far from the shoulder. The profile scales use the parameterization introduced in Section 6.1:
μJ(c) = Qcteff(c)/2 , μS(c) = Qcteff(c) , (124) with the effective exponent
1 􏰇 c − c0 􏰈 teff(c)=tmin+(1−tmin)·2 1−tanh w . (125)
The profile function interpolates between teff = 1 (canonical scales) for c ≪ c0 and teff = tmin (nearly fixed scales) for c ≫ c0.
The central transition point c0 is motivated by the crossing structure visible in Figure 3. Resummation is most important where the singular contribution Bsing dominates over the non- singular piece BNS. As shown in Figure 3, Bsing = BNS at c ≈ 0.04 (C ≈ 0.77), and Bsing crosses zero at c ≈ 0.12 (C ≈ 0.79). Beyond this point, the singular logarithms are no longer the dominant contribution and fixed-order perturbation theory becomes more appropriate. We therefore choose the central transition point c0 = 0.08, roughly midway between these two crossings, corresponding to C ≈ 0.78.
The central parameter values are:
• c0 = 0.08: the transition point, corresponding to C ≈ 0.78
• w = 0.05: the transition width, chosen to give a smooth but localized transition
