 2.2 The Collapse of the Fact/Value Dichotomy
Putnam's critique extends beyond reference to challenge the fundamental distinction between facts and values that underwrites the claim to scientific objectivity. In The Collapse of the Fact/Value Dichotomy (2002), Putnam demonstrates that the very concepts we use in science including "coherence," "plausibility," "reasonableness," and "simplicity" are irreducibly value-laden.
"The logical positivists maintained that ethical statements are 'cognitively meaningless,' but their own notion of 'cognitive significance' presupposed epistemic values they could not acknowledge without undermining their position" (Putnam, 2002, p. 31). The selection of what counts as a relevant observation, what constitutes a satisfactory explanation, what degree of precision is required all involve value judgments that cannot be eliminated from scientific practice.
Putnam's analysis of thick ethical concepts like "cruel," "courageous," or "just" that combine descriptive and evaluative content reveals that many scientific concepts function similarly. Terms like "species," "ecosystem," or even "cause" carry normative implications about what patterns matter, what relationships are significant, what differences make a difference. As Putnam notes in Ethics Without Ontology (2004): "Description and evaluation are interwoven and interdependent. We cannot factor our language into a 'purely descriptive' part and a 'purely evaluative' part" (Putnam, 2004, p. 62).
2.3 The Critique of Scientific Method
Putnam's engagement with the methodology of science challenges both the traditional accounts of scientific method and their contemporary sophistications. In "The 'Corroboration' of Theories" (1974), Putnam argues that neither deductive nor inductive logic can account for scientific practice: "The idea that science proceeds by deduction from axioms or by induction from particular observations are both myths. Science proceeds by what Peirce called 'abduction' the creation of explanatory hypotheses which involves imagination, not just logic" (Putnam, 1974, p. 250).
His critique of Carnap's inductive logic in Mathematics, Matter and Method (1975) demonstrates that probability assignments to scientific theories cannot be objective in the required sense: "There is no such thing as the degree of confirmation of a theory on given evidence. Different persons with different background beliefs will assign different probabilities, and there is no way to say that one assignment is more 'rational' than another in any absolute sense" (Putnam, 1975, p. 270).
But Putnam goes further than showing the limits of formal methodology. In Realism with a Human Face (1990), he argues that the very idea of a scientific method that could be specified independently of particular scientific practices is incoherent: "There is no scientific method, if by 'method' one means a set of rules that can be stated in advance and that will generate scientific knowledge when followed. Science is a human activity, and like all human activities, it involves skills that cannot be fully formalized" (Putnam, 1990, p. 185).
2.4 Internal Realism as Alternative
Against the God's Eye View, Putnam develops what he calls "internal realism" or "pragmatic realism" a position that acknowledges the reality of the world while denying we can describe it from a perspective-free standpoint. In The Threefold Cord (1999), Putnam articulates this position: "Internal realism says that we can think and talk about things as they are, but always from within a conceptual scheme. There is no God's Eye View available to us; there are only the various points of view of actual persons reflecting various interests and purposes" (Putnam, 1999, p. 43).
This position maintains standards, evidence constrains theoretical choices, some frameworks prove more adequate for particular purposes, and truth retains its regulatory force within conceptual schemes. Putnam consistently rejects the idea that all conceptual schemes are equally valid. Rather, it's the recognition that truth and reference make sense only within conceptual frameworks that we cannot step
11

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 outside of to validate. As he argues in Renewing Philosophy (1992): "To say that truth is relative to a conceptual scheme is not to say that 'anything goes,' but to acknowledge that what we call 'truth' depends on the conceptual resources we have available" (Putnam, 1992, p. 120).
Putnam's famous thought experiment of brains in vats, presented in Reason, Truth and History, illustrates this point. The statement "we are brains in vats" cannot be true when uttered by us, not because we can verify that we're not brains in vats, but because reference requires causal connections that would be absent in the vat scenario. "The Brain in a Vat hypothesis is self-refuting, not because we can prove we're not brains in vats, but because the conditions necessary for the hypothesis to be meaningful are incompatible with its truth" (Putnam, 1981, p. 15).
2.5 Conceptual Relativity and Scientific Ontology
Putnam's doctrine of conceptual relativity, developed most fully in The Many Faces of Realism and Ethics Without Ontology, challenges the idea that science discovers the one true ontology of the world. His famous example involves counting objects: "Consider a world with three individuals. How many objects are there? Three? Seven (the three individuals plus their mereological sums)? The question has no determinate answer independent of a conceptual scheme" (Putnam, 1987, p. 18).
This extends to scientific ontology. In Philosophy in an Age of Science (2012), Putnam argues: "Quantum mechanics doesn't tell us what the world is like independent of measurement; it tells us what we can expect when we make measurements. The idea that there must be a determinate way things are 'anyway' is a metaphysical addition to physics, not something required by it" (Putnam, 2012, p. 103).
Putnam's analysis of quantum mechanics is particularly revealing. He shows that different interpretations of Copenhagen, many-worlds, and hidden variables are not competing descriptions of the same reality but different conceptual schemes that parse the phenomena differently. "The question 'which interpretation describes reality as it really is?' presupposes the God's Eye View. From within physics, we can only ask which interpretation is more useful for which purposes" (Putnam, 2005, p. 624).
2.6 The Fact of Conceptual Plurality
In his later work, particularly The Threefold Cord and Ethics Without Ontology, Putnam emphasizes what he calls "the fact of conceptual plurality" the recognition that we inevitably employ multiple, sometimes incompatible conceptual schemes. "We describe the world using intentional concepts in psychology, mechanical concepts in physics, functional concepts in biology and there is no super-science that could reduce all these to one fundamental level" (Putnam, 1999, p. 38).
This plurality, far from being a defect that inquiry ought to overcome, follows from the different purposes our conceptual schemes are made to serve. In "Aristotle After Wittgenstein" (1994), Putnam writes: "The idea that there must be exactly one true and complete description of how the world is constitutes a regulative ideal that we can neither satisfy nor coherently abandon. We are condemned to plurality" (Putnam, 1994, p. 63).
2.7 Science Without Spectators
Putnam's critique culminates in a vision of science as a human practice rather than a view from nowhere. In Pragmatism: An Open Question (1995), he writes: "Science is not spectatorship but interaction. We are not outside the universe looking in; we are part of the universe we seek to understand. This doesn't make science subjective, but it does mean that the ideal of a 'view from nowhere' is incoherent" (Putnam, 1995, p. 11).
This interactionist view connects with American pragmatist tradition, particularly Dewey's experimentalism. In The Collapse of the Fact/Value Dichotomy, Putnam explicitly endorses Dewey's view: "Knowledge is not passive contemplation but the result of inquiry, and inquiry is always motivated
12

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 by human needs and interests. The idea of knowledge as a 'copy' of reality makes no sense; knowledge is successful practice" (Putnam, 2002, p. 97).
2.8 The Ethics of Belief
Putnam's rejection of the God's Eye View carries ethical implications that reach well beyond epistemology. In Jewish Philosophy as a Guide to Life (2008), he argues: "The pretense to a God's Eye View is constitutes both an intellectual error and an ethical failure since the pretense denies our responsibility for the conceptual choices we make and their consequences it denies our responsibility for the conceptual choices we make and their consequences" (Putnam, 2008, p. 99).
This connects with his critique of scientism in Philosophy in an Age of Science: "The attempt to reduce all legitimate knowledge to scientific knowledge proves both mistaken and dangerous as it impoverishes understanding while legitimating the dismissal of ethical, aesthetic, and spiritual concerns as 'merely subjective'. It impoverishes our understanding and legitimates the dismissal of ethical, aesthetic, and spiritual concerns as 'merely subjective'" (Putnam, 2012, p. 127).
2.9 Realism Without Metaphysics
In his final major work, Naturalism, Realism, and Normativity (2016), Putnam articulates a "realism without metaphysics" that maintains scientific achievements while abandoning the God's Eye View: "Science discovers truths about the world through conceptual frameworks that make discovery possible as the truths emerge from the interaction between world and concepts. Reality and mind are not opposites but correlates" (Putnam, 2016, p. 91).
This position avoids both metaphysical realism and relativism through what Putnam calls "sophisticated realism": "The world emerges through interaction where we encounter resistance that shapes our concepts while our concepts determine what appears as meaningful phenomena. It is something we interact with, and our concepts are tools for that interaction, not mirrors of metaphysical structures" (Putnam, 2016, p. 108).
The implications for scientific practice are significant. As Putnam notes in "Science and Philosophy" (2012): "Scientists need not pretend to occupy a God's Eye View to do excellent science. Indeed, recognizing that we always operate from particular perspectives, with particular purposes, using particular conceptual resources, can make us better scientists, more aware of our assumptions, more open to alternatives, more responsive to evidence that doesn't fit our frameworks" (Putnam, 2012, p. 143).
Part III: Bateson's Ecology of Information and the Observer Problem
Gregory Bateson's work in cybernetics and systems theory reveals how the fundamental concepts of information science themselves require an observing system that determines what counts as information. His famous definition of information as "a difference which makes a difference" (Bateson, 1972, p. 315) exposes the observer-dependence built into the very structure of information theory, undermining claims to observer-independent data or computation.
3.1 Information as Difference for an Observer
In Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972), Bateson demonstrates that information cannot exist without an observing system capable of registering differences. His analysis begins with the map-territory distinction: "The map is not the territory, and the name is not the thing named" (Bateson, 1972, p. 455). But Bateson goes further, showing that what gets encoded in the map, which counts as a difference worth marking, depends entirely on the observing system's capacities and purposes.
13

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 Bateson's example of a blind man with a stick makes the point. Where does the blind man's self begin? At the handle of the stick? At the tip? Bateson argues: "The stick is a pathway along which differences are transmitted under transformation, so that to draw a delimiting line across this pathway is to cut off a part of the systemic circuit which determines the blind man's locomotion" (Bateson, 1972, p. 318). The information system includes the observer, the instrument, and the environment in an irreducible circuit.
This analysis exposes a confusion at the root of computational approaches to cognition. The computer metaphor assumes that data exists independently, waiting to be processed. But Bateson shows that data becomes information only when there is a system for which certain differences matter. As he writes in Mind and Nature (1979): "Information consists of differences that make a difference. The letter that you do not receive contains no information. The sound of the tree falling in the forest with no one to hear makes no difference" (Bateson, 1979, p. 99).
3.2 The Impossibility of Raw Data
Bateson's work exposes the illusion of "raw data" that underlies claims to objectivity in information science and cognitive science. In his communication theory work with Jurgen Ruesch, Communication: The Social Matrix of Psychiatry (1951), Bateson argues that "all information exists through coding, and every code embodies decisions about what to register, how to encode it, and what thresholds determine a difference" (Ruesch & Bateson, 1951, p. 169). The selection of what to encode, how to encode it, and what thresholds determine a registerable difference all involve decisions that cannot be derived from the data itself.
This becomes particularly clear in Bateson's analysis of learning and communication in cetaceans. In his dolphin communication studies, Bateson observed that what counts as a signal depends entirely on the interpretive framework of the receiver: "The dolphin's click trains carry information only relative to a system capable of distinguishing variations in frequency, amplitude, and timing. What is 'data' for one observing system is noise for another" (Bateson, 1972, p. 372).
The implications extend to all claims about information processing. When cognitive scientists speak of the brain "processing information," they obscure the fact that what counts as information depends on the system's organization, history, and context. As Bateson notes: "The neural impulse that travels along an axon does not contain information in itself. It becomes information only in relation to the system that can be affected by it" (Bateson, 1979, p. 109).
3.3 Recursive Observation and Levels of Learning
Bateson's theory of learning levels, developed in "The Logical Categories of Learning and Communication" (1972), demonstrates how observation itself operates at multiple recursive levels, each creating its own context for what counts as information. Learning 0 involves response to stimuli; Learning I involves change in response patterns; Learning II involves change in the pattern of patterns; Learning III involves change in the system that organizes Learning II.
Each level creates a different observational stance: "The phenomenon of Learning II shows that what counts as 'the same' context is itself learned and therefore observer dependent. The experimental rat that has learned to learn (Learning II) perceives different information in the maze than the naive rat, even though the 'data' remains unchanged" (Bateson, 1972, p. 293).
This recursive structure reveals why the view from nowhere is impossible even in principle. Every observation occurs from within a learned framework that determines what can be observed. As Bateson writes: "The observer's understanding of what he observes is always mediated by his premises about the nature of knowledge and the nature of the world. These premises are partly conscious and partly unconscious, and they themselves are products of previous learning" (Bateson, 1972, p. 314).
14

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 3.4 The Double Bind and the Paradox of Objectivity
Bateson's concept of the double bind, developed with his research team in "Toward a Theory of Schizophrenia" (1956), illuminates the paradoxical demands of objectivist epistemology. The double bind occurs when a system receives contradictory injunctions at different logical levels, with a prohibition against recognizing the contradiction.
The demand for a view from nowhere creates precisely such a double bind: "Be an observer without being anywhere in particular; have a perspective that is not a perspective; know without the conditions that make knowing possible" (Bateson et al., 1956, p. 256). The scientist is told to eliminate subjective factors while using necessarily subjective capacities of observation, pattern recognition, and interpretation.
Bateson argues this double bind produces what he calls "epistemological pathology": "The attempt to achieve a perspectiveless perspective leads to a systematic blindness about the conditions of one's own observation. The observer who claims to see from nowhere cannot see their own seeing" (Bateson, 1972, p. 489).
3.5 Mind as Ecological System
In Mind and Nature: A Necessary Unity (1979), Bateson develops an ecological understanding of mind that makes the view from nowhere conceptually impossible. Mind, for Bateson, is not contained within individual observers but consists of the total system of organism-plus-environment engaged in recursive interaction.
"The individual mind is immanent but not only in the body. It is immanent also in pathways and messages outside the body; and there is a larger Mind of which the individual mind is only a subsystem"
(Bateson, 1972, p. 467). This larger mind includes the instruments of observation, the contexts of interpretation, and the social systems that determine what observations matter.
This ecological view transforms how we understand scientific observation. The telescope, the laboratory, the scientific community, and its history of concepts all participate in what can be observed. As Bateson writes: "The microscope, the stained slide, the trained eye, the history of cell theory all these are parts of the mental system that 'discovers' cellular structure. The structure is not revealed to a passive observer but emerges from the total system of observation" (Bateson, 1979, p. 133).
3.6 Information Theory Against Itself
Bateson's critique is particularly powerful because it emerges from within information theory and cybernetics rather than from external philosophical criticism. His work with the Macy Conferences on cybernetics, alongside Norbert Wiener, John von Neumann, and Warren McCulloch, positioned him at the center of the computational revolution. Yet his analysis shows how the foundational concepts of this revolution undermine their own claims to objectivity.
In "Cybernetic Explanation" (1972), Bateson writes: "The engineers and mathematicians who developed information theory imagined they were creating a neutral measure of order and disorder. But their mathematics required decisions about what to count as a symbol, what to count as noise, what channel to measure across. Each decision introduces the observer's purposes and categories into what pretends to be observer-free measurement" (Bateson, 1972, p. 408).
The confusion between map and territory that Bateson identifies in information science reflects a deeper category error treating differences detected by a particular observing system as properties of the world independent of observation. This error, Bateson argues, pervades cognitive science: "When we say the brain 'processes information,' we forget that what counts as information depends on the total system of brain-body-environment. We mistake our analytical divisions for natural joints" (Bateson, 1979, p. 217).
