 Part IV: The Philosophical Archaeology of Perspectivism
4.1 Nietzsche's Genealogy of the "Pure" Gaze
Friedrich Nietzsche's assault on the possibility of perspectiveless knowledge precedes and anticipates the twentieth-century critiques of objectivity. His genealogical method reveals that what presents itself as "pure" observation emerges from specific historical conditions and serves particular forms of life. In On the Genealogy of Morals (1887), Nietzsche writes: "There is only a perspective seeing, only a perspective 'knowing'; and the more affects we allow to speak about one thing, the more eyes, different eyes, we can use to observe one thing, the more complete will our 'concept' of this thing, our 'objectivity,' be" (Nietzsche, 1887/1967, III, §12).
This formulation radically reconceives objectivity. Rather than the elimination of perspective, Nietzsche proposes that what we call objectivity emerges from the multiplication and integration of perspectives. The dream of perspective-free knowledge represents, for Nietzsche, a particular perspective that denies its own perspectival character what he calls "the longest lie" (Nietzsche, 1887/1967, III, §24).
In The Gay Science (1882), Nietzsche traces this denial to what he terms "the metaphysical need" , the desire for a world behind the world, a true world beyond appearances. "The 'apparent' world is the only
one: the 'true' world is merely added by a lie" (Nietzsche, 1882/1974, §344). The scientist who claims to observe reality as it truly is perpetuates the theological dream of God's perspective while denying its theological character.
Nietzsche's notebooks from the 1880s, published posthumously as The Will to Power, develop the physiological basis of perspectivism: "That things possess a constitution in themselves quite apart from interpretation and subjectivity is a quite idle hypothesis: it presupposes that interpretation and subjectivity are not essential, that a thing freed from all relationships would still be a thing" (Nietzsche, 1901/1967, §560). Knowledge emerges from the living body's needs, drives, and affects not from a disembodied eye.
4.2 The Ascetic Ideal and Scientific "Objectivity"
Nietzsche's analysis of the ascetic ideal in the third essay of On the Genealogy of Morals reveals how scientific objectivity inherits and secularizes religious self-denial. The scientist who claims to eliminate subjective factors practices a form of asceticism denying the body, the affects, the personal in favor of "pure" knowledge.
"Science today is a hiding place for every kind of discontent, disbelief, gnawing worm, despectio sui, bad conscience it is the unrest of the lack of ideals, the suffering from the lack of any great love" (Nietzsche, 1887/1967, III, §23). The claim to observe from nowhere masks a particular somewhere in the perspective of life that denies life, that seeks to escape the conditions of living observation.
In Beyond Good and Evil (1886), Nietzsche extends this critique: "The objective man is indeed a mirror: he is accustomed to submit before whatever wants to be known, without any other pleasure than that found in knowing and 'mirroring forth'" (Nietzsche, 1886/1966, §207). This supposedly neutral mirroring is itself a stance, a way of being in the world that shapes what can appear.
16

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 4.3 Merleau-Ponty's Critique of Pensée de Survol
Where Nietzsche's genealogy reveals the historical construction and life-denying character of the "pure" gaze, Maurice Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology demonstrates its impossibility through careful attention to the structures of perception itself. The ascetic ideal that Nietzsche unmasks as a perspective that denies its own perspectival character finds its phenomenological counterpoint in what Merleau-Ponty identifies as the irreducible presence of the lived body the corps vécu that cannot be erased from the scene of knowing, no matter how strenuously the observer attempts to achieve transparent observation.
Maurice Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology provides a systematic alternative to what he calls "pensée de survol" high-altitude thinking or surveying thought that imagines it can hover above the world to observe it from no particular position. In The Visible and the Invisible (1964), Merleau-Ponty writes: "The error of the philosophies of reflection is to believe that the thinking subject can absorb into its thinking or appropriate without remainder the object of its thought, that our being can be brought down to our knowledge" (Merleau-Ponty, 1964/1968, p. 45).
This high-altitude thinking, which Merleau-Ponty also calls "kosmotheoros" (world-spectator), assumes the possibility of complete coincidence between thought and being. Against this, Merleau-Ponty argues that perception always occurs from within the world it perceives: "The world is not an object such that I have in my possession the law of its making; it is the natural setting of, and field for, all my thoughts and all my explicit perceptions" (Merleau-Ponty, 1945/2012, p. lxxiv).
In Eye and Mind (1961), Merleau-Ponty specifically addresses scientific observation: "Science manipulates things and gives up living in them. It makes its own limited models of things; operating upon these indices or variables to effect whatever transformations are permitted by their definition, it comes face to
face with the real world only at rare intervals" (Merleau-Ponty, 1961/1964, p. 159). The scientific gaze that claims to see from nowhere actually sees from a highly specific perspective the perspective of operational thinking that reduces the world to manipulable variables.
4.4 The Lived Body as Ground of Perception
Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology reveals that all observation originates from the lived body (corps vécu), which is always already situated, oriented, and engaged with the world. In Phenomenology of Perception (1945), he demonstrates that the body, far from being one object set down among others in the world, is the very condition through which a world appears at all: "The body is our general medium for having a world" (Merleau-Ponty, 1945/2012, p. 146).
This embodied perspective cannot be eliminated or transcended. "Far from my body's being for me no more than a fragment of space, there would be for me no space at all if I had no body" (Merleau-Ponty, 1945/2012, p. 104). Every observation, including scientific observation, occurs from a bodily position that provides the zero-point of orientation the here from which there appears, the now from which then becomes meaningful.
The attempt to achieve a view from nowhere requires forgetting this embodied ground. In The Prose of the World (1969), Merleau-Ponty writes: "Objective thought ignores the subject of perception. This is because it presents itself with the world ready-made, as the setting of every possible event, and treats perception as one of these events" (Merleau-Ponty, 1969/1973, p. 54). The scientific observer who claims to eliminate perspective must suppress awareness of their own perceiving body.
17

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 4.5 The Chiasm and the Impossibility of Pure Observation
Merleau-Ponty's concept of the chiasm or intertwining (entrelacs) demonstrates why pure observation is impossible in principle. The observer and observed are not separate entities but intertwined aspects of a single flesh (chair). In The Visible and the Invisible, he writes: "The seer and the visible reciprocate one another and we no longer know which sees and which is seen" (Merleau-Ponty, 1964/1968, p. 139).
This intertwining appears clearly in the famous example of one hand touching another. The touching hand can become the touched, the perceiver can become the perceived. "My body as a visible thing is contained within the full spectacle. But my seeing body subtends this visible body, and all the visibles with it. There is reciprocal insertion and intertwining of one in the other" (Merleau-Ponty, 1964/1968, p. 138).
Scientific observation attempts to suppress this reversibility, to maintain a rigid distinction between observer and observed. But this suppression does not eliminate the chiasm; it merely renders it invisible. The microscope, the telescope, the laboratory all extend the perceiving body rather than replacing it. As Merleau-Ponty notes: "Instruments are annexed to my body, they dilate the scope of my being in the world" (Merleau-Ponty, 1945/2012, p. 154).
4.6 The Depth of the World
Against high-altitude thinking, Merleau-Ponty proposes that we always perceive from within what he calls the "depth" (profondeur) of the world. Depth is not a third dimension added to height and width but "the experience of the reversibility of dimensions, of a global 'locality' where everything is in the same place at the same time" (Merleau-Ponty, 1964/1968, p. 267).
This depth cannot be surveyed from above because we are always already immersed in it. In Signs (1960), Merleau-Ponty writes: "We never have before us pure individuals, indivisible glaciers of being, nor essences without place and without date. Not that they exist elsewhere, beyond our grasp, but because
we are experiences, that is, thoughts that feel behind themselves the weight of the space, the time, the very Being they think" (Merleau-Ponty, 1960/1964, p. 20).
Scientific observation that claims to eliminate depth, to spread everything out on a single plane for inspection, loses precisely what it seeks to understand. "When I think of the Cartesian cogito, I do not thereby place myself at the disposal of a transparent thought; I am caught up in a thickness of duration and spatiality which I cannot survey from above" (Merleau-Ponty, 1960/1964, p. 21).
4.7 Perspectivism as Condition of Truth
What Putnam demonstrates through logical analysis as the incoherence of the God's Eye View, and what Bateson reveals through information theory as the observer-dependence of any difference that makes a difference, Nietzsche and Merleau-Ponty establish through genealogical and phenomenological investigation: the perspectival, embodied character of any world-disclosure whatsoever. The convergence of these critiques from analytic philosophy, cybernetics, genealogy, and phenomenology suggests that the impossibility of the view from nowhere, rather than belonging to any single discipline as a local insight, is a structural feature of knowledge itself.
Both Nietzsche and Merleau-Ponty argue that perspectivism, so far from being a limitation that knowledge must labour to overcome, is the condition that makes truth possible in the first place. Nietzsche writes in his notebooks: "The perspective character of the world extends as far as we can possibly establish indeed, we cannot establish any limit to its perspectival character" (Nietzsche, 1901/1967, §374).
18

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 Merleau-Ponty echoes this in arguing that situatedness enables rather than prevents knowledge: "The world appears to me as perspective only because I am situated in it. If I could survey it from nowhere, it would not appear at all" (Merleau-Ponty, 1945/2012, p. 333). The very structure of appearing requires a perspective from which something appears.
This transforms our understanding of scientific knowledge. Rather than approaching truth by eliminating perspective, science advances by explicitly acknowledging and systematically varying perspectives. As Merleau-Ponty writes in Adventures of the Dialectic (1955): "Knowledge is not the intellectual possession of a mental object but the taking of a stand, the adoption of a perspective" (Merleau-Ponty, 1955/1973, p. 198).
Part V: The Epistemological Impossibility of Neutral Observation
5.1 Phenomenotechnique: How Instruments Create Their Objects
Gaston Bachelard's concept of phenomenotechnique, developed across his works but particularly in Le Nouvel Esprit Scientifique (1934) and La Formation de l'esprit scientifique (1938), strikes at the notion that scientific instruments provide transparent access to reality. For Bachelard, "instruments are nothing but theories materialized" (Bachelard, 1934/1984, p. 13). They do not discover phenomena that exist independently; they produce phenomena through their specific technical constitution.
Take the electron, that paradigmatic object of modern physics. Bachelard argues that the electron does not exist independently of the apparatus that detects it. In L'Activité rationaliste de la physique contemporaine (1951), he writes: "The electron existed before man; but before man, it did not exist as an
electron. It existed as an unknown reality, lost in the phenomenal reality of matter" (Bachelard, 1951, p. 104). The electron as a scientific object with its specific properties of charge, mass, and spin comes into being through the instrumental practices that constitute it as observable.
The cloud chamber provides a concrete example. When we say we "observe" particle tracks in a cloud chamber, what exactly are we observing? Condensation trails in supersaturated vapor, certainly. But the identification of these trails as "electron paths" requires an entire theoretical apparatus: the physics of ionization, the thermodynamics of supersaturation, the electromagnetic theory that relates charge to condensation nucleation. As Peter Galison demonstrates in Image and Logic (1997), different detection instruments constitute particles differently: "The bubble chamber physicist and the wire chamber physicist may both study 'particles,' but the objects of their investigation are as different as their instruments" (Galison, 1997, p. 433).
This goes beyond any interpretive overlay laid upon neutral observation: the phenomena literally do not exist outside the instrumental context that produces them. Bachelard emphasizes this point through his analysis of the Michelson-Morley experiment. The null result that supposedly disproved the ether was not a simple observation but required extraordinary instrumental precision and theoretical sophistication. The interferometer had to be isolated from vibrations, temperature variations, and mechanical strains that would otherwise swamp the effect being sought. As Bachelard notes: "The Michelson experiment is not an observation of nature; it is a production of a phenomenon that does not exist naturally" (Bachelard, 1934/1984, p. 16).
19

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 5.2 The Rupture with Common Experience
Bachelard's notion of epistemological rupture (rupture épistémologique) reveals another impossibility in the view from nowhere: scientific knowledge does not refine common observation but breaks radically with it. In La Formation de l'esprit scientifique (1938), Bachelard argues that "scientific observation is always polemical; it confirms or denies a prior thesis, a preexisting model, an observational protocol" (Bachelard, 1938/2002, p. 16).
The scientific concept of temperature illustrates this rupture. Common experience knows heat and cold through bodily sensation, the warmth of sun on skin, the chill of winter air. Scientific temperature, measured by thermometers, has no direct relationship to these sensations. Mercury expansion in a graduated tube measures something that never appears to direct experience. Moreover, the development from mercury thermometers to thermocouples to pyrometers to cosmic background radiation detection shows that "temperature" is not one thing observed through different instruments but different phenomena constituted by different instrumental practices.
Bachelard's student Georges Canguilhem extends this analysis in La Connaissance de la vie (1965), showing how the biological concept of reflex required breaking with everyday understanding of voluntary and involuntary movement. The reflex arc, as a scientific object, "does not exist in lived experience; it exists only in the physiological laboratory" (Canguilhem, 1965/2008, p. 133). The knee-jerk reflex that seems so natural and obvious is actually invisible without the specific experimental setup that isolates it from the complex totality of bodily movement.
This rupture with common experience, far from being a regrettable necessity, is part of what constitutes scientific knowledge. As Bachelard argues: "Science is not a refinement of common knowledge but its contradiction" (Bachelard, 1938/2002, p. 14). The view from nowhere claims to transcend the limitations of particular perspectives, but it actually constructs entirely new observational domains that have no continuity with ordinary experience.
5.3 Epistemological Obstacles and the Psychoanalysis of Objective Knowledge
Bachelard's concept of epistemological obstacles (obstacles épistémologiques) reveals the psychological and cultural impediments that must be overcome to achieve scientific knowledge. At a deeper level it shows that these obstacles, rather than being external hindrances to some pure observation, are part of what constitutes the observational act itself.
In La Formation de l'esprit scientifique, Bachelard identifies several fundamental obstacles:
The obstacle of primary experience: The immediate, sensory encounter with phenomena that seems most real is actually the greatest impediment to scientific understanding. Fire appears to be a common experience as a flickering, consuming, warming presence. For chemistry, fire is rapid oxidation, a concept that shares nothing with the lived experience of flame. The vividness of primary experience must be actively suppressed for the scientific concept to emerge.
The obstacle of general knowledge: The tendency to explain through overly broad generalizations that seem to explain everything but actually explain nothing. The 18th-century concept of "affinity" in chemistry appeared to explain why substances combine, but as Bachelard shows, it was merely a projection of human emotional categories onto matter. "To say that acid has an affinity for base is to attribute to chemicals a tendency that properly belongs to the chemist" (Bachelard, 1938/2002, p. 62).
The obstacle of verbal knowledge: The confusion of words with understanding. Bachelard analyzes how the word "sponge" became an explanatory principle in pre-scientific thought; the sponge-like nature of matter supposedly explained absorption. But this verbal explanation blocked real investigation into porosity, capillary action, and surface tension.
20

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 The obstacle of unitary and pragmatic knowledge: The desire to reduce all phenomena to a single principle or to immediate utility. The phlogiston theory persisted not because it explained combustion well but because it unified apparently diverse phenomena under one concept.
These obstacles are psychological necessities that structure pre-scientific thought, rather than simply errors waiting to be corrected. Their overcoming requires what Bachelard calls a "psychoanalysis of objective knowledge" a systematic examination of the unconscious commitments that shape observation.
5.4 The Social Production of Objectivity
Bachelard's later work, particularly Le Rationalisme appliqué (1949), emphasizes that scientific objectivity is achieved through collective technical practices within what he calls the "scientific city" (cité scientifique), rather than by individual observers transcending their subjectivity. Objectivity is a social achievement, not an individual transcendence.
The scientific city has its own technical culture, its own language, its own standards of rationality that must be learned through long apprenticeship. As Bachelard notes: "To enter the scientific city, one must undergo a genuine intellectual mutation" (Bachelard, 1949, p. 24). This mutation involves learning to see through instruments, to think through mathematics, to suppress immediate experience in favor of mediated construction.
Helen Longino's Science as Social Knowledge (1990) develops this insight, showing how objectivity emerges through critical interaction within scientific communities rather than through individual methodological rigor. "Objectivity is secured by the social character of inquiry rather than by the logical features of scientific propositions" (Longino, 1990, p. 74). The peer review process, replication attempts, and critical scrutiny do not eliminate perspective but multiply perspectives within a shared framework.
But this social production of objectivity operates within strict boundaries. As Pierre Bourdieu demonstrates in Science of Science and Reflexivity (2001), the scientific field has specific entry requirements, educational credentials, mastery of technical languages, access to instruments that
exclude most perspectives from the outset. "Scientific objectivity is the product of the scientific field's specific social conditions of production" (Bourdieu, 2001/2004, p. 76). The view from nowhere is actually the view from a very specific somewhere: the laboratory, the university, the funded research program.
5.5 Incommensurability and the Impossibility of Neutral Comparison
Thomas Kuhn's concept of incommensurability, introduced in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) and refined in subsequent work, provides another angle on the impossibility of neutral observation. Incommensurability means that competing paradigms cannot be compared through neutral observation because they constitute different observational worlds.
The transition from Aristotelian to Galilean physics exemplifies this incommensurability. For Aristotelian physics, a swinging stone on a string exhibits constrained fall of the stone trying to reach its natural place (the earth's center) while being prevented by the string. For Galilean physics, the same phenomenon is pendulum motion, a nearly perfect embodiment of the principle of inertia. As Kuhn argues: "The two groups of scientists see different things when they look from the same point in the same direction" (Kuhn, 1962/1970, p. 150).
This is not a matter of different interpretations of the same observation. The observation itself is paradigm-dependent. In The Essential Tension (1977), Kuhn clarifies: "The point is not that the world changes with a change of paradigm. Rather, it is that scientists work in a different world" (Kuhn, 1977, p. 338). The Aristotelian physicist and the Galilean physicist do not observe the same pendulum and describe it differently; they observe different phenomena constituted by their respective paradigms.
21

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 Paul Feyerabend, in Against Method (1975), radicalizes this insight, arguing that incommensurability makes the idea of scientific progress through neutral observation incoherent. "There is no neutral observation language that could be used to formulate the observable consequences of competing theories" (Feyerabend, 1975, p. 268). Every observation is theory-laden, every instrument embodies theoretical commitments, every experimental protocol assumes what it claims to test.
5.6 The Underdetermination of Theory by Evidence
The Duhem-Quine thesis, formulated independently by Pierre Duhem in La Théorie physique (1906) and Willard Van Orman Quine in "Two Dogmas of Empiricism" (1951), establishes that observation alone can never determine theoretical truth because theories always face experience as corporate bodies.
Duhem's original formulation focused on physics: "The physicist can never subject an isolated hypothesis to experimental test, but only a whole group of hypotheses; when the experiment is in disagreement with his predictions, it teaches him that at least one of the hypotheses constituting this group is unacceptable and ought to be modified; but the experiment does not designate which one should be changed" (Duhem, 1906/1954, p. 187).
Take the discovery of Neptune. When Uranus's orbit deviated from Newtonian predictions, astronomers faced a choice: abandon Newton's law of gravitation or postulate an unseen planet. The decision to maintain Newton and search for a new planet was not determined by observation but by the paradigm's robustness and the community's commitment to it. As Imre Lakatos argues in The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes (1978), "It is not that we propose a theory and Nature may shout NO; rather, we propose a maze of theories, and Nature may shout INCONSISTENT" (Lakatos, 1978, p. 130).
Quine extends this argument to all knowledge: "Our statements about the external world face the tribunal of sense experience not individually but only as a corporate body" (Quine, 1951, p. 41). Any
recalcitrant observation can be accommodated by adjusting other parts of our theoretical network. The choice of what to adjust is underdetermined by the observation itself.
This underdetermination persists through the structure of observation itself, where multiple incompatible interpretations remain consistent with any finite set of data points. As Larry Laudan demonstrates in "Demystifying Underdetermination" (1990), "For any finite body of evidence, there are indefinitely many mutually incompatible theories that entail that evidence" (Laudan, 1990, p. 320). The view from nowhere would require observation to uniquely determine theory, but the Duhem-Quine thesis shows this is impossible in principle.
5.7 The Experimenter's Regress
Harry Collins's concept of the experimenter's regress, developed through his studies of gravitational wave detection and documented in Changing Order (1985), reveals a fundamental circularity in experimental observation that makes neutral observation impossible.
The problem is this: to know whether an experimental apparatus works correctly, we need to know what correct results look like. But to know what correct results look like, we need a correctly functioning apparatus. Collins studied the attempts to detect gravitational waves in the 1970s, showing how different research groups could not agree on whether detections had occurred because they could not agree on what a properly functioning detector should register.
As Collins documents: "The existence of gravitational waves was the very phenomenon that was in question, so it could not be used as a calibration standard" (Collins, 1985, p. 84). Joseph Weber claimed to have detected gravitational waves with his aluminum bar detectors. Other groups, using similar but not identical equipment, failed to replicate his results. Was Weber's equipment more sensitive, or was it detecting artifacts? Without independent access to gravitational waves, there was no neutral way to decide.
22

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 The regress was only terminated through social negotiation within the physics community a consensus emerged that Weber's results were artifacts, not because this was proven observationally but because the community decided what would count as a legitimate detector. As Collins argues: "The experimenter's regress is terminated not by Nature but by social negotiation" (Collins, 1985, p. 91).
5.8 The Theory-Ladenness of Observation
Norwood Russell Hanson's argument for the theory-ladenness of observation, presented in Patterns of Discovery (1958), directly challenges the possibility of neutral observation. Hanson argues that "there is more to seeing than meets the eyeball" (Hanson, 1958, p. 7) all observation is conceptually organized from the outset.
Hanson's famous example involves two microbiologists looking at a prepared slide. One sees Golgi bodies, the other sees artifacts of staining technique. They are looking at the same slide through the same microscope, but they do not see the same thing. Their different theoretical backgrounds constitute different observations. As Hanson writes: "Observation of x is shaped by prior knowledge of x" (Hanson, 1958, p. 19).
This is not a psychological point about interpretation but an epistemological point about the nature of observation itself. In Perception and Discovery (1969), Hanson extends this analysis: "The theory-observation distinction as commonly drawn is not tenable... theories and observations are not independent; theories, in fact, structure observations" (Hanson, 1969, p. 75).
Alan Chalmers, in What Is This Thing Called Science? (1976), provides a compelling example through the history of microscopy. When early microscopists observed cells, they saw them as hollow chambers (hence "cells" from the Latin cella for small room). Later observers, with different theoretical frameworks, saw the same preparations as complex structures with nuclei, organelles, and membranes. The observations changed not because the microscopes improved but because the theoretical framework evolved.
5.9 Constructivism and the Laboratory Manufacture of Facts
The laboratory studies movement, initiated by Bruno Latour and Steve Woolgar's Laboratory Life (1979) and continued in Karin Knorr Cetina's The Manufacture of Knowledge (1981), provides ethnographic evidence for the construction rather than discovery of scientific facts.
Latour and Woolgar spent two years observing work in a neuroendocrinology laboratory, documenting how a scientific fact (the structure of Thyrotropin Releasing Hormone) emerged through material and social practices. They show that "the laboratory is a system of inscription devices that transforms material substances into written documents" (Latour and Woolgar, 1979, p. 51). What eventually becomes accepted as an objective fact about nature begins as ambiguous traces on recording devices, subjected to intensive interpretation, negotiation, and transformation.
The insight that matters here is that the fact does not exist independently of the practices that constitute it. TRH(Thyrotropin Releasing Hormone) as a scientific object with its specific amino acid sequence Pyro-Glu-His-Pro-NH2 came into being through a complex process involving bioassays, chromatography, mass spectrometry, and extensive argumentation about what counted as adequate evidence. As Latour and Woolgar observe: "The artificial reality, which participants describe in terms of an objective entity, has been constructed through material operations" (Latour and Woolgar, 1979, p. 243).
Knorr Cetina's study of a plant protein laboratory extends this analysis, showing how scientific objects are "culturally constructed in the laboratory" (Knorr Cetina, 1981, p. 4). She documents how decisions about what to measure, how to measure it, what counts as signal versus noise, what requires control, are all made through local, contingent reasoning rather than universal methodology.
23

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 5.10 Instrumental Realism and the Mediation of Reality
Ian Hacking's "experimental realism," developed in Representing and Intervening (1983), attempts to salvage scientific realism by grounding it in experimental manipulation rather than observation. Hacking argues that we should believe in electrons not because we observe them but because we can spray them: "We are completely convinced of the reality of electrons when we regularly set out to build and often enough succeed in building new machines that use various well-understood causal properties of electrons to interfere in other more hypothetical parts of nature" (Hacking, 1983, p. 265).
The move from observation to intervention transforms rather than eliminates mediation as instruments now shape what can be produced rather than what can be detected. As Nancy Cartwright argues in How the Laws of Physics Lie (1983), our ability to manipulate electrons depends on highly idealized models that may not correspond to reality: "The fundamental laws of physics do not describe true facts about reality. Rendered as descriptions of facts, they are false; amended to be true, they lose their fundamental, explanatory force" (Cartwright, 1983, p. 3).
Davis Baird's Thing Knowledge (2004) develops a complementary analysis, arguing that scientific instruments embody knowledge that cannot be fully articulated in propositional form. A mass spectrometer "knows" how to separate ions by mass-to-charge ratio in a way that cannot be completely
captured in theoretical description. This instrumental knowledge is not neutral but embodies specific ways of engaging with materiality.
Part VI: The Hermeneutic Prison of All Knowledge
6.1 Dilthey's Critique of Historical Reason
Wilhelm Dilthey's project of a "critique of historical reason," conceived as a parallel to Kant's critique of pure reason, establishes fundamental differences between the natural sciences (Naturwissenschaften) and the human sciences (Geisteswissenschaften) that reveal the limited scope of any attempted view from nowhere. In Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften (1883), Dilthey argues that "nature we explain, psychic life we understand" (Dilthey, 1883/1989, p. 144).
This distinction operates at the ontological level by structuring what can appear as meaningful rather than organizing already given content. Natural objects, insofar as they are conceived as external to consciousness, can be subjected to causal analysis. But human expressions, texts, actions, institutions are manifestations of lived experience (Erlebnis) that require understanding from within. As Dilthey writes in Der Aufbau der geschichtlichen Welt (1910): "Life cannot be brought before the judgment seat of reason" (Dilthey, 1910/2002, p. 223).
The point that matters is that understanding (Verstehen) constitutes its own form of rigor appropriate to meaningful phenomena that would be destroyed by reduction to causal explanation (Erklären). It is a distinct form of cognition appropriate to its objects. When we understand a historical text, we are not tracking causal relations but entering into meaningful connections. The historian reading Thucydides does not explain the Peloponnesian War through covering laws but understands it through imaginative re-experiencing of the meaningful contexts within which historical agents acted.
Dilthey's concept of the hermeneutic circle reveals why this understanding cannot achieve a view from nowhere. In "Die Entstehung der Hermeneutik" (1900), he writes: "The whole of a work must be understood from the individual words and their combinations, but full understanding of the individual part presupposes understanding of the whole" (Dilthey, 1900/1996, p. 252). This circular movement between parts and whole constitutes the structure through which meaning emerges.
Take the interpretation of a scientific text, Darwin's Origin of Species, for instance. To understand any particular passage, we must grasp Darwin's overall argument. But to grasp the overall argument, we must
24

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 understand the particular passages. Understanding begins from within inherited meanings and questions where every starting point already carries interpretive commitments that shape what can appear. We enter the circle with our pre-understanding and modify it through encounters with the text.
6.2 Life as the Unsurpassable Horizon
Dilthey's late philosophy, particularly in Die Kategorien des Lebens (1910), develops the concept of life (Leben) as the ultimate horizon that cannot be transcended. Life is not biological existence but the totality of meaningful experience within which all understanding occurs. As Dilthey argues: "Life is the
fundamental fact that must form the starting point of philosophy. It is that which is known from within, it is that behind which we cannot go" (Dilthey, 1910/2002, p. 360).
This bears heavily on the possibility of a view from nowhere. Every attempt to achieve objective knowledge occurs within life where the living researcher studying life employs the very processes they seek to explain. The scientist studying cognition is using cognition. The theorist analyzing society is embedded in society. The philosopher examining experience is having experience. There is no Archimedean point outside life from which to observe life neutrally.
Rudolf Makkreel, in Dilthey: Philosopher of the Human Studies (1975), clarifies this point: "Life presents itself as a complex of meaningful relations whose understanding requires articulating immanent structures rather than reducing to component elements" (Makkreel, 1975, p. 378). The attempt to achieve a view from nowhere is an attempt to step outside life to observe it externally but this stepping outside would still occur within life.
6.3 The Historical Character of Understanding
Dilthey's insight into the thoroughly historical character of understanding undermines any claim to timeless, perspectiveless knowledge. In Das geschichtliche Bewusstsein und die Weltanschauungen (1911), he argues that "man knows himself only in history, never through introspection" (Dilthey, 1911/1985, p. 279). Even self-knowledge is historically mediated.
Historical mediation constitutes reason itself as the categories and questions through which reason operates emerge from historical development. Historical situatedness constitutes the very possibility of understanding. We understand ancient Greek philosophy not by transcending our historical position but by bringing our contemporary questions into dialogue with Greek texts. The meaning that emerges is neither purely Greek nor purely contemporary but emerges in the encounter between horizons.
The implications extend to natural science. The scientist's concepts, methods, and questions emerge from specific historical contexts. Newtonian mechanics was not a timeless discovery but emerged from the particular problem-situation of 17th-century natural philosophy. Quantum mechanics arose from specific experimental anomalies encountered in early 20th-century physics. As Jos de Mul argues in The Tragedy of Finitude (2004): "Even the natural sciences, insofar as they are human undertakings, are interpretive practices embedded in historical horizons" (de Mul, 2004, p. 234).
6.4 Gadamer's Radicalization: Prejudice as Enabling Condition
Hans-Georg Gadamer's Wahrheit und Methode (1960) radicalizes Dilthey's insights, arguing that the Enlightenment's "prejudice against prejudice" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 272) itself prevents understanding of how understanding actually works. For Gadamer, prejudices (Vorurteile) provide the initial orientation from which questions arise and significance appears as they function as the tacit background making explicit interpretation possible.
The Enlightenment ideal, which underlies the aspiration to a view from nowhere, demands the elimination of all prejudices to achieve objective knowledge. But Gadamer demonstrates that this demand is incoherent: "The historicity of our existence entails that prejudices, in the literal sense of the
25

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 word, constitute the initial directedness of our whole ability to experience" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 278).
Think about how we approach any text or phenomenon. We necessarily bring expectations about what we might find, categories through which to organize our observations, languages in which to articulate our understanding. These prejudices constitute the conditions through which understanding becomes possible by providing the anticipatory structures that allow phenomena to show themselves. Without
expectations, we could not recognize anything as significant. Without categories, we could not organize experience. Without language, we could not articulate findings.
The key insight is that prejudices function as starting points for dialogue that can be revised through encounters with what challenges them. Through encounters with texts, phenomena, or other perspectives, our prejudices are challenged, modified, confirmed, or overturned. Understanding emerges through putting our prejudices at risk in genuine encounters, rather than through eliminating them.
6.5 The Fusion of Horizons
Gadamer's concept of the fusion of horizons (Horizontverschmelzung) provides an alternative to the view from nowhere that acknowledges the necessarily perspectival character of understanding. Every act of understanding involves the encounter between the interpreter's horizon and the horizon of what is interpreted.
A horizon, in Gadamer's technical sense, is "the range of vision that includes everything that can be seen from a particular vantage point" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 301). It encompasses the prejudices, expectations, and possibilities available from a particular historical-cultural position. The horizon is not a fixed boundary but a moving limit that expands through encounter.
When a contemporary physicist reads Newton's Principia, they bring their horizon quantum mechanics, relativity, contemporary mathematics into encounter with Newton's horizon, absolute space and time, corpuscular philosophy, geometric demonstration. Understanding emerges through a fusion of horizons where contemporary questions encounter historical texts, generating meanings available to neither perspective alone.
This fusion constitutes the ontological structure of understanding through the way meaning emerges through temporal distance and interpretive engagement. As Gadamer writes: "Understanding is always the fusion of these horizons supposedly existing by themselves" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 305). That "supposedly" carries the weight: the horizons do not exist independently, but only in relation to each other through acts of understanding.
6.6 Tradition as the Medium of Understanding
Gadamer's rehabilitation of tradition challenges the Enlightenment assumption that reason can operate independently of traditional contexts. Tradition constitutes the medium within which reason operates, providing the concepts, problems, and standards through which rational inquiry proceeds. As Gadamer argues: "We stand always within tradition, and this is no objectifying process i.e., we do not conceive of what tradition says as something other, something alien. It is always part of us" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 282).
Scientific traditions exemplify this embeddedness. The physicist working on quantum mechanics inherits not just theories and equations but ways of approaching problems, standards of explanation, exemplary problem-solutions, instrumental techniques, and mathematical formalisms. This tradition provides the enabling conditions for physics through the mathematical frameworks, experimental practices, and theoretical questions that make physical investigation possible.
26

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 Thomas Kuhn's analysis of scientific paradigms, though developed independently, converges with Gadamer's account of tradition. What Kuhn calls "normal science" is work within an established tradition that provides the framework within which problems are identified, addressed, and solved. Revolutionary science involves not escaping tradition altogether but shifting from one traditional framework to another.
6.7 The Linguistic Nature of Understanding
Gadamer's claim that "being that can be understood is language" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 470) reveals another impossibility in the view from nowhere: all understanding is linguistically mediated. The claim here is not the trivial one that we merely express understanding in language; it reaches deeper, holding that language is the medium in which understanding occurs.
Language constitutes the medium within which reality becomes articulate and available for understanding. Rather, language is the medium in which reality becomes understandable. As Gadamer writes: "Language is not just one of man's possessions in the world; rather, it depends on the fact that man has a world at all" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 440).
This linguistic mediation extends to scientific observation. When the astronomer observes stellar spectra, they see absorption lines only because they possess the linguistic-conceptual framework of spectroscopy. Without the concepts of wavelength, emission, absorption, and atomic transition, there would be only meaningless patterns. The language constitutes what can appear as meaningful phenomena since 'electron spin' creates rather than labels an observable feature.
John McDowell, in Mind and World (1994), develops a complementary argument through his critique of the "myth of the given." McDowell argues that "we cannot really understand the relations in virtue of which a judgment is warranted except as relations within the space of concepts" (McDowell, 1994, p. 7). Even supposedly direct observations are conceptually structured, and concepts are linguistically constituted.
6.8 The Problem of Application
Gadamer's analysis of application (Anwendung) as an integral moment of understanding further undermines the possibility of neutral observation. In the hermeneutic tradition, understanding always involves application to the interpreter's situation. Application emerges simultaneously with understanding as we understand something precisely through grasping how it applies to our situation.
Legal hermeneutics provides the paradigm case. When a judge interprets a law, they must understand it in application to a particular case. The law's meaning is not fixed in advance but emerges through application. Similarly, Gadamer argues, all understanding involves application: "Understanding here is always application" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 308).
This principle extends to scientific understanding. When scientists apply theories to new phenomena, they are not mechanically extending fixed meanings but creating meaning through application. The application of Newtonian mechanics to planetary motion, fluid dynamics, or quantum systems involves creative interpretation that constitutes the theory's meaning rather than simply revealing it.
6.9 Dialogue as the Structure of Understanding
For Gadamer, genuine understanding has the structure of dialogue, a dialogical encounter with what has something to say, rather than monological observation of mute objects. This dialogue is not metaphorical but describes the actual structure of interpretive encounter.
In dialogue, understanding emerges through dialogue where our prejudices encounter resistance and transformation through engagement with the other's claims. Instead, we risk our prejudices in genuine encounters, allowing them to be challenged while simultaneously challenging what we encounter. The meaning that emerges belongs neither to us nor to the text but emerges in the between-space of dialogue.
27

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 This dialogical structure applies even to natural scientific investigation. The experiment constitutes active questioning of nature where apparatus and procedures embody specific questions that determine what nature can answer. As Heidegger argues in "The Question Concerning Technology" (1954): "Modern physics is not experimental physics because it applies apparatus to the questioning of nature. Rather the reverse is true. Because physics, already as pure theory, sets nature up to exhibit itself as a coherence of forces calculable in advance, it therefore orders its experiments precisely for the purpose of asking whether and how nature reports itself when set up in this way" (Heidegger, 1954/1977, p. 21).
6.10 Dilthey's Categories of Life
Dilthey's late work develops categories specific to life that cannot be reduced to the categories of natural scientific explanation. In Der Aufbau der geschichtlichen Welt, he identifies categories such as meaning (Bedeutung), value (Wert), purpose (Zweck), and development (Entwicklung) that structure historical understanding differently from causal explanation.
These categories emerge from life's self-articulation through the ways living beings organize and express their experience. Meaning constitutes the way events present themselves within the context of life through how they connect to purposes, values, and ongoing stories. A scientific discovery has meaning not as an isolated event but within the context of a research program, a disciplinary tradition, a cultural moment. This meaning requires understanding the connections between events and the life-context within which they gain significance within which the discovery emerges.
The category of development (Entwicklung) differs fundamentally from mere change. Development implies an unfolding of potential, a movement toward realization that can only be understood retrospectively. The development of quantum mechanics from Planck's quantum hypothesis to full quantum field theory is not mere succession but meaningful development that can only be grasped by understanding the internal logic of the research program.
6.11 The Effective History
Gadamer's concept of effective history (Wirkungsgeschichte) reveals that we never encounter objects or texts in their pristine originality but always as mediated through their history of effects. Wahrheit und Methode argues: "Understanding is, essentially, a historically effected event" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 299).
Shakespeare's Hamlet cannot be understood as it was in 1600 because it comes to us through four centuries of interpretation, performance, criticism, and cultural influence. These effects constitute the text as it exists for understanding since each reading adds to the tradition through which the text continues to speak. Similarly, Newton's laws come to us through centuries of application, refinement, criticism, and pedagogical transmission that constitute their meaning for us.
This principle applies equally to natural phenomena. The electron comes to us through a century of experimental investigation, theoretical development, and technological application. The electron as a scientific object emerges through its effective history comprising the accumulation of experimental techniques, theoretical frameworks, and instrumental practices that make it observable.
6.12 The Hermeneutic Situation
The concept of situation (Situation) in Gadamer's hermeneutics emphasizes the always-already positioned character of understanding. We never begin from a neutral starting point but always find ourselves thrown into a situation with its particular possibilities and limitations.
As Gadamer writes: "The very idea of a situation means that we are not standing outside it and hence are unable to have any objective knowledge of it. We are always within the situation, and to throw light on it is a task that is never entirely completed" (Gadamer, 1960/2004, p. 301).
28

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 The scientist in the laboratory is in a situation funded by particular institutions, equipped with particular instruments, trained in particular traditions, motivated by particular questions. This situation provides the enabling condition for research through the questions, tools, and frameworks that make investigation possible. Research emerges from and depends upon institutional support, instruments, training, and inherited questions that constitute its conditions of possibility.
Jean-Luc Nancy, in The Experience of Freedom (1988), extends this analysis: "Situation is not what surrounds a pre-given subject, but the opening within which something like a subject can occur" (Nancy, 1988/1993, p. 67). The researcher doesn't have a situation; they emerge as a researcher through the situation.
6.13 Truth as Disclosure
Gadamer's conception of truth as disclosure (Wahrheit as aletheia) rather than correctness (Richtigkeit) provides an alternative to the correspondence theory assumed by the view from nowhere. Truth is not the correct representation of pre-existing facts but the event of unconcealment in which something shows itself.
This conception, derived from Heidegger but given hermeneutic specificity by Gadamer, understands truth as what emerges in the encounter between interpreter and interpreted. A great artwork doesn't represent pre-existing truth but opens new truth through its working. Similarly, scientific theories don't simply correctly describe reality but open new domains of phenomena for investigation.
As Gadamer argues in "What is Truth?" (1957): "The event of truth is not adequately characterized by the concept of correspondence... Truth is rather the unconcealment of what is" (Gadamer, 1957/1994, p. 42). This unconcealment always occurs from particular perspectives, within particular traditions, through particular languages. There is no unconcealment from nowhere.
Part VII: The Violence and Productivity of Situated Knowledge
7.1 The Corpse-Making of Objectification
The attempt to achieve objective knowledge through eliminating subjective perspective commits what we might call epistemological violence it kills its objects to know them. This violence is literal in biological science, where living organisms must often be killed, fixed, stained, and sectioned to become observable. But it extends metaphorically throughout the sciences, where dynamic processes are frozen, relationships are severed, and contexts are stripped away to achieve "objective" observation.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe recognized this violence in his critique of Newtonian optics. In Zur Farbenlehre (1810), Goethe argues that Newton's experimental approach destroyed the phenomena it claimed to investigate: "The Newtonian doctrine, in order to exist, must destroy the phenomena of color as they appear to the eye" (Goethe, 1810/1970, p. 302). By passing light through prisms in darkened
rooms, Newton created artificial conditions that eliminated color as lived experience: the play of light on surfaces, the warmth of yellows, the coolness of blues.
Henri Bergson extends this critique in L'Évolution créatrice (1907), arguing that intellectual analysis necessarily spatializes time, fragments continuity, and immobilizes movement: "The intellect is characterized by a natural inability to understand life" (Bergson, 1907/1998, p. 165). To study life, science must arrest it, transforming durée (lived duration) into a series of static states. The butterfly pinned in the display case reveals morphology but conceals flight.
Maurice Merleau-Ponty, in La Structure du comportement (1942), demonstrates this through analysis of reflex theory in physiology. The reflex arc stimulus leads to response through fixed neural pathways that appear clear in the isolated preparation. But as Merleau-Ponty shows: "The reflex does not exist as such;
29

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 it is constructed by scientific analysis" (Merleau-Ponty, 1942/1963, p. 31). In living behavior, there are no isolated reflexes but integrated responses shaped by the whole organism's engagement with its environment.
This violence emerges from the structure of objectification itself, which requires eliminating everything that ties phenomena to particular contexts, relationships, and meanings.. The view from nowhere requires eliminating everything that ties phenomena to particular contexts, relationships, and meanings. But these connections often constitute the phenomena themselves. The migrating bird's behavior makes no sense without its ecological relationships. The cell's function cannot be understood outside its tissue context. The ritual's meaning disappears when extracted from its cultural setting.
7.2 What Neutral Observation Cannot See
The aspiration to neutral observation systematically blinds itself to dimensions of reality that only appear from particular perspectives. These are not subjective additions to objective facts but aspects of reality itself that require situated engagement to become visible.
Consider pain. The neuroscientist can observe nociceptor activation, map pain pathways, identify neurotransmitters involved in pain signaling. But pain itself, the lived experience of hurting, remains invisible to neutral observation. As Elaine Scarry argues in The Body in Pain (1985): "To have pain is to have certainty; to hear about pain is to have doubt" (Scarry, 1985, p. 13). Pain can only be known from the inside, from the irreducibly first-person perspective of the sufferer.
This extends beyond subjective experience to intersubjective phenomena. Trust, for instance, cannot be observed neutrally. As Annette Baier demonstrates in Moral Prejudices (1994), trust involves a distinctive kind of vulnerability that can only be understood from within relations of trusting and being trusted. The attempt to study trust "objectively" through game theory or neuroscience captures behavioral correlates but misses trust itself, the lived experience of placing oneself in another's hands.
Feminist philosophers have shown how the supposedly neutral perspective systematically overlooks phenomena visible from women's social positions. Sara Ruddick's Maternal Thinking (1989) argues that the practice of mothering develops distinctive cognitive capacities attentive love, concrete thinking, narrative understanding invisible to abstract masculine reason. These are not inferior modes of thought but ways of knowing appropriate to preserving and fostering life.
7.3 Standpoint Epistemology and Epistemic Advantage
Feminist standpoint epistemology, developed by scholars like Nancy Hartsock, Sandra Harding, and Patricia Hill Collins, argues that marginalized perspectives possess epistemic advantages for understanding social reality. This epistemology maintains that marginalized perspectives gain
epistemic advantage through direct experience of power's operations and contradictions, revealing structures that dominant positions have incentive to obscure or naturalize.
Nancy Hartsock's "The Feminist Standpoint" (1983) argues that women's position in capitalist patriarchy provides superior understanding of gender and class relations: "A standpoint is not simply an interested position (interpreted as bias) but is interested in the sense of being engaged" (Hartsock, 1983, p. 285). The dominant group's perspective appears universal because it has the power to enforce its partiality as neutrality. The subordinated group, needing to understand both the dominant worldview and their own experience, develops a dual consciousness that sees more.
Patricia Hill Collins's Black Feminist Thought (1990) extends this analysis through the concept of the "outsider within" Black women in academia who are simultaneously inside and outside dominant institutions. This position enables what Collins calls "intersectional consciousness" the ability to see how race, gender, class, and other systems of oppression interconnect in ways invisible to those who experience only one dimension of marginalization or none at all.
30

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 The epistemic advantage is not automatic but achieved through struggle. As Donna Haraway argues in "Situated Knowledges" (1988): "The standpoints of the subjugated are not 'innocent' positions. On the contrary, they are preferred because in principle they are least likely to allow denial of the critical and interpretive core of all knowledge" (Haraway, 1988, p. 584). Those who must fight for recognition cannot afford the luxury of believing in neutral observation.
7.4 The View from Below
The view from below from positions of marginalization, oppression, and exclusion reveals dimensions of reality systematically obscured by the view from above. This is not merely a different perspective on the same reality but access to realities that dominant perspectives actively suppress.
James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State (1998) demonstrates how high-modernist planning, attempting to impose geometric order from above, systematically destroys local knowledge essential for human flourishing. The colonial administrator viewing forests as timber resources cannot see the complex ecological relationships that forest dwellers navigate. The urban planner seeing slums as a disorder cannot perceive the intricate social networks that make marginal communities viable.
María Lugones's "Playfulness, 'World'-Travelling, and Loving Perception" (1987) develops the concept of "world-travelling" , the ability to shift between different cultural worlds and see oneself through different frameworks. This constitutes a survival skill developed by those who must navigate between dominant and subordinate worlds, requiring constant code-switching and perspective-shifting. The migrant worker, the colonized subject, the assimilated immigrant develops what Lugones calls "a plural self" capable of seeing what those secure in single worlds cannot perceive.
Enrique Dussel's Philosophy of Liberation (1977) argues that genuine philosophical insight emerges not from the center but from the periphery, not from totality but from exteriority. The poor, the excluded, the colonized occupy a position of exteriority to dominant systems that allows them to see these systems' violence and limitations. As Dussel writes: "The face of the poor, of the dominated, of the tortured is the starting point of philosophy" (Dussel, 1977/1985, p. 43).
7.5 Indigenous Epistemologies and Relational Knowledge
Indigenous epistemologies provide profound alternatives to the view from nowhere by grounding knowledge in relationships rather than abstraction. These are not pre-modern perspectives awaiting development but sophisticated ways of knowing that reveal the poverty of disconnected observation.
Vine Deloria Jr. 's The Metaphysics of Modern Existence (1979) contrasts Western emphasis on time with Indigenous emphasis on space. Western science seeks universal laws that apply everywhere and always. Indigenous knowledge focuses on particular places and the relationships that constitute them. As Deloria argues: "The structure of the physical world is a function of the complex of relationships that constitute a place" (Deloria, 1979, p. 34).
Linda Tuhiwai Smith's Decolonizing Methodologies (1999) shows how Indigenous research methodologies proceed through relationships rather than objectification. Knowledge is not extracted from informants but emerges through reciprocal engagement. The researcher is not a neutral observer but a participant in networks of obligation. As Smith writes: "Indigenous methodologies tend to approach cultural protocols, values and behaviors as an integral part of methodology" (Smith, 1999, p. 15).
Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's As We Have Always Done (2017) articulates Nishnaabeg epistemology, where knowledge emerges through land-based practices, intergenerational transmission, and embodied engagement with territory. This is not folklore or traditional ecological knowledge as understood by Western science but a comprehensive intellectual tradition with its own standards of validity. Simpson writes: "Intelligence in Nishnaabeg thought comes from the connections and relationships, from the web of connections, not from separation and isolation" (Simpson, 2017, p. 22).
31

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 7.6 The Carnal Knowledge of Embodied Cognition
The phenomenological tradition, particularly Merleau-Ponty's work, demonstrates that perception and cognition are fundamentally embodied processes that cannot be abstracted into a view from nowhere. The body is not a container for consciousness but the medium through which the world and self mutually constitute each other.
In Phénoménologie de la perception (1945), Merleau-Ponty argues that perception occurs through what he calls the "intentional arc" the body's directedness toward the world: "The body is our general medium for having a world" (Merleau-Ponty, 1945/2012, p. 146). We perceive depth not through geometric calculation but through our body's potential for movement. We grasp objects not through mental representation but through motor intentionality.
This embodied perspective is always situated gendered, racialized, aged, abled or disabled in particular ways. Iris Marion Young's "Throwing Like a Girl" (1980) shows how feminine body comportment in patriarchal society involves "inhibited intentionality" a holding back from full bodily engagement with the world. This is not a natural feminine essence but the embodied effect of social positioning.
Drew Leder's The Absent Body (1990) analyzes how illness and disability reveal dimensions of embodiment invisible to the healthy. The person with chronic pain develops intimate knowledge of bodily processes that remain background for others. The wheelchair user knows space differently not as abstract geometry but as concrete accessibility or barrier.
7.7 Emotional Knowledge and Affective Attunement
The exclusion of emotion from legitimate knowledge represents one of the views from nowhere's most impoverishing effects. Emotions are not obstacles to clear perception but modes of disclosure that reveal aspects of reality invisible to detached observation.
Alison Jaggar's "Love and Knowledge" (1989) argues that emotions are "ways of being aware of our world" that can provide epistemic resources unavailable to dispassionate reason. Anger at injustice reveals moral dimensions of situations that appear neutral to those not affected. Love enables knowledge of particularity that abstract reason necessarily misses. As Jaggar writes: "Emotions may be helpful and even necessary rather than inimical to the construction of knowledge" (Jaggar, 1989, p. 156).
Sara Ahmed's The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004) shows how emotions are not private feelings but social and cultural practices that shape what bodies can do. Fear orients bodies away from some objects and toward others. Happiness functions as a promise that directs life courses. Disgust establishes boundaries between self and other. These emotional orientations constitute rather than distort knowledge of the social world.
Nel Noddings's Caring (1984) develops an ethics of care based on the emotional engagement of caring relations rather than abstract principles. The one-caring knows the cared-for through attention, motivational displacement, and affective engagement that cannot be achieved through neutral observation. This is not sentimental substitution of feeling for thought but recognition that certain ethical truths only appear through emotional engagement.
7.8 The Imaginal and Symbolic Dimensions
Henry Corbin's concept of the mundus imaginalis the imaginal world points to dimensions of reality that the view from nowhere cannot access because they exist between the purely physical and purely mental. The imaginal is not imaginary (unreal) but a genuine ontological realm where symbolic forms have creative power.
In Creative Imagination in the Sufism of Ibn Arabi (1969), Corbin argues that the imaginal realm is where "spiritual beings are corporealised and corporeal beings are spiritualised" (Corbin, 1969, p. 4).
32

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 This is where visions occur, where symbols operate, where meaning and matter interpenetrate. The view from nowhere, recognizing only material facts and mental representations, cannot access this intermediate realm.
Carl Jung's work on active imagination and symbolic reality, particularly in The Red Book (2009), demonstrates how psychic reality operates through images that are neither literal facts nor mere fantasies. The encounter with archetypal images in dreams, visions, and creative work provides knowledge of psychic depths invisible to rational consciousness. As Jung writes: "Image and meaning are identical; and as the first takes shape, so the latter becomes clear" (Jung, 2009, p. 231).
James Hillman's archetypal psychology extends this insight, arguing in Re-Visioning Psychology (1975) that the soul speaks in images that cannot be reduced to concepts: "To understand anything at all, we must have an image of it" (Hillman, 1975, p. 23). The attempt to achieve imageless, conceptually pure knowledge eliminates precisely what makes understanding possible.
7.9 Participatory Knowledge and the Between
Martin Buber's distinction between I-Thou and I-It relationships, developed in Ich und Du (1923), reveals modes of knowledge unavailable to objectifying observation. The I-It relation treats the other as an object, seeking to know through categorization and control. The I-Thou relation encounters the other as presence, knowing through participation rather than observation.
Buber writes: "The relation to the You is unmediated. Nothing conceptual intervenes between I and You" (Buber, 1923/1970, p. 62). This is not mystical fusion but genuine encounter where knowledge emerges in the between-space of relation. The teacher knows the student, the therapist knows the client, the researcher knows the subject not through detached observation but through participatory engagement.
Jorge Ferrer's Participatory Turn in Transpersonal Theory (2002) extends this to spiritual knowledge, arguing that spiritual knowing is not observation of transcendent objects but participatory enactment of spiritual realities. Different contemplative practices meditation, prayer, ritual, psychedelic experience don't reveal the same reality from different angles but participate in bringing forth different spiritual worlds.
Richard Tarnas's Cosmos and Psyche (2006) argues for what he calls "participatory epistemology" the recognition that "the human mind is ultimately the organ of the world's own self-revelation" (Tarnas, 2006, p. 488). Knowledge emerges not through the subject observing the object but through the world knowing itself through human participation.
7.10 The Productivity of Constraint
Situated knowledge is not diminished knowledge but knowledge enriched by constraint. The view from somewhere, precisely because it is limited, achieves depths and intensities unavailable to the impossible view from nowhere.
Maurice Blanchot's concept of the "essential solitude" of writing, developed in L'Espace littéraire (1955), shows how creative knowledge emerges through limitation. The writer confronts the blank page from their particular situation, their language, their moment, their obsessions. This situatedness is not an obstacle to universal significance but its condition. As Blanchot writes: "To write is to make oneself the echo of what cannot cease speaking" (Blanchot, 1955/1982, p. 27).
Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari's concept of "minor literature," developed through their study of Kafka, shows how marginalized positions generate revolutionary potential. Writing from the margin of German-language literature as a Prague Jew, Kafka achieves what major literature cannot: "A minor literature doesn't come from a minor language; it is rather that which a minority constructs within a major language" (Deleuze and Guattari, 1975/1986, p. 16).
33

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 Édouard Glissant's Poetics of Relation (1990) develops the concept of opacity as productive resistance to transparency. The demand for transparency that everything be made clear, visible, understandable is a colonial demand for control. Opacity preserves the irreducible particularity that generates genuine diversity. As Glissant argues: "Opacities can coexist and converge, weaving fabrics whose texture may vary" (Glissant, 1990/1997, p. 190).
Conclusion: The Situated Ground of All Knowledge
The attempt to achieve a view from nowhere does not transcend the limitations of situated knowledge but destroys the very conditions that make knowledge possible. This investigation has demonstrated through converging lines of analysis, historical, epistemological, hermeneutic, and phenomenological, that the aspiration to perspectiveless knowledge is not merely practically unattainable but conceptually incoherent.
The historical analysis revealed that what presents itself as the absence of perspective, scientific objectivity, is actually the product of specific metaphysical decisions made during the Scientific Revolution (Koyré, 1957; Burtt, 1924). The shift from finite cosmos to infinite universe (Koyré, 1957), the mathematization of nature (Galilei, 1623), the bifurcation of reality into primary and secondary qualities (Locke, 1689), these were not discoveries of how reality truly is but impositions of a particular framework that subsequently naturalized itself. The view from nowhere is not the absence of somewhere but the universalization of a very particular place that has forgotten its origins (Husserl, 1936).
The epistemological investigation established that observation is never neutral registration but always technical production within theoretical frameworks (Bachelard, 1934). Instruments do not reveal pre-existing facts but participate in constructing what can appear as factual (Hacking, 1983). Paradigms constitute the observational space within which phenomena become visible (Kuhn, 1962). The theory-ladenness of observation (Hanson, 1958), the underdetermination of theory by evidence (Duhem, 1906; Quine, 1951), and the experimenter's regress (Collins, 1985) combine to make neutral observation impossible in principle, not merely in practice.
The hermeneutic analysis demonstrated that all understanding occurs within horizons of meaning that cannot be transcended (Gadamer, 1960). The distinction between understanding and explanation reveals different modes of cognition appropriate to different domains, not a hierarchy from inferior to superior knowledge (Dilthey, 1883). Prejudice and tradition are not obstacles to understanding but its enabling conditions (Gadamer, 1960, pp. 278-279). The fusion of horizons that occurs in genuine understanding is not the achievement of a perspectiveless position but the productive encounter between situated perspectives (Gadamer, 1960, p. 306).
The examination of situated knowledge revealed both what the view from nowhere destroys and what the view from somewhere makes possible. The attempt at objectification kills living phenomena (Bergson, 1907), spatializes time (Bergson, 1889), fragments continuity (James, 1890). Yet situated knowledge, from marginalized standpoints (Collins, 1990; Hartsock, 1983), from Indigenous epistemologies (Deloria, 1979; Smith, 1999), through embodied cognition (Merleau-Ponty, 1945; Varela et al., 1991), via emotional attunement (Jaggar, 1989; Ahmed, 2004), through imaginal perception (Corbin, 1969), reveals dimensions of reality invisible to the supposedly neutral gaze. The view from below sees the violence obscured by the view from above (Scott, 1998; Dussel, 1977). Relational knowledge grasps connections that analytical separation destroys (Kimmerer, 2013; Simpson, 2017).
This does not lead to relativism, the claim that all perspectives are equally valid, but to what Haraway (1988, p. 590) calls "situated objectivity." Some positions reveal more than others, not because they approximate a view from nowhere but because they are better positioned to perceive particular dimensions of complex reality (Harding, 1991). The path forward is not the impossible transcendence of situatedness but the multiplication of perspectives, the cultivation of dialogue between different situated
34

The View from Nowhere, which is also Somewhere M. Nourizadeh
 knowledge, the creation of conditions for productive encounter between different ways of knowing (Santos, 2014).
The view from nowhere promises everything and delivers nothing, a complete knowledge that destroys what it claims to know. The view from somewhere promises nothing and delivers everything, partial, situated, embodied knowledge that preserves and reveals the phenomena in their living complexity. The task is not to achieve an impossible nowhere but to inhabit our somewhere more consciously, more critically, more creatively, recognizing both its limitations and its unique revelatory power.
We remain where we have always been, somewhere, in bodies, in history, in language, in culture, seeing from here what cannot be seen from there, blind here to what is visible there. This is not a failing to be corrected but the human condition to be inhabited (Merleau-Ponty, 1945). The aspiration to escape this condition through achieving a view from nowhere is not merely impossible but destructive. It is time to abandon this aspiration and embrace instead the difficult, partial, but genuine knowledge available from somewhere we inhabit.
The view from nowhere is the emperor's new clothes of epistemology, a magnificent nothing that everyone pretends to see. The view from somewhere is all we have, all we have ever had, and, properly understood, all we need.
