14.1 Introduction and Overview

The aim of the chapter is to highlight promising theoretical and methodological innovations that work to understand and address inequities in postsecondary physics contexts. In particular, we move beyond a focus on the individual and identity as the main lens. We instead show how a focus on relations between people, communities, and institutions can unsettle physics education research (PER) and offer new avenues for scholarly investigation. In particular, if PER researches education, then its hegemonic contexts, interests, goals, and methods play a role in defining what education means. The broad overview we provide in this chapter of questions and re-orientations for all of these pieces of PER pushes then toward reconceptualizing what counts as education within PER, moving toward relationships, community, and critical critique as core to the idea of education.

This chapter takes up and responds to two important contexts. First, PER and physics equity work more broadly has primarily been conducted in ways which support seeing science education as a process in service of developing capital (see, for example, Pierce, 2012) and, consequently, have focused on “diversity” and “inclusion” issues like binarized gender inequalities. Second and more specifically, PER has traditionally focused on a genre of research that prioritizes learning standard physics knowledge and practices in the university classroom and student laboratories—a context which has only recently started to challenge the colonial, enlightenment values of physics research at large, instead continuing to train and socialize individuals into these practices. In this chapter, then, we focus on how attending to efforts that grapple with “politicized” questions and themes, and the social backgrounds to the research in the community, can broaden the field of (postsecondary) physics education research. We look at examples of action and learning in a variety of contexts, which responds to the call to pluralize the typical focus of PER on classroom contexts.

14.1.1 Positionality
As researchers, we acknowledge that research is a subjective endeavor that is situated in our varied positionalities. All four authors bring varying relations with ancestors, the lands we live on, and physics as a subject, to our scholarship on physics education. We recognize that we have White racialized identities, and are/have always been settlers; all four of us living and working in colonial states. We understand that engaging in research means also recognizing those privileges and colonized perspectives in our research and work. Our epistemological positionalities are aligned with research that seeks to identify and challenge issues of power, equity, and social justice in physics contexts, particularly in academia. Some of us position ourselves as insiders to physics, while others are outsider to physics but benefit from positions as insiders to postsecondary physics.

14.1.2 Research Context for Postsecondary Physics Education
Often motivating physics education research is the goal to have more (and more diverse) people in STEM. Why do we need more people working in STEM? An answer to that question involves complex, entangling ideas about scientists and engineers as contributing to economic growth with considerations about the significance of STEM professionals for a country’s defense capabilities and national security (Fensham, 1985; Lövheim, 2016, 2021). To complicate matters further, utilitarian arguments concerning a perceived need for more STEM professionals are often interspersed with arguments drawing on equity and social justice (DeBoer, 2013). This emphasis on “getting more qualified professionals into STEM fields” has led to research on barriers that under-represented groups face in STEM, and solutions to support their trajectories into the “STEM pipeline,” rather than questions about the STEM pipeline itself. In physics education research in particular, the issue of the uneven distribution of women and men in physical sciences has received considerable attention. Looking back, notable works include Laura McCullough’s research on gender differences in physics assessments (e.g., McCullough, 2004), the work on highlighting and reducing gender gaps in higher education physics (e.g., Pollock et al., 2007), and research in secondary schools investigating “physics identity” and strategies to encourage girls to enter university-level physics programs (e.g., Hazari et al., 2013). Such work has been pivotal in uncovering binarized gender inequities in physics, and in postsecondary physics education especially.

Casting the net wider, feminist critiques of science (e.g., Fox, 1985; Prescod-Weinstein, 2020) and studies of physics communities from anthropological points of view (e.g., Traweek, 1988; Hasse, 2002) have provided complementary perspectives on the intersection between gender and the epistemology and practices of physics. This contrasts to much equity work in physics education oriented work in the context of postsecondary physics that has, implicitly or explicitly, relied on notions of gender as something static and binary (Traxler et al., 2016). Lately, this work has diversified to include both a recognition of a wider set of social categories (e.g., Barthelemy’s (2020) work on LGBT+ physicists) and expanding theoretical vantage points, such as critical race theory (e.g., Hyater-Adams et al., 2018) and intersectionality (e.g., Avraamidou, 2020a). Such identity-oriented perspectives have lately gained a lot of traction in physics education research (Gonsalves & Danielsson, 2020) for understanding connections between gender and who is recognized as a particular kind of physics student or physicist. As useful as this work has been in uncovering nuances of exclusionary practices in physics, we cannot but wonder where the perspectives’ limits are in terms of reimagining teaching, learning, and research practices in physics. Therefore, in this chapter, rather than give an overview of equity-oriented research in postsecondary physics education research to date, we look forward toward future possibilities. We seek to identify strands in the contemporary research that we see as auspicious for engaging a diversity of learners and disrupting harmful norms and practices in postsecondary physics contexts.

14.1.3 Grounding Lens and Showcasing Innovations
In this chapter, we cover three innovations: theoretical innovations; methods and practices; and rethinking impact. In these sections, we draw into PER context developments that have taken place elsewhere in academic scholarship; and demonstrate their use and future potential uses within postsecondary physics DBER. We have selected some examples from different frameworks which are themselves expansive, and we recommend that the references we include here can act as a guide for those interested in reading and thinking with these theoretical frameworks at large.

Our view of postsecondary contexts will include not just higher education programs and university students’ experiences in physics, but also learning in professional communities, informal learning spaces in postsecondary physics institutions, and community engaged physics research. Learning and education have long been conceived of expansively (e.g., Sandlin et al., 2011) to include extra-institutional contexts; de-institutionalizing the conception of teaching and learning and liberating knowledge development. In expanding our focus beyond traditional learning institutions, we draw inspiration from Herrenkohl et al. (2019) who argue for a “learning humanities” that puts relationships at the center of inquiry. Thus, we move away from examining the cognitive dimensions of physics learning, and from the examination of practices shaping identity work, to instead explore how relationships are centered in (in)formal physics practices, and how practices which place relationships at the center can transform forms of engagement in physics. Thus, we no longer wish to answer questions about how to get more qualified people into physics. Instead, we seek to learn from research and practices that ask questions about obligations vis-a-vis physics practices, responsibilities that physicists and physics students have to act in the world (in relation to human and more-than-human actors), and mechanisms that retain those who are qualified in the profession. Our focus on relationships pulls informal learning contexts into consideration as vital sites of postsecondary physics education, where new, existing, and non-members of the field learn to navigate the profession.

Thus, In Sect. 14.2, we cover theoretical innovations that engage with critical race and critical Whiteness theories and queer theory, as well as exploring expansively other theoretical innovations elsewhere in science learning contexts that we see innovative futures in for postsecondary physics education research. In Sect. 14.3, we demonstrate how mentorship communities and professional development networks offer novel methods and practices toward futures in postsecondary physics communities that are not structured simply around “including” new folks into existing communities of practice. Finally, in Sect. 14.4, we pull to the fore how innovation in what university outreach is and how it is studied in PER contexts, and in the practices and research of citizen science exercise can expand postsecondary physics education. We conclude the chapter looking forward to innovation in futures in postsecondary PER.

14.2 Theoretical Innovations Adopted Recently in PER

In this section, we show how innovations in application of theoretical lenses offer critical perspectives on PER and innovative futures toward which we can expand physics education (and the research that studies these practices expansively).

14.2.1 Critical Race Theory and Critical Whiteness
Recent developments in postsecondary PER have seen an uptake of critical perspectives on race in physics education, drawing on critical race theory, intersectionality, and critical Whiteness (Rosa & Mensah, 2016; Hyater-Adams et al., 2019; Avraamidou, 2020b, 2022; Robertson & Hairston, 2022). Critical race theory (CRT) describes racism as an everyday ordinary occurrence, understanding that race structures social interactions, and that racism is normalized in social systems, social institutions, and social norms. This normalization of racism is an important principle that CRT seeks to make visible as a structuring feature of society (Delgado, 1995). As race, through the lens of CRT, is produced in social interactions, to understand racism research must center the voices of People of Color (Delgado & Stefancic, 2017). Rosa and Mensah (2016) documented the voices of Black women in physics, by utilizing one of the key principles of CRT: counterstories. In centering the stories of Black women in physics, telling counterstories confronts the dominant stories of those who are in power in physics. These counterstories revealed obstacles that Black women face in physics, such as ordinary racism and microaggressions, and frames these obstacles, such as feelings of isolation and decreased self-efficacy, mechanisms of exclusion which compromised their learning and performance in physics. Rosa and Mensah argue that traditional narratives in research about persistence in physics overplays “academic achievement…and downplays the role of the racial social climate in STEM fields” (p. 11).

The counterstories enabled by the CRT lens reveal how racism functions specifically in students’ performance and persistence in physics, and challenges the dominant narratives that place student deficits as a key feature that interventions in the field should seek to address. In this study, Hyater-Adams et al. (2019) adopt a CRT lens to investigate how Black folks identify as physicists, developing a framework (critical physics identity, CPI) to describe such identities. The framework draws on the basic tenets of science identity framings (featuring the importance of recognition, performance, and competence) but also combines these with Nasir’s (2011) model of racialized identities that foregrounds the importance of relational, ideational, and material resources in the construction of identity. The findings showed that all participants strongly identified with physics, but experienced difficulties performing their physics identities due to similar structural barriers as those described by Rosa and Mensah. The value of this framework which places race at the analytical centre is that it provides a means to capture the counterstories of Black participants, while identifying the structural obstacles that impact Black students’ performances in physics.

Drawing on intersectionality theory, Avraamidou (2020b, 2022) challenges the prioritizing of the “politics of recognition” in physics identity research, asking researchers to consider where the power resides in research that seeks to learn about how recognition supports insider identity work in physics. Avraamidou’s use of intersectionality—which develops an understanding of how the way people experience society is shaped by the overlap of their different identities that are inextricably interlinked and not separable (Nash, 2011)—in this research highlights the often problematic ways that the concept of recognition is mobilized in identity research (in PER and science education research more broadly). Recognition has emerged as a strong analytical concept in identity research investigating the underrepresentation of women and racialized people in physics (e.g., Hazari et al., 2010). However, Avraamidou (2022) points out, recognition has been largely mobilized as a binary concept (either one is recognized as a physics person, or not), which neglects the multiple, intersecting ways that identity positions can yield various forms of recognition, non-recognition, or misrecognition that are not fixed between different contexts. Thus, Avraamidou argues, there is a need to attend to the politics of recognition in identity research, and especially to attend to the ways that current conceptualizations of recognition “leaves open the possibility of women in physics seeking recognition from the very people and institutions that are responsible for their underrepresentation” (p. 62).

Robertson and Hairston (2022) operationalize Critical Whiteness theory to examine how White supremacist ideology can structure interactions in physics classrooms. The authors draw on CRT and literature from Critical Whiteness studies to identify “markers for whiteness” and to analyze how these show up in introductory physics classrooms. This research examines micro-interactions between students, a teacher, a whiteboard, and a physics concept to analyze the interactions and the teacher’s attention. Mobilizing several concepts from CWT, the authors demonstrate how interactions in the classroom center Whiteness in a way that elevates dominant voices, ideas, and ideologies while marginalizing others. These interactions, and those described in follow-up interviews about the class, demonstrate how meritocracy is intertwined with Whiteness in ways that are valued among students and the teacher. These ideologies are likely to be silencing to many of those participating in the class, yet they are reproduced by students in interactions. This new research in physics education is a radical departure for the field. The response to its publication signals the troubling relationship physics education has with race and racial ideology. Shortly after this paper’s publication, the editors of Physical Review Physics Education journal published an editorial supporting the research and their choice to publish it, and admonishing the “harassing, intimidating, and diminishing tweets and emails in response to the publication of the article” (Henderson & Thoennessen, 2022). The authors have since published subsequent work employing a CWT framework that demonstrates how faculty members teaching in mainstream physics programs will adopt “race evasive frames” (e.g., grit or equal opportunity) to discuss representation and success in ways that maintain race-neutrality and the minimization of racism in physics (Robertson et al., 2023).

14.2.2 LGBT+ Research and Queer Theorising
Where early equity and diversity work in PER was almost exclusively focused on binarized gender, recent work has instead expanded to consider the experiences of LGBT+Footnote 1 physicists and the constructions of gender and sexuality. Rather than only accounting for the experience of cis women and cis men, this research reports on the experiences of trans and non-binary physicists. A notable series of papers by Ramón S Barthelemy and colleagues (Barthelemy, 2020; Barthelemy et al., 2022a, 2022b) report from an online quantitative and qualitative survey of LGBTQ+ physicists, exploring LGBTQ+ physicists and physics students experiences of exclusionary behavior and harassment. While those respondents who could be out about their LGBTQ+ identity were more comfortable with their institution (Barthelemy et al., 2022a), in the 71 qualitative responses that reported on experiences of exclusionary behavior and harassment for cis and trans physicists, Barthelemy (2020) found that the majority were based on non-normative gender expression, including for cis physicists, and being a woman. Their data demonstrate that nearly half of the transgender respondents experienced the most exclusionary behavior (with one fifth reporting at least one experience of this in the past year), and over one third of transgender respondents considering leaving their workplace. This finding is echoed in a survey of astronomy and planetary scientists, where Richey et al. (2019) found that although LGBTQPAN women and gender minorities were more likely to feel unsafe at work due to their race, sexual orientation, and gender identity than cisgender, straight women.

To date, this line of research has focused on the experiences of LGBT+ students and scientists, and contributes to broadening the discussion about diversity and inclusion in PER beyond binary gender; demonstrating the need to take into account the intersection of different axes of power. There have been, for example, vital calls to adapt survey practices and institutional policies to take a complex approach to gender, specifically moving beyond gender as something binary, discrete, or that can be easily discernible through names or other external characteristics (Rasmussen et al., 2019; Strauss et al., 2020). Similarly, raising the profile in PER projects of both LGBTQ+ physics students and physicists through developing resources about prominent LGBTQ+ folks (e.g., 500 Queer Scientists, n.d.), or of popular culture figures engaging with physics such as Amrou Al-Kadhi describing quantum mechanics’ non-binary state as “beautiful, strange and glorious” (Al-Kadhi, 2024) has been a vital step toward developing both representation and identity-confirmation in postsecondary physics education.

However, we might distinguish this work on LGBTQ+ visibility and recognition, to practices that embed queer theory and queer approaches to both PER and postsecondary physics education contexts. In postsecondary informal science education contexts, Armstrong (2022) has demonstrated the use of queer theorizing to unpack “hidden” narratives that both discuss LGBTQ+ identities and moved to apply critical queer perspectives on physics and other science research for tour guide attendees in a museum. This demonstrates the potential of queer theorizing in postsecondary physics education where it seeks to deconstruct dominant narratives around gender and sexuality, dismantling binary constructions such as heterosexual/homosexual and masculine/feminine. Elsewhere, work to theorize queer epistemologies of identities in physics contexts is taking shape (see, for example, Armstrong & Danielsson, 2023, and Orthia & Roberson (2023)). In a recent anthology, Letts and Fifield (2019), who have collected STEM education writings engaging with queer theories over two decades, state that “Queer theorizing uncovers and incites paradoxical relations of the normal and strange in ways of knowing, feeling, and being …[and attends to] processes that normalize and naturalize (and abnormalize and denaturalize) particular manifestations of human subjects, society, culture, and nature.” (p. 4). This can be seen in Helene Götschel’s (2019) physics university classroom. She seeks to teach queering of physics by, for example, “scrutinizing what is supposed to be normal and what is invisible or silenced, making the familiar strange, reflecting on the discursive production of physical knowledge” (p. 126). In this way, Götschel also discusses how our understanding and storying of the world through physics sometimes relies on binary, heteronormative gender systems; reflective of Barad’s work to use queer to rethink the very ontology of physics (Barad, 2011).

14.2.3 Theories Used More Widely in Other Science Learning Contexts
In addition to these two theoretical vantage points, we note that there are a range of innovations that have been taken up elsewhere in both non-physics postsecondary science education and physics education at other levels, and here we gesture toward the possibilities for postsecondary physics education research by engaging with these rich bodies of work. Collectively these (along with the queer and critical race theory and Whiteness sections) share a willingness to look at physics as a system of knowledge that is part of larger social systems and to critically to engage with social justice in the context of physics education (Cochran et al., 2021).

Well integrated into research on early-years learning contexts, posthumanism and other theories which include matter offer theoretical innovation for postsecondary PER by emphasizing the co-emergence of learning between learners and matter. Introducing this into theorizing of postsecondary offers mechanisms to engage with how, in contexts beyond the classroom, engagement and experience are often a priority. This is in direct contrast to the formal classroom where “often concepts are afforded more ontological power and are considered more real than the lifeworld experiences of the learner” (Milne, 2019). Particularly rich in theorizing around elements of the natural environment, for example, in exploration of water by Elkin Postila (2022), or engaging learners in ethical education in science (e.g., Scantlebury & Milne, 2020), these approaches offer the potential to draw attention to dimensions of physics education practice that are currently under-theorized in the postsecondary domain. Such work directs our attention to the formation of identity through intra-action with matter (Barad, 2007), and in the social engagement with the nonhuman world. However, an emphasis on the genealogies of posthumanism as the mode of engaging with the interaction of human and non-human worlds in other science learning overlooks and erases theorizing by Indigenous scholars and with Indigenous knowers (Todd, 2016). For example, ​​the Turtle Island Institute (founded by Melanie Goodchild (Goodchild 2023)) supports a Virtual Teaching Lodge that engages in Indigenous-led teaching of science specifically beyond the university classroom; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Astronomy project works with teacher education in the postsecondary context at the University of Melbourne (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Astronomy, 2022).

Agitating for greater engagement in the implications of physics being part of a settler colonial project in the education that is provided about physics is part of activist work within the field (see Sect. 14.3: Methods and Practices for more details). Deliberate engagement with, and challenge to, entitlement to Indigenous land and access for physics research can be seen in relation to large astronomical science operations (e.g., Casumbal-Salazar, 2017; Neilson, 2019; Goodyear-Ka’ōpua, 2020; Maile, 2021). But, thus far, the impacts of including such critiques in physics education, for example, in the content of classroom work or ethical skills for engaging communities of practice, has been undertheorized in PER. Such work could unpack what work postsecondary learning does or could do to (re)shape beliefs that physics as a body of knowledge is modern, contemporary, progressive, future-oriented and that those attributes are good, desirable, and/or inevitable; highlighting where or how learners both within and the beyond the field are socialized to believe this to be the case. In this way, we call for innovative futures in physics education that move research past the support of colonial states and assimilatory equity that currently dominates the field. All of these critiques encourage us to ask: What will it take in PER to interrogate how colonial, capitalist, and extractivist practices, systems, and theories exist in physics?

14.3 Methods and Practices of Physics Education

We highlight postsecondary contexts that expand the concept of “physics education” to include learning beyond teaching in the classroom. Our contribution here is to move a focus on methods and practices of physics education in the university classroom context to more varied social contexts. We exemplify by one practice in the context of under-graduate students and one in the context of professional learning, but recognize that these practices also are powerful across contexts and that the distinction between “professional” and “student” is porous and not clearly defined.

14.3.1 Physics Learners: Mentorship and Training Programs
Socialization into the field of physics has been an important and long-standing focus of research in PER (e.g., Danielsson, 2012; Gonsalves, 2014), theorizing at how learners learn to belong in the research field. Socialization takes place in many venues. Beyond learning through university classrooms, mentorship and training programs can provide such socialisation events. A wave of programs focus on providing opportunities for more inclusive socialization for those who come from minoritized backgrounds into the field. However, even well-intentioned mentorship provided by people outside the community from which the junior participants come from, and especially that undertaken by White scholars, can potentially be alienating. Counter-narrative led research by Martinez-Cola (2020) demonstrates that Students of Color are subject to imbalance mentoring relationships that, especially in their worst cases, do not see challenging of community norms in developing a place within the community for the mentees, instead trying to fit those outside into existing norms. While there are some White mentors who act as “Allies” (as Martinez-Cola describes them) to disrupt community norms through inviting mentees to events, introducing them to their community, co-authoring with them, she makes the point that these are infrequent persons in the academy. Rather, many mentors “collect” students (then extractively utilize mentees for personal gain) or “nightlight” mentees (by shining guiding lights for mentees without recognizing systemic challenges) in mentoring relationships which socialize students in harmful ways.

To support physics learners, developing communities can be vital. Community change can be supported, convened, led, and populated by the minoritized groups that are historically excluded. These projects offer a different idea about what it means to be socialized into the field, in what we might call “by-with-for PER projects,” led by community members, for community members, with community members as active agents in their development (an adaptation of Simon, 2016). For example, at the California Academy of Sciences, a summer intern program for queer youth, “STARS” (Striving for Trans Inclusion and Anti-Racism in Science Learning) lead by trans and/or BIPOC museum workers to forge paths that see queer identities as part of postsecondary science fields. As an intern on the program, Eli Ramos (2021) gathered the experiences of their colleagues on this program. Ramos notes that many colleagues were united in their “ostracization by race or gender” from science community spaces prior to the program. However, STARS interns described how development “alongside other people of color and LGBTQ+ people has been instrumental to us” allowing them not to have “to explain the basics of my identity and justifying my personhood”—which “was a relief” (Ramos, 2021). Elsewhere, participants at Space Science in Context reported their experience of not having to explain or justify themselves in a conference setting (based on racialized, ableist, or misogynistic judgements) as being integral to finding a community in space sciences that encouraged them to see they belonged in the field (Persaud & Armstrong, 2022). Such experiences describe the relief of not having to do what Murray et al. have theorized as the additional “imposter work” that minoritized folks often undertake to survive and thrive in postsecondary science education contexts (Murray et al., 2022) by being outside the social conditions that make them outsiders to the science community at large. This shift in focus from the individual to the system of relations that maintain the internalization of “feeling like a fraud despite one’s achievements” (p. 7) rejects the need for individualized success narratives that often belie the privileges that are required to experience overcoming such exclusions. As Hodari et al. (2022) urge in their paper on socialization in physics training it “costs us so little to counter those experiences with cues that tell them we are happy they [minoritized students] are there” (p. 21).

14.3.2 Physics Professionals and Communities: Reshaping Professionalism Through Community Building and Action
Other postsecondary physics learning spaces (re)develop norms within professional STEM communities, which are by members of the profession, for their peers, in community with them. Although the distinction is somewhat arbitrary from the section (what does “to be within the field” mean as opposed to becoming part of the field, for instance), in this section, we focus on professional development and community building projects and programs. In their paper, Hodari et al. (2022) note while much research focuses on undergraduate contexts, late-postgraduate and postdoctoral positions in physics fields are key times where researchers are socialized into the field. It is during these periods that “historically marginalized scientists are often excluded or kept out of these professional networks that are tied to increased productivity, which in turn affects their professional success” (p. 4).

Thus, the development of space to reshape social norms of the field from within are vital, which can lead to relearning what participation within the professional physics field could be. These take a wide range of guises from labs within institutions, to trans-national digital communities. From digital community building of projects such as #BlackinSTEM, Particles for Justice (n.d.), Pride in STEM (n.d.), Shutdown STEM (n.d.), VanguardSTEM (2021) leading to off-line action, to projects such as the Astronomers for Planet Earth which encourages climate conscious research and conference participation (Burtscher et al., 2022); or to local institutional LGBTQ+ STEM community action across science departments at UCL (Lock et al., 2025); it is possible to expand the focus on professional community change. We unite these projects in their work to support relearning behaviors within the postsecondary physics community, through supporting, validating, and focusing change in the community and institutions at large through reshaping ideas about how physicists can be within the community. In their work on the experiences on Women of Color in STEM, Ong et al. (2018) describe how such communities can be theorized as counter spaces for Women of Color, instrumental for “facilitating their educational preparation and readying them for careers and beyond” (p. 216).

14.4 Rethinking the Impacts of Informal Postsecondary Learning Contexts

While existing literature in the field addresses the impact of informal learning primarily on the participants in such projects who are from “the public,” we here make an intervention to draw attention to the work that is being done by those developing informal learning practices and the opportunities that this provides to reshape their understandings and knowledge of physics. We focus particularly on reconceptualizing who is learning the practices through the example of University outreach and what is being learned through exploring innovative citizen science projects.

14.4.1 University “Outreach”
Engagement with informal learning in postsecondary physics contexts has been shown to impact university students’ identity work in their physics programs in ways which expand the sense of what physics identity is or ought to be. These programs can be meaningful opportunities for students to build community and find a sense of belonging within their university programs. Research investigating the impacts of university students’ experiences as facilitators of physics outreach projects suggests that informal physics learning experiences can have positive impacts on students’ identity work outside of the constraints that are usually found in academic physics settings (Fracchiolla et al., 2020). Participating in a physics outreach community of practice provides opportunities for students to be recognized as members in the physics community in new ways, and expanding their participation beyond the normative practices of university physics (Prefontaine et al., 2021). This is not limited to university students. Outreach practices of researchers also provide new spaces to negotiate their science identities through creating and sustaining multiple science identities theorized as giving researchers the opportunity to experiment with developing shifting and contingent identity performances in university science outreach (Davies, 2021). Additionally, research specifically investigating women’s involvement in facilitating informal physics programs found that participants gained increased opportunities for internal and external recognition, thus providing opportunities for them to “curate their own sense of expertise” which improved their confidence in their chosen major (Randolph et al., 2021, p. 363).

These programs also provide resources for youth who are engaged in learning that facilitates their own socialization into physics. For example, research into the significance of “university adjacent” informal physics learning programs suggests that university outreach programs provide numerous resources that contribute to youths’—especially young women’s—identity work vis-a-vis physics (Gonsalves et al., 2022). Programs identified as university-adjacent (such as outreach programs, internships, summer schools, and public lectures) can provide opportunities for youth to begin to see themselves as physics people, and to learn about the lives of physicists beyond the classroom or even the lab. While we acknowledge the importance of these practices to contribute to pluralizing the people who participate in physics, we also wish to point to these as often elite and difficult to access programs for many minoritized students.

14.4.2 Citizen Science
“Citizen science” designates a wide range of different activities involving public participation in science. This can include, for example, amateur naturalists collecting observational data about birds (Parrish et al., 2019), people classifying images of galaxies (Reed et al., 2013; Lingard et al., 2020), or monitoring of radioactivity in food (Reiher, 2016; Andersson-Sundén et al., 2019). Today, citizen science is typified by distributed fieldwork or crowd-sourcing of data analysis (McQuillan, 2014), with the common goal of “educating” the public about science. Research in PER related to these activities have hegemonically, thus, looked at the “success” of various projects against such goals. But citizen science has an epistemically transformative potential: challenging the very foundation of the modern regime of scientific knowledge production where the work of professional scientists is separated from the lay public, who are understood as—at best—consumers of science. The involvement of lay people in science not only changes who participates in the knowledge production, it can also transform how this is done as well as where and why—including lay people in experimental research not just in collection of observations (Strasser et al., 2019). Strasser and colleagues instead attend to “striking” importance of the perceptive and affective qualities employed by participants during citizen science projects, despite “knowing that [these attributes’] exclusion was a key element in the formation of modern science, based on the ideal of objective, rational, and disinterested knowledge” (2019, p. 65).

McQuillan (2014) takes this potential further, arguing for citizen science as nomadic science focused on the local, the situated, and the culturally reflective. In this nomadic science also lies a potential for community activism, to enact science as a bottom-up practice, attentive to local needs and practices (McQuillan, 2014). For example, the Public Lab (n.d.) seeks to pursue environmental justice through community science and open technology. Through low-cost tools, people are able to participate in the building of community knowledge about environmental health based on physics experimental techniques (e.g., do-it-yourself spectrometers used to detect oil pollution). Another example of citizen science within physics is the Original Research By Young Twinkle Students (ORBYTS) program, where secondary school students have been involved in original research on exoplanets, supervised by PhD students and postdocs (Dunn, 2021). Part of the data used comes from data obtained by citizen astronomers, thereby linking junior research, school students, and citizen scientists. One aim with the ORBYTS program is to by involving school students in state-of-the-art research empower them to participate in STEM and challenge ideas about who can be a producer of scientific knowledge (Sousa-Silva et al., 2017).

14.5 Conclusions, Contributions to the Field, and a Call to Innovative Futures

Throughout this chapter, one of our overarching contributions has been to (re)conceptualize what counts as education within the field of physics education research by introducing and highlighting theories, methods, and contexts that are a departure from hegemonic PER. In our selection of cases, we particularly ask what it means to think of education beyond the normative postsecondary contexts of the university classroom, with a greater focus on learning in its expansiveness to capture experiences, knowledge transfers, skills, and behaviors. Not only does this transformation open a range of new practices and sites of subjectivities to the purview of PER, it also moves beyond a conceptualisation of postsecondary education that is narrowly focused on those for whom physics remains a central part of their lives. Instead, this view allows exploration of the value of understanding what physics learning might mean for those beyond the field. Thus, we call for innovative moves in postsecondary PER: from the individual to networks of relationships, from a specifically university classroom context to more varied social contexts, and from support of socializing people into physics more efficiently into critiquing colonial physics at its core. This transformation of physics education research and practices is a call to think critically not only about the sites of physics learning that are researched, but also the goals of the research practice. We call for innovative futures in PER that resist reproducing oppressive, colonialist, extractive cultures, or the goals of improving “diversity and inclusion” in physics, for example, and instead invest in imagining sociocultural change beyond increasing representation.

The Cringe vs. The Fringe vs. Those That Impinge
Observations and delineations on when "cranky" is a strict superset of "crank"
CURT JAIMUNGAL
SEP 07, 2025

There’s a bias on YouTube: if you have some novel “outsider” theory, it’s generally seen as considerably positive, and those who represent “the academy” (whatever that means) are portrayed as ossifying fools who don’t recognize what’s new. This is unfair. Not all work in the sciences needs to be “revolutionary.” Even if that were the case, the original idea being proposed isn’t revolutionary to begin with; it’s tentative and conjectural.

On the other hand, those with original proposals primarily become intertwined with the pejorative of “crackpots.” They’re seen as narcissists suffering from Dunning‑Kruger, obsessed with a single idea, attention‑seeking, sour‑grapes, queue‑jumping interlopers who don’t know the physics, podcast entertainers rather than scientists, and mavericks who undermine scientific integrity with their often ill‑intentioned, self‑delusional egotism.

Not all those positing new‑fangled results are maltreated revolutionaries. Similarly, not all are “crackpots” (a derisive term I’m not a fan of, as derision actually contributes to an anti‑science sentiment, since at minimum, hostile approaches trigger opposition, while beliefs remain woefully unchanged. See Song et al. (2018) and Van’t Riet et al. (2017).)

Many people ask me some variation of this: “Curt… How has Theories of Everything changed your worldview / beliefs? You’ve spoken to 200+ professors in various fields… Do you, Curt, have a personal theory of everything?”

Well, outside of the “cringe physics” joke called SCHLONG Theory, the answer is no. I don’t have answers. I don’t have proposals. What I do have, though, are a series of observations I’d like to share.

Share

Concerning the YouTube channel, people tune in to listen to the cognoscenti; not me. The guests are the ones with actual acumen, views, and justifications for their views, etc. They’re like an electron, with the properties of charge, spin, and mass, etc.

Asking what my views are would be treating me like an electron. I’m nowhere near the level of any of the people I’ve interviewed. Instead of an electron, the channel is more suitably characterized as an electric field. For instance, I see the movement of electrons. I may change an electron’s state from one position to another or from one spin to another, etc., so that it can be viewed or comprehended more palatably, etc.

NOTE: I did not say the electron field… that would be God.

You can ask what the charge and mass of an electron are, but it’s a category error to ask what the charge or mass of the electric field is. It’s a different beast entirely. Thus, instead of my own theories, what I have are observations.

Much of work in the sciences is about refinements and distinctions. That is to say, concepts we used to think were univocal have become further delineated. You can see examples of this when it comes to consciousness, where you have phenomenal consciousness, access consciousness, etc. We used to call something nucleons, then refined to protons and neutrons made of different quarks, etc. Progress is made via unification, yes, but on the other hand (like the above examples) progress is made when something you thought was “the same” is actually seen as multiple distinguished phenomena.

I think what’s occurring in our modern YouTube discourse is a collapsing of discrepancies to “one thing,” with that thing being “crackpot” (much like one’s mom calls every gaming console Nintendo). Let me propose a different taxonomy, along with the concomitant family resemblances and tests to discern the difference.

The academy (again, whatever that means) is usually seen as the “Orthodox.” This is quite foolish, since there are plenty of tenured professors who have views that go steeply against the majority of their colleagues. For the sake of this article, I will call the stereotypical refractory member of the Orthodox by a different name: The Hinge.

Then there is what is not a part of The Hinge. Often this is merely called “crackpot,” but let’s split it into three:

The Cringe
The Fringe
Those That Impinge
…there's also The Unhinged (explained later)
“The Cringe” is what most would strongly associate with “crackpottery” (again, a term I dislike because of its counter‑productively contemptuous nature, and thus I’m using it in scare‑quotes).

The mistake is to think The Cringe is the full set.




TLDR: I’ll get into more about these differentiating features as we continue, but the TLDR is that you can think of this as the distinction between the different answers to the question of “what is a vector?”:

The Cringe (or “crackpot”) would say “something with a magnitude and direction,” with position and “momentum” being an example.
The Fringe physicist may say “it’s an element of a vector space where a vector space is defined by satisfying the axioms of so‑and‑so,” and they’d still say position and momentum are examples.
Those That Impinge, however, will agree with the axiomatic definition of a vector space but note that position is a point in a manifold, and momentum is a covector defined via the fiber derivative (ie, Legendre map). If they’ve had enough wine, perhaps they’d say something fancy about the terminal object of Vect_k.
This is the highly compressed “rule of thumb” napkin version of this distinction.

Thanks for reading! This post is public so feel free to share it.

Share

Some Disclaimers…

To be clear, I’m not claiming that there are zero problems with any of those in the “heterodox” in terms of their theories. I’m not claiming that people should stop what they’re doing and work on their theories. I’m not claiming that I endorse them as being true, especially since they virtually all contradict one another. They can’t all be true. I’m not claiming that those in the prevailing avenues like loop quantum gravity or string theory etc. are incorrect in their approaches.

Do I think “the academy is broken yo!”? No. Broken means what, specifically? And relative to what, specifically? And is it all of the “academy”? Just a subfield? Or a subfield within that? I don’t subscribe to the “broken” thesis, nor do I subscribe to the “we’re in crisis” thesis. I would love for an interventionalist, longitudinal study to be conducted, and I would happily consult with such a study’s conductor on how we can have objective precise measures on these subjective imprecise claims.

This disclaimer may seem completely unnecessary to ~95% of people who read this. There may, however, be a subset who thinks that unless one collapses all these distinctions down to “crackpot”, this is some back‑door manner of saying the “establishment” (whatever that means) is wrong, or that there’s some major “crisis” (a word I dislike) that the academy is ignoring via gate-keeping. Let me be clear: I don’t believe any of this! I personally like and value “gate-keeping!” Virtually everything needs a gate / boundary (your skin is a productive example of one). I don’t believe there is a crisis, and I don’t believe that there is not a crisis. I’m agnostic on this, and I would want to know what the specific definition would be and what studies would demonstrate there is / isn’t, that aren’t merely correlational but causal, etc.

What follows are my present deliberations, of course subject to change as they do regularly. I’ll be providing no “shoulds” in this essay and, in place of a normative stance that would require plenty of information, counter‑arguments, rebuttals to those, investigations with historians of science, thinking through consequences, and looking through studies and conducting them, etc. Thus, this is not rigorous argumentation. I will instead provide observations. These observations are of how different aggregations are more aptly aggregated, as well as how these groups interact with / encroach on / view one another.

NOTE: Why this Cringe / Fringe / Impinge terminology, nominally? As I mentioned, it fits better than mere “crank” vs. “intransigent insider,” or something like “heterodox vs. orthodox,” which are all terms each person defines differently anyhow. The Hinge, however, has literal hinges because they have office doors on campus. Those That Impinge are those that go against or theoretically collide. The Fringe is self‑explanatory. The Cringe, on the other hand, is something I apologize for because it’s just too straightforward a rhyme for me to pass up, even though I’m violating my own rules of decorum by this insignia. Forgive me!

…With that out of the way, let’s get to it.

What We Can Learn From Philosophers…

There’s a philosopher named Kane Baker and he has a video on philosophy vs. public interaction where many of his thoughts echo the sentiments I’ve noticed expressed by other physicists:

There’s a good reason philosophers don’t do enough of [YouTube videos, podcasts, etc.]. Philosophy is an academic discipline, and academic success is measured by strict standards. The primary (and perhaps the single) criterion, aside from networking and luck, is publishing articles in journals and books that expand the discipline’s frontiers. Those works aren’t written for laypeople; they’re often incomprehensible without specialized training and interest only a handful of specialists. The intended audience of journal articles and scholarly books is specialists in the same field, and that’s pretty much all that matters for an academic career. That’s what you’ve got to do: publish in specific journals or produce books in that style.

Something I adore about philosophers that I didn’t discover until fairly recently is “the principle of charity.” This means a philosopher is trained to interpret a speaker’s statements in the most rational way possible and, for any argument, to consider the strongest interpretation. For me, however, that requirement is too stringent, and you can instead relax it to what I call “the method of veridical representation.” That simply means double‑checking whether what’s being disproved truly represents the speaker’s views.

There’s no established term for this, which is why I coined “the method of veridical representation,” and it’s something I aim to do on the podcast. You’ll frequently hear me say, “Okay, just a moment… are you saying X, or are you saying Y?” or “If A is true in your model, wouldn’t that entail that B is true? Why or why not?” This ensures my model of someone isn’t a phantasm but actually reflects what the interlocutor believes. Only recently did I learn that, in philosophy, it’s considered a common practice of intellectual rigor to email someone prior to critiquing them, to ensure the critique addresses what they actually intend, and not some doppelganger.

I first noticed method with a critique of Nancy Cartwright’s Dapped World, where the critic began by thanking Nancy Cartwright directly for her contributions / clarifications to the critique. That’s insane! This sort of private correspondence where one demonstrates that they’re not merely debunking but extending / clarifying, prior to publication, is quite wild and something that I didn’t know was the norm in philosophy.

The above disposition was also echoed by someone else on Substack, who I don’t know, but showed up on my feed:

Jessie Ewesmont: “Laypeople are almost always surprised to hear how common it is for philosophers to email or talk to each other and be like: ‘Hey, I’m writing a paper about why your view is wrong. Can you confirm I haven’t misrepresented it in my gloss here? Also, any cutting objections you want to raise so I can rethink my paper to account for it before Reviewer #2 puts me on blast for missing such an obvious objection?’ This is part of why presenting at conferences is so important. It’s a chance to get your work heard by a wide variety of smart people, who will then provide these remarks in Q&A.”

That’s a standard I absolutely adore.

You can see where I’m going with this. It’s not like this in physics. Instead, it’s more common to collapse the separations of The Cringe / The Fringe / Those That Impinge.

Let’s clarify how one can tell where one stands…

Proficiency Tests and Family Resemblance…

What I’ve observed is that these groups can be largely classified by the following:

The Cringe

Characterized by those who write in Microsoft Word and are essentially the sole reason the caps lock button stays in business
They tend to be fans of picture proofs, circles / spirals / diagrams on paper
They tend to believe (mostly) everyone except them is corrupt, even disrespecting others inside The Cringe
They tend to be able to write down Schrödinger’s equation, though they most likely would not be able to derive the ground state of an electron confined to an infinite square well in non-relativistic quantum mechanics
When they email you, it tends to be private messages one-on-one
The Fringe

They tend to be part of long chains, with others from The Hinge who regret that their email address is public. Satan’s greatest spawn is the CC feature.
They too tend to write in Microsoft Word, yes, but are at least aware that LaTeX is preferred
They can manipulate Schrödinger’s equation just fine
They tend to be obsessed with one or two unconventional historical figures who were silenced and see themselves as continuing their work.
They tend to dislike natural units and see that as concealing the “true” physics
They think (mostly) experiments matter and tinker away, perhaps even finding obscure anomalous effects but not knowing the theory behind them. Their experimental setups have coils abound.
They can list two or three different solutions to general relativity and prove they satisfy the EFE.
They’re also often obsessed with alternative forms of Maxwell’s equations and gravity. This is likely due to the energy scales involved, since the EM field is readily toyed with in one’s garage using tabletop experiments, and they either conduct such experiments themselves or are heavily influenced by those who do.
Tend to be engineers rather than theoreticians
They also tend to be obsessed with the concept of zero‑point energy.
An example would be the extended electrodynamics crowd. They can manipulate curl, divergence, and write PDEs, yes. They’re doing something mathematical, but they may think that all that matters are the E and M fields and write down an equation like this:

without seeing why this breaks gauge invariance (or why breaking gauge invariance is even a problem to begin with). And yes, what I wrote here doesn’t even work dimensionally (you have a 3‑form equal to a 1‑form), but they’d tend not to notice that immediately.

Those That Impinge (Proficiency Test) 

These are people who can answer the below questions with ease, scoring 80 % or greater. For the remaining 20 % they’d at least know roughly what it means and how to find the answer without the aid of an LLM.

Do you recognize all of these Top 30 List of Theoretical Physics Topics?
Spin(4) is isomorphic to what other groups, and how so exactly?
You get Einstein’s conception of special relativistic energy by doing what (exactly) to the Newtonian one, and if they can’t be analogized as such, then why not? How does this extend (or not extend) to the general‑relativistic case?
Can you explain what the standard model Lagrangian terms all represent / their importance / what would happen if you removed some term, etc.?
Can you explain promotion of classical observables on phase space to quantum operators? How do you deal with ambiguities?
Why is the large N limit so relevant to AdS / CFT?
What is a generating functional? How is it different from a generating function?
What’s at least one reason saying quantum field theory is about “fields” is misleading?
Is gauge fixing a problem? Why or why not?
How do you formulate quantum mechanics equivalently with real numbers (and no reference to complex numbers)?
What’s S‑duality?
What’s the problem with naive discretization of spacetime given the symmetries of electrodynamics?
What’s a cotangent bundle?
How is quintessence related to the Bianchi identities (problems with a variable cosmological constant), and why must it be a scalar field if our universe is isotropic?
What’s the renormalization group?
Of course, these lists are best when dynamic because anyone can overfit any particular test by sheer memorization of answers. Thus, you can ask any physics professor to look at the above questions and then generate, for each class, a few new questions that people within that class would be able to answer if they possess a genuine understanding rather than purely committing answers to memory.

The above deals with proficiency, and I believe The Cringe and The Fringe are classified in your mind without issue. Those That Impinge, on the other hand, require some more explication.

Here's the family resemblance that unifies them over and above technical aptitude:

Those That Impinge (Family Resemblance)

They tend to disbelieve one or more of the foundational pillars of the mainline approaches. Perhaps extra spatial dimensions, perhaps inflation, perhaps something to do with unitarity or the consistency of quantum mechanics itself.
They’re often not fans of the culture of The Hinge, while respecting the theories of The Hinge.
They tend to have PhDs or even professorships in the same field or closely adjacent fields.
They also tend to have at least one extremely hypothetically hazardous concept (for instance, Penrose with his consciousness / uncomputability / quantum link).
They tend to find the gauge groups of the Standard Model extremely peculiar. It bothers them.
They seem to be more concerned with the 4 spacetime dimensions of our world whereas The Hinge is more comfortable with exploring toy models as avenues for new insights
They tend to construe “orthodox” fundamental physics (whatever that means) as having long‑standing beliefs that have been unsuccessful in some rooted manner:
For instance, here’s Neil Turok from 2010: “I think the last 20 or 30 years we’ve seen huge bandwagons in physics. String theory is another bandwagon. By and large these bandwagons have failed (well not by and large, totally they have failed, they have failed to deliver).”
Actually, when I was speaking to Roger Penrose, he didn’t even want to talk about the state of modern fundamental physics because it would “upset him too much” and ruin his dinner. This was in front of Matt O’Dowd from PBS Spacetime.



They tend not to consider the quantity of arXiv papers (or the accumulation of citations) as an indication of a field’s health.
They tend to be fond of using words like “stagnation” to describe the state of fundamental physics research—or some variant of it—and claim that the issue isn’t individual but somehow “systemic.”
For instance, David Deutsch just yesterday said Conjecture Institute podcast: “One of the problems is that the whole system is institutionally biased against fundamental innovation, and that’s not anyone’s fault. It’s simply because the method of choosing recipients goes through a bureaucratic process where the people judging it are asked to make a judgment on things they can’t possibly know.”
Broadly speaking, they’re concerned with foundational questions rather than mathematically‑inspired model‑building .
For instance, George Ellis and Joe Silk wrote about this in a 2014 Nature commentary titled Defend the Integrity of Physics. They were concerned that some theorists were willing to abandon empirical testing and declared that this trend wasn’t something nice.
They tend to be snickered at by their colleagues off‑air.
For instance, I’ve heard both graduate students and other professors say Penrose is “off his rocker.” This is a verbatim quote, twice, from two different people, not counting the other phrases. It’s one thing to find faults A, B and C with a proposal; it’s another to disparage the person.
Importantly, those who impinge are not people who believe they have a simple two‑page proof of the Riemann hypothesis or the Yang–Mills mass gap, nor do they think Oneness is the answer to the universe, nor that there's a rank‑3 tensor Love field. Not yet, at least!
There are also rules that Those Who Impinge are not supposed to break: One is that you’re not supposed to call your theory a “theory of everything” (or anything close to grandiose).

Some people may say that all Stephen Wolfram needs to do is publish on the arXiv, but even if he does, the criticisms don’t stop. Suppose he does; then they’ll say, “Well, it needs to be in a peer‑reviewed journal.” Suppose he does; then they’ll say, “Well, it’s not in a respectable peer‑reviewed journal.” Suppose he does, then they’ll say, “Well, the citation count is trifling.” Suppose it’s substantive, then they’ll say, “Well, it’s only cited by people who actually don’t matter.” And on and on, until at some point, they’re implicitly admitting that unless they get the go‑ahead from those at the top of the hierarchy (effectively knighting it), they themselves won’t publicly suggest legitimate new work.

Understandably, it’s easier to catch a late train going to a socially acceptable place and say “sorry,” than it is to buy a ticket early for a train which hinders one’s career prospects.

The motto is to always put something forward as a series of tentative results, and it will be better received, even if it’s the exact same content. Thus, what’s being objected to isn’t always the inside (merit‑worthy or otherwise), but the wrapper. In other words, we think, “Don’t judge a book by its cover, but please do judge a theory by the pride of its proposer.”

Those That Impinge also tend to be on the older side. It may have something to do with being publicly grouped here as an Impinger not being super‑fantastic for their career prospects; thus they already have income elsewhere outside a tenured position and aren’t actively seeking one. If they were actively seeking a position, they’d have to be much more careful about the aforementioned “wrapping” of their ideas than about the ideas themselves.

Something I didn’t know until recently was that collaborating publicly with a controversial figure lowers your own perceived credibility (a sort of “contagion” effect measured in lab studies of reputational risk; see Mongeon & Larivière (2016), Costly Collaborations).

Now, it’s worth disclaiming explicitly here once more: observations on culture, incentives, and dispositions are an entirely separate matter from the objective scientific merit of any given proposal. The former should in no way be mistaken for an endorsement of the latter.

With that out of the way, let’s consider the dispositional gulf…

The Epistemic Divide…

Throughout the above, I have focused on the differences between the three groups, but for now I’d like to focus on the difference between the third and the fourth—namely, between those hard working on the established theories (The Hinge) versus those that aren’t (Those That Impinge). Yes, they differ in terms of research direction, but they also differ dispositionally.

Those That Impinge tend to have near forceful conviction in their ideas, whereas, for the most part, those who aren’t (The Hinge) view themselves as participants in a process of accumulative knowledge‑building, where that knowledge may or may not ultimately relate to the real physical world. This process is thought of like a roulette wheel.

I know this first‑hand: if you were to ask them, “Would you bet money that your research is actually going to lead to a breakthrough / be proven to be on the correct track?” what do you think they would say? My experience is that they wouldn’t be willing to bet money on it, at least not large sums proportionate to the odds even if it’s according to their own stated odds.

The logic is understandable, of course. It’s something approximating “No one knows the future, let alone the future in fundamental physics, so let’s each research what we each think is promising and have the entire enterprise of the academy be akin to an investor who holds a diversified portfolio of different bets (most of which will go nowhere, but some of which will, hopefully, pay off large at some undetermined point in the future).”

This distributed approach (thousands of researchers making additive contributions without the strong individual conviction to bet large sums of their own cash) produced quantum electrodynamics, then the standard model, gravitational‑wave detection, and virtually every major physics breakthrough since 1950! This means that this portfolio model, and peer-review with its error-correcting mechanisms, serve major functions that the lone Impinger approach can’t.

Yet this feels like an unsatisfying answer, not just to you reading this… but to them as well. Something is off. It seems like the soul is lost in the transition from being K‑selected to R‑selected. This is true even in companies. In the beginning, what matters most is who your co‑founder is. That’s when you have a small family in your group—maybe two or three people. What matters after that is who your first employee is, and then, as your company grows, who your first investors are, etc. However, once the company reaches the level where you have hundreds or even thousands of employees, you become R‑selected and you’ve automated away your soul. This innate soul / heart that we sense from the figures who drew us to this field in the first place (people like Einstein, Schrödinger, etc.) is what gets automated away once the enterprise becomes R‑selected in that particular subfield. This is likely a major contributor behind why AI “art” (or AI output in general) isn’t considered to have heart. It may just be that automation devours spirit.

Of course, all of the above observations should be caveated with addenda like “for the most part,” because there are exceptions everywhere. (I think this is my first “should” in this essay.)

An interesting consideration is that those with little certainty that what they are pursuing is correct are generally takers of money. They get money in order to make their contributions. That’s good! People should be paid to follow their flame! (I think this is my second “should” in this essay!) On the other hand, for Those That Impinge, it’s the opposite. They believe in their theories with perhaps a standard deviation or more higher conviction than a generic Hinger, so much so that they themselves pay to do their research! Garrett Lisi, for instance, pays. He does not get paid. Garrett had to get his money independently. Stephen Wolfram pays to do his research. One may say he “puts his money where his mouth is.” Those That Impinge also pay with their intellectual credibility.

Something that is considerably difficult for people outside the academy to appreciate is that there’s “alternate theory latitude” and then there’s “academic cred.” In order to get that latitude, you have to spend your academic cred. To spend that cred, you have to earn that academic cred. A PhD in the relevant field is the minimum way to do so, but even that is just nickels and dimes. A tenured position is an honest way to earn such academic cred, and it’s of course better if it’s tenured at a “respectable” university, or even better, the IAS, etc. There’s an unspoken hierarchy.

Yes, this can be “polluted,” as David Deutsch pointed out yesterday, but perhaps that's the exception. One wants to omit as much foolish work as possible and produce as much fruitful work as possible. Academic cred tends to be incentive‑aligned in this admirable direction.

Every approach has failure modes. For instance, with the self‑funded Impingers, if you’ve made a panoply of money, you can just spend your way to research rather than having to “earn it” through traditional means such as peer validation. The wealthy person can continue to put out nonsensical research without the same fear of reputational stakes. There are problems all around.

Who Cares About The Public? They’re Mostly Idiots, Right?…

Interestingly, even though science as a whole serves the public, there are zero “public engagement” requirements for scientists. This is beneficial in a sense because public engagement is its own separate skill that would otherwise detract from the difficult, deep work of diligently pursuing your subject in the lab, at the blackboard, collaborating, networking, interrogating yourself and other fields, conducting studies, etc. And that’s where the bulk of scientific work is birthed. That’s not the interesting part. The interesting part is that academics who succeed publicly—say, Brian Cox, Neil deGrasse Tyson, or anyone else who becomes popular—are spending their academic cred on public engagement. They’re not earning it. This is supported by the literature (see Watermeyer (2015)).

In other words, you’ll often hear, “Yeah, but so‑and‑so isn’t a ‘true’ scientist. They’re not ‘highly respected’ in the field.” Those sentiments aren’t confined to comment sections or Reddit threads; I’ve heard working researchers voice them about colleagues who receive public attention. Not that what science communicators do is of little value—indeed, it’s of tremendous value! Indeed, even the scientists who consider themselves the true contributors were inspired by the more public‑facing people; the popularizers are, at minimum, the soil from which the scientific academy grows. But something you’ve probably noticed, especially if you’re an academic, is that many scholars are blinded to what isn’t academically valued or “prestigious.” Many tie much of their personal worth to prestige, and anything that reduces that prestige (such as becoming popular or not producing work respected by peers) is not only avoided but generally looked down upon. I’ve heard that accusation of “yeah, he’s great with the public but he’s not highly respected in the field,” thrown at Brian Greene, and Brian, in my opinion (not that he needs my opinion), is a fantastic, formidable physicist! He’s highly respected by me for the twin prongs of his work with Plesser and his wonderfully articulate and his charitably warm cordiality. There’s basically no one who possesses all these qualities simultaneously except him.
