Subscribe
This pattern appears across many fields. Last week I watched the OJ Simpson’s Netflix documentary, and one of the lawyers lamented another lawyer for being a “celebrity lawyer.” They noted that lawyers who receive ample media attention tend to be looked down upon, not because of the quality of their work or whether they uphold justice, but simply because the more spotlight falls on them, the more they’re resented by others who feel they deserve less attention.

You can see this even with the term “public intellectual.” It’s a dirty word in The Hinge. You’ll encounter it even when the public intellectual in question was revered by peers and students prior to fame. The only public intellectuals we can laud as being of quality are those no longer practicing, such as Chomsky or Russell.

Hobbes wrote about this phenomenon succinctly several centuries ago: “Competition of praise inclineth men to a reverence of antiquity. For men contend with the living, not with the dead; hoping the glory of the latter obscures the former.”

Then there’s Kane Baker, who said in 2023:

There are certainly philosophers doing public‑engagement work, especially since COVID, with more online presence, YouTube channels, and podcasts. That’s wonderful, but none of this work is rewarded with better career prospects. We’re encouraged to do it, yet it’s seen as altruistic. To be clear, this YouTube channel has been harmful to my academic career. If I had spent my time creating scholarly articles instead of this content, I’d be in a far stronger position. The time I spend on this channel is completely useless for furthering an academic career, and I’m not special—any philosopher producing public‑facing content is, from a career standpoint, wasting time.

Science, like philosophy, values publication of articles that expand the discipline’s frontiers and are accessible only to highly trained specialists. It’s “publish or perish,” but in a very narrow sense—only a specific kind of publication matters, and that’s the case in science as well.

Scientists value this exclusively because their work has direct practical applications that interest the public. Discovering new mechanisms for DNA methylation could lead to medical therapies; a new technique for analyzing cosmic‑ray data can produce striking Milky Way images for books or TV, engaging the public. By compelling scientists to focus exclusively on expanding the discipline’s boundaries, we also achieve public engagement—public interest follows when theories have direct practical applications.

That’s not the case for philosophy. Expanding philosophy’s frontiers with specialist journal articles has no direct practical utility. Nobody outside academia has a reason to care. Philosophers won’t cure cancer or build particle accelerators, nor will they achieve convergence on theories that other disciplines can readily build upon, as computer engineers have done with quantum mechanics. Science embeds a public‑facing aspect that philosophy lacks.

The suggestion, then, is to change incentives so that public‑engagement work becomes relevant to career success. Journal publications should still matter, but criteria should expand to count projects like this channel. Obviously, this is a very self‑serving position—or maybe it isn’t, because I don’t know. I may not pursue academia, and I’m not that bothered; there are other things I can do with my life. But I care about philosophy as a discipline. I want people to be more interested in it, and I think the way to achieve that is to change the criteria for success.

There’s no need to change philosophy’s content. Philosophers can continue doing what they’ve always done. I’ve found that topics expected to interest only specialists can engage laypersons when presented accessibly.

Much of what Kane said I’ve also found to be the case. Consider feeding into an LLM one of the transcripts from one of the most popular videos on the Theories of Everything channel, say with Claudia de Rham or Ted Jackobson, etc., and ask it, “At what level is this aimed at, given the material? Is it high schoolers? Is it a general undergrad?” You’ll find that most often it’s for a PhD‑level audience in the same relevant field, yet they have 100,000s of views. This is the specialty of the channel, and it’s toward this that I aim.

To close the loop, it may be that these differing epistemic stances (portfolio diversification versus concentrated conviction) are distinct, yes, but are potentially complementary in fundamental physics. It’s not about “which is correct.”

It also may very well be that if you start thinking of yourself as a lottery ticket, then you view your colleagues as a lottery ticket. If that happens, your accountability is minimized, because who cares if what you’re personally pursuing is likely of little value? After all, the same applies to everyone else, and besides, this is just the “natural process.”… But perhaps in fundamental physics it’s not the natural process; perhaps it never was; perhaps it never should be. Perhaps when you view yourself as an unlikely barcode, you view the general public as that as well. And perhaps that’s a horrible, unproductive, deleterious view of your brothers and sisters.

The Climbing Rules and Field Extension Closure…

Defenders of the university system portray science (and, in particular, the quest for a TOE) as the quest to scale a mountaintop. There’s an objective, singular peak that represents ultimate scientific truth. Publicly, there’s an emphasis on collective progress toward the apex, with the scientific community portrayed as cooperative climbers equipped with the necessary tools and knowledge to ascend.

The problem is that the tools of science are not necessarily the same as the tools of the academy. Science is concerned with being objectively correct, and the academy is concerned with that, yes, but also with ensuring you don’t step on the wrong toes, have grant acquisitions, that you achieve a certain citation count, that you’re invited to certain conferences, etc.

Just yesterday, Deutsch recounted meeting the committee member who approved his quantum‑computing grant: “I said if ‘I were to apply today under today's criteria would you have been able to give me the grant?’ The committee member replied, ‘No chance. No chance because you wouldn't have been able to fill out none of the boxes. Literally none.’”

To Deutsch and other Impingers, the community isn’t about scaling the mountain; it’s more akin to a regulated sport, imposing strict norms and methodologies (akin to climbers using regulated equipment and adhering to safety protocols).

On the other hand, there are people outside this established framework who employ unconventional methods, perhaps seen as irrational. Those That Impinge aren't tied to the same incentive structure. These outsiders are seen by the defenders as disregarding the communal rules and are portrayed as undermining the integrity of the scientific pursuit, but actually, these Impingers are undermining the integrity of the academic pursuit (and that's different). We resist integrating mavericks who can scale higher more quickly, dangerously. Free soloing isn't allowed.

The idea is that relaxing academic standards for one outsider risks a floodgate effect.

I think what else is happening is that when you have a finite field extension, you don’t just let in a single irrational root. If you append the square root of two to the rationals, it’s not just about appending the square root of two. You also have to append one plus the square root of two, three halves minus the square root of two, etc. To keep closure and consistency, you have to let in a slew of poppycock elements. When you let in one outsider, you open the floodgates.

Those That Impinge don’t (necessarily) play by the same rules. Why would The Hinge play chess with you if you’re allowed to move your pawn more than one space after the first move? Why would they play in the field extension when they can form a Galois group, keep their academic rational field fixed, and allow all those irrational people to merrily mix about themselves instead?

Another useful distinction is the philosophical difference between vehicle and object. A vehicle is the means by which something is achieved. The object is what’s being achieved (or the “referent”). I think what’s going on is that someone like Gregory Chaitin views the academy as a vehicle with the object being “science”. He may say that those that defend The Hinge may implicitly view it oppositely, with the academy as the object and science as the vehicle. That is, your answer to the following question determines if you lie in Those That Impinge or The Hinge:

Is science the goal, with academic employment / prestige serving as the vehicle toward it? Or is academic employment / prestige the goal, with science being the instrument toward it?




People Over Projects and Some Unhinged Notes…

David Deutsch recommends funding people (rather than projects) and doing so without conditions. I don’t know if this is the correct approach, and hopefully sometime soon I can speak with David Deutsch on the podcast about it.

His view does seem to be supported by a large‑scale study by Wu, Wang & Evans (2019), who analyzed 65+ million papers, patents, and software products from the 50s to the 2010s. They found that smaller teams tended to disrupt science and technology with new ideas, while larger teams tended to develop existing ones. Turns out even Nobel‑Prize‑winning papers had nearly three times as high a probability of being from small teams compared to the control group.

Y Combinator also runs on this “fund founders, not companies” mentality, so it’s not entirely foreign.

Deutsch caveats this with, “But I guess it’s not going to be feasible for all kinds of research because some kinds of research involve the collaboration of five people or 50 people, and then it’s extremely disadvantageous to have a hierarchy.” Again, the interview just launched yesterday, and the link is here.

I'd like to end with some more from Kane Baker on his views on if journals should be the sole method of furthering philosophy:

Journal publication is not the only way to develop new ideas. Indeed, the weight that’s given to such publications, the fact that we take this to be the only way of legitimately contributing new ideas, I think that might actually stifle creativity in some ways because journals can be quite conservative. There are several features, I think, of academic journals that might tend to stifle the development of new ideas. Here are some of them.

First of all, if you try to publish in a journal, you’re going to be required to address topics that are considered important or relevant, which is to say topics that professional philosophers happen to find interesting at the moment. You’re going to be limited, probably, by whatever the current philosophical fads are. You’re going to be forced to frame issues in terms of the tradition that has prevailed beforehand. I mean, just consider how, for decades, many philosophers in Western universities were very dismissive of work that was seen as continental. No doubt there are plenty of reasonable criticisms of continental philosophy, but it seems like it wasn’t really given a fair hearing. By placing a bit more emphasis on non‑peer‑reviewed work, we may make it easier for philosophers to overcome these kinds of biases and bring new ideas into the discourse.

Second, when you publish in journals, there’s a requirement that you demonstrate familiarity with the literature. In many ways, that’s a good thing. But what this means is that in practice, if you come up with a new idea, you have to respond to all of the major alternatives. This can take a lot of time. Maybe you don’t want to devote that much time to it. It would be a lot easier to just throw out the idea in a blog post, for instance. It could still be a genuinely new contribution, right? Even if you’re not in the mood for shaping something into the sort of article that could be published in a journal, you can still make a new contribution by putting the idea out there in some other way.

Finally, there is some interesting evidence that progress slows in large fields. I will link this in the description. It’s the study “Slowed Canonical Progress in Large Fields of Science” by Chu and Evans. They focus on the sciences, but the results may generalize to other fields as well. One of their findings is, and I quote, “When the number of papers published per year in a scientific field grows large, citations flow disproportionately to already well‑cited papers. The list of most‑cited papers ossifies, new papers are unlikely ever to become highly cited, and when they do, it is not through a gradual, cumulative process of attention gathering, and newly published papers become unlikely to disrupt existing work.” These findings suggest that the progress of large scientific fields may be slowed, trapped in existing canon.

Now, if that’s right, and if that does generalize to philosophy as well, then we have the somewhat surprising result that by incentivizing philosophers to produce work beyond journal publications—and so by reducing the amount of time spent on journal publication—we might actually promote progress within journal publication. Fewer people publishing articles might be the best way to promote progress within that area. That’s just a suggestion. Again, that evidence is very unclear at the moment, I believe.

Anyway, the general point is that methods of public engagement do provide avenues for exploring genuinely novel ideas. Here are a couple of examples. One is from Oxford’s The Practical Ethics Blog, the post “Why Philosophers Should Write More Accessibly.” This post introduced a new concept of epistemic injustice called “respondent injustice.” That concept could have been worked into an academic article, but it was presented on a blog, and it’s still a new idea and a new argument. Other examples, taken from my own channel, include a video on the philosophy of rainbows in which I give an empiricist account of rainbows, serving as a response to Bas van Fraassen, and a video on the incoherence of morality, the first part of which presents my own moral incoherence argument. I don’t think either of these ideas is publishable in their current form, and I don’t think I’ll ever bother to shape them up to make them publishable. Still, I think these are contributions that expand the frontier; they present new ideas in the same way journal articles are supposed to.

From my interview with economist and physicist Prof. Robin Hanson: “Academia’s main social role is credentialing impressive associations. Academia talks as if its main product were intellectual progress or insight, but plausibly its main actual product is prestige. There’s a huge demand for prestige, and they seem to be successfully supplying that demand.”

Prof. Robin Hanson believes one should replace narrative peer judgment with long‑horizon prediction markets (or other “information prizes”) that pay out if work is still judged valuable in 50–200 years. This is an interesting proposal, but I can see issues such as hyperbolic discounting and the fact that “valuable” is operationally undefined. He may have responses to these, though, as he’s incredibly sharp and well‑read.

Thomas Gieryn (1983) has a term called boundary‑work. This is something I’ve only come across recently. Boundary-work is where one emphasizes that “real” science is what they do, and casts the dissenters as “pseudo” or “deviant” practitioners to be excluded from legitimate science. It’s not enough to dispassionately find faults / no-go theorems being violated / contradiction with experiment. Instead, connotations of debasement and degradation accompany the denunciative denotations.

Essentially, Gieryn found that it consists of the so‑called in‑group (“we are serious scientists with standards”) and denigrates the out‑group (those who flout our norms). Of course, I’m aware that even my own delineation here of The Fringe vs. The Cringe vs. etc. is itself a boundary! Such bounds seem to be inevitable. The issue is the function of each, and whether the attitudes some of these clusters have for one another are productive / counterproductive. What Phillips & Zuckerman (2001) found is the interesting observation is that the “boundary policing” tends to not be generated from people who are existing tenured professors. This is decidedly unexpected because you would think the most push back would be from the most credentialed people. The reason that readily comes to mind is that those who are tenured are concerned with more important matters than commenting on speculative theories; this is true. However, this isn’t the sole reason. The other reason is that it’s actually in the incentives for people who are not tenured academics to perform the boundary policing in order to signal that they are a part of what is within whatever boundary. To put it simply, an alternative method of accumulating academic cred is to formulate a crackpot index and to designate others as being it.

Thus, The Hinge isn’t causing any of these boundary issues at all! It’s more like a certain cluster, let’s say The Unhinged, who want to be seen as a part of The Hinge do the boundary work to pronounce that they’re defenders. It’s also understandable as the immune system of not wanting that contagion effect referenced earlier, of course.

Those perceived as outsiders have the boundary enforced on them (“you’re not one of us, so your opinions don’t count”), whereas insiders or allies are given leeway to roam intellectually. Again, these don’t just seem to be mere dispassionate, rational assessments of theories / propositions. I’ve observed that perceived political alignment also matters for how much someone is shot down. It’s positioned as if it’s theory obliteration, but it seems more like the theory is collateral damage, with the intended target being something else.

This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.


Subscribe
I offer the above observations for what I believe to be a more fruitful and accurate classification than the traditional “in = good” and “out = crank”. Of course, reasonable people disagree about these characterizations, culpability, causes, and consequences.

TLDR: I don’t like short tweetable chunks, so you should read the entire essay above but if I had to truncate it into something fashionable it would be: Fundamental physics research is like a manifold with boundary, but some want to think it’s a closed manifold. ∂M impinges. The tangent space is fringe. The disconnected component is cringe. What unhinges isn’t ∈ M but wants to be, and indicates by being some function which takes {M} → {M - ∂M}.

I want to hear from you in the Substack comment section below. I read each and every response.

The Cringe vs. The Fringe vs. Those That Impinge
Observations and delineations on when "cranky" is a strict superset of "crank"
CURT JAIMUNGAL
SEP 07, 2025

There’s a bias on YouTube: if you have some novel “outsider” theory, it’s generally seen as considerably positive, and those who represent “the academy” (whatever that means) are portrayed as ossifying fools who don’t recognize what’s new. This is unfair. Not all work in the sciences needs to be “revolutionary.” Even if that were the case, the original idea being proposed isn’t revolutionary to begin with; it’s tentative and conjectural.

On the other hand, those with original proposals primarily become intertwined with the pejorative of “crackpots.” They’re seen as narcissists suffering from Dunning‑Kruger, obsessed with a single idea, attention‑seeking, sour‑grapes, queue‑jumping interlopers who don’t know the physics, podcast entertainers rather than scientists, and mavericks who undermine scientific integrity with their often ill‑intentioned, self‑delusional egotism.

Not all those positing new‑fangled results are maltreated revolutionaries. Similarly, not all are “crackpots” (a derisive term I’m not a fan of, as derision actually contributes to an anti‑science sentiment, since at minimum, hostile approaches trigger opposition, while beliefs remain woefully unchanged. See Song et al. (2018) and Van’t Riet et al. (2017).)

Many people ask me some variation of this: “Curt… How has Theories of Everything changed your worldview / beliefs? You’ve spoken to 200+ professors in various fields… Do you, Curt, have a personal theory of everything?”

Well, outside of the “cringe physics” joke called SCHLONG Theory, the answer is no. I don’t have answers. I don’t have proposals. What I do have, though, are a series of observations I’d like to share.

Share

Concerning the YouTube channel, people tune in to listen to the cognoscenti; not me. The guests are the ones with actual acumen, views, and justifications for their views, etc. They’re like an electron, with the properties of charge, spin, and mass, etc.

Asking what my views are would be treating me like an electron. I’m nowhere near the level of any of the people I’ve interviewed. Instead of an electron, the channel is more suitably characterized as an electric field. For instance, I see the movement of electrons. I may change an electron’s state from one position to another or from one spin to another, etc., so that it can be viewed or comprehended more palatably, etc.

NOTE: I did not say the electron field… that would be God.

You can ask what the charge and mass of an electron are, but it’s a category error to ask what the charge or mass of the electric field is. It’s a different beast entirely. Thus, instead of my own theories, what I have are observations.

Much of work in the sciences is about refinements and distinctions. That is to say, concepts we used to think were univocal have become further delineated. You can see examples of this when it comes to consciousness, where you have phenomenal consciousness, access consciousness, etc. We used to call something nucleons, then refined to protons and neutrons made of different quarks, etc. Progress is made via unification, yes, but on the other hand (like the above examples) progress is made when something you thought was “the same” is actually seen as multiple distinguished phenomena.

I think what’s occurring in our modern YouTube discourse is a collapsing of discrepancies to “one thing,” with that thing being “crackpot” (much like one’s mom calls every gaming console Nintendo). Let me propose a different taxonomy, along with the concomitant family resemblances and tests to discern the difference.

The academy (again, whatever that means) is usually seen as the “Orthodox.” This is quite foolish, since there are plenty of tenured professors who have views that go steeply against the majority of their colleagues. For the sake of this article, I will call the stereotypical refractory member of the Orthodox by a different name: The Hinge.

Then there is what is not a part of The Hinge. Often this is merely called “crackpot,” but let’s split it into three:

The Cringe
The Fringe
Those That Impinge
…there's also The Unhinged (explained later)
“The Cringe” is what most would strongly associate with “crackpottery” (again, a term I dislike because of its counter‑productively contemptuous nature, and thus I’m using it in scare‑quotes).

The mistake is to think The Cringe is the full set.




TLDR: I’ll get into more about these differentiating features as we continue, but the TLDR is that you can think of this as the distinction between the different answers to the question of “what is a vector?”:

The Cringe (or “crackpot”) would say “something with a magnitude and direction,” with position and “momentum” being an example.
The Fringe physicist may say “it’s an element of a vector space where a vector space is defined by satisfying the axioms of so‑and‑so,” and they’d still say position and momentum are examples.
Those That Impinge, however, will agree with the axiomatic definition of a vector space but note that position is a point in a manifold, and momentum is a covector defined via the fiber derivative (ie, Legendre map). If they’ve had enough wine, perhaps they’d say something fancy about the terminal object of Vect_k.
This is the highly compressed “rule of thumb” napkin version of this distinction.

Thanks for reading! This post is public so feel free to share it.

Share

Some Disclaimers…

To be clear, I’m not claiming that there are zero problems with any of those in the “heterodox” in terms of their theories. I’m not claiming that people should stop what they’re doing and work on their theories. I’m not claiming that I endorse them as being true, especially since they virtually all contradict one another. They can’t all be true. I’m not claiming that those in the prevailing avenues like loop quantum gravity or string theory etc. are incorrect in their approaches.

Do I think “the academy is broken yo!”? No. Broken means what, specifically? And relative to what, specifically? And is it all of the “academy”? Just a subfield? Or a subfield within that? I don’t subscribe to the “broken” thesis, nor do I subscribe to the “we’re in crisis” thesis. I would love for an interventionalist, longitudinal study to be conducted, and I would happily consult with such a study’s conductor on how we can have objective precise measures on these subjective imprecise claims.

This disclaimer may seem completely unnecessary to ~95% of people who read this. There may, however, be a subset who thinks that unless one collapses all these distinctions down to “crackpot”, this is some back‑door manner of saying the “establishment” (whatever that means) is wrong, or that there’s some major “crisis” (a word I dislike) that the academy is ignoring via gate-keeping. Let me be clear: I don’t believe any of this! I personally like and value “gate-keeping!” Virtually everything needs a gate / boundary (your skin is a productive example of one). I don’t believe there is a crisis, and I don’t believe that there is not a crisis. I’m agnostic on this, and I would want to know what the specific definition would be and what studies would demonstrate there is / isn’t, that aren’t merely correlational but causal, etc.

What follows are my present deliberations, of course subject to change as they do regularly. I’ll be providing no “shoulds” in this essay and, in place of a normative stance that would require plenty of information, counter‑arguments, rebuttals to those, investigations with historians of science, thinking through consequences, and looking through studies and conducting them, etc. Thus, this is not rigorous argumentation. I will instead provide observations. These observations are of how different aggregations are more aptly aggregated, as well as how these groups interact with / encroach on / view one another.

NOTE: Why this Cringe / Fringe / Impinge terminology, nominally? As I mentioned, it fits better than mere “crank” vs. “intransigent insider,” or something like “heterodox vs. orthodox,” which are all terms each person defines differently anyhow. The Hinge, however, has literal hinges because they have office doors on campus. Those That Impinge are those that go against or theoretically collide. The Fringe is self‑explanatory. The Cringe, on the other hand, is something I apologize for because it’s just too straightforward a rhyme for me to pass up, even though I’m violating my own rules of decorum by this insignia. Forgive me!

…With that out of the way, let’s get to it.

What We Can Learn From Philosophers…

There’s a philosopher named Kane Baker and he has a video on philosophy vs. public interaction where many of his thoughts echo the sentiments I’ve noticed expressed by other physicists:

There’s a good reason philosophers don’t do enough of [YouTube videos, podcasts, etc.]. Philosophy is an academic discipline, and academic success is measured by strict standards. The primary (and perhaps the single) criterion, aside from networking and luck, is publishing articles in journals and books that expand the discipline’s frontiers. Those works aren’t written for laypeople; they’re often incomprehensible without specialized training and interest only a handful of specialists. The intended audience of journal articles and scholarly books is specialists in the same field, and that’s pretty much all that matters for an academic career. That’s what you’ve got to do: publish in specific journals or produce books in that style.

Something I adore about philosophers that I didn’t discover until fairly recently is “the principle of charity.” This means a philosopher is trained to interpret a speaker’s statements in the most rational way possible and, for any argument, to consider the strongest interpretation. For me, however, that requirement is too stringent, and you can instead relax it to what I call “the method of veridical representation.” That simply means double‑checking whether what’s being disproved truly represents the speaker’s views.

There’s no established term for this, which is why I coined “the method of veridical representation,” and it’s something I aim to do on the podcast. You’ll frequently hear me say, “Okay, just a moment… are you saying X, or are you saying Y?” or “If A is true in your model, wouldn’t that entail that B is true? Why or why not?” This ensures my model of someone isn’t a phantasm but actually reflects what the interlocutor believes. Only recently did I learn that, in philosophy, it’s considered a common practice of intellectual rigor to email someone prior to critiquing them, to ensure the critique addresses what they actually intend, and not some doppelganger.

I first noticed method with a critique of Nancy Cartwright’s Dapped World, where the critic began by thanking Nancy Cartwright directly for her contributions / clarifications to the critique. That’s insane! This sort of private correspondence where one demonstrates that they’re not merely debunking but extending / clarifying, prior to publication, is quite wild and something that I didn’t know was the norm in philosophy.

The above disposition was also echoed by someone else on Substack, who I don’t know, but showed up on my feed:

Jessie Ewesmont: “Laypeople are almost always surprised to hear how common it is for philosophers to email or talk to each other and be like: ‘Hey, I’m writing a paper about why your view is wrong. Can you confirm I haven’t misrepresented it in my gloss here? Also, any cutting objections you want to raise so I can rethink my paper to account for it before Reviewer #2 puts me on blast for missing such an obvious objection?’ This is part of why presenting at conferences is so important. It’s a chance to get your work heard by a wide variety of smart people, who will then provide these remarks in Q&A.”

That’s a standard I absolutely adore.

You can see where I’m going with this. It’s not like this in physics. Instead, it’s more common to collapse the separations of The Cringe / The Fringe / Those That Impinge.

Let’s clarify how one can tell where one stands…

This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.


Subscribe



Proficiency Tests and Family Resemblance…

What I’ve observed is that these groups can be largely classified by the following:

The Cringe

Characterized by those who write in Microsoft Word and are essentially the sole reason the caps lock button stays in business
They tend to be fans of picture proofs, circles / spirals / diagrams on paper
They tend to believe (mostly) everyone except them is corrupt, even disrespecting others inside The Cringe
They tend to be able to write down Schrödinger’s equation, though they most likely would not be able to derive the ground state of an electron confined to an infinite square well in non-relativistic quantum mechanics
When they email you, it tends to be private messages one-on-one
The Fringe

They tend to be part of long chains, with others from The Hinge who regret that their email address is public. Satan’s greatest spawn is the CC feature.
They too tend to write in Microsoft Word, yes, but are at least aware that LaTeX is preferred
They can manipulate Schrödinger’s equation just fine
They tend to be obsessed with one or two unconventional historical figures who were silenced and see themselves as continuing their work.
They tend to dislike natural units and see that as concealing the “true” physics
They think (mostly) experiments matter and tinker away, perhaps even finding obscure anomalous effects but not knowing the theory behind them. Their experimental setups have coils abound.
They can list two or three different solutions to general relativity and prove they satisfy the EFE.
They’re also often obsessed with alternative forms of Maxwell’s equations and gravity. This is likely due to the energy scales involved, since the EM field is readily toyed with in one’s garage using tabletop experiments, and they either conduct such experiments themselves or are heavily influenced by those who do.
Tend to be engineers rather than theoreticians
They also tend to be obsessed with the concept of zero‑point energy.
An example would be the extended electrodynamics crowd. They can manipulate curl, divergence, and write PDEs, yes. They’re doing something mathematical, but they may think that all that matters are the E and M fields and write down an equation like this:

without seeing why this breaks gauge invariance (or why breaking gauge invariance is even a problem to begin with). And yes, what I wrote here doesn’t even work dimensionally (you have a 3‑form equal to a 1‑form), but they’d tend not to notice that immediately.

Those That Impinge (Proficiency Test) 

These are people who can answer the below questions with ease, scoring 80 % or greater. For the remaining 20 % they’d at least know roughly what it means and how to find the answer without the aid of an LLM.

Do you recognize all of these Top 30 List of Theoretical Physics Topics?
Spin(4) is isomorphic to what other groups, and how so exactly?
You get Einstein’s conception of special relativistic energy by doing what (exactly) to the Newtonian one, and if they can’t be analogized as such, then why not? How does this extend (or not extend) to the general‑relativistic case?
Can you explain what the standard model Lagrangian terms all represent / their importance / what would happen if you removed some term, etc.?
Can you explain promotion of classical observables on phase space to quantum operators? How do you deal with ambiguities?
Why is the large N limit so relevant to AdS / CFT?
What is a generating functional? How is it different from a generating function?
What’s at least one reason saying quantum field theory is about “fields” is misleading?
Is gauge fixing a problem? Why or why not?
How do you formulate quantum mechanics equivalently with real numbers (and no reference to complex numbers)?
What’s S‑duality?
What’s the problem with naive discretization of spacetime given the symmetries of electrodynamics?
What’s a cotangent bundle?
How is quintessence related to the Bianchi identities (problems with a variable cosmological constant), and why must it be a scalar field if our universe is isotropic?
What’s the renormalization group?
Of course, these lists are best when dynamic because anyone can overfit any particular test by sheer memorization of answers. Thus, you can ask any physics professor to look at the above questions and then generate, for each class, a few new questions that people within that class would be able to answer if they possess a genuine understanding rather than purely committing answers to memory.

The above deals with proficiency, and I believe The Cringe and The Fringe are classified in your mind without issue. Those That Impinge, on the other hand, require some more explication.

Here's the family resemblance that unifies them over and above technical aptitude:

Those That Impinge (Family Resemblance)

They tend to disbelieve one or more of the foundational pillars of the mainline approaches. Perhaps extra spatial dimensions, perhaps inflation, perhaps something to do with unitarity or the consistency of quantum mechanics itself.
They’re often not fans of the culture of The Hinge, while respecting the theories of The Hinge.
They tend to have PhDs or even professorships in the same field or closely adjacent fields.
They also tend to have at least one extremely hypothetically hazardous concept (for instance, Penrose with his consciousness / uncomputability / quantum link).
They tend to find the gauge groups of the Standard Model extremely peculiar. It bothers them.
They seem to be more concerned with the 4 spacetime dimensions of our world whereas The Hinge is more comfortable with exploring toy models as avenues for new insights
They tend to construe “orthodox” fundamental physics (whatever that means) as having long‑standing beliefs that have been unsuccessful in some rooted manner:
For instance, here’s Neil Turok from 2010: “I think the last 20 or 30 years we’ve seen huge bandwagons in physics. String theory is another bandwagon. By and large these bandwagons have failed (well not by and large, totally they have failed, they have failed to deliver).”
Actually, when I was speaking to Roger Penrose, he didn’t even want to talk about the state of modern fundamental physics because it would “upset him too much” and ruin his dinner. This was in front of Matt O’Dowd from PBS Spacetime.



They tend not to consider the quantity of arXiv papers (or the accumulation of citations) as an indication of a field’s health.
They tend to be fond of using words like “stagnation” to describe the state of fundamental physics research—or some variant of it—and claim that the issue isn’t individual but somehow “systemic.”
For instance, David Deutsch just yesterday said Conjecture Institute podcast: “One of the problems is that the whole system is institutionally biased against fundamental innovation, and that’s not anyone’s fault. It’s simply because the method of choosing recipients goes through a bureaucratic process where the people judging it are asked to make a judgment on things they can’t possibly know.”
Broadly speaking, they’re concerned with foundational questions rather than mathematically‑inspired model‑building .
For instance, George Ellis and Joe Silk wrote about this in a 2014 Nature commentary titled Defend the Integrity of Physics. They were concerned that some theorists were willing to abandon empirical testing and declared that this trend wasn’t something nice.
They tend to be snickered at by their colleagues off‑air.
For instance, I’ve heard both graduate students and other professors say Penrose is “off his rocker.” This is a verbatim quote, twice, from two different people, not counting the other phrases. It’s one thing to find faults A, B and C with a proposal; it’s another to disparage the person.
Importantly, those who impinge are not people who believe they have a simple two‑page proof of the Riemann hypothesis or the Yang–Mills mass gap, nor do they think Oneness is the answer to the universe, nor that there's a rank‑3 tensor Love field. Not yet, at least!
There are also rules that Those Who Impinge are not supposed to break: One is that you’re not supposed to call your theory a “theory of everything” (or anything close to grandiose).

Some people may say that all Stephen Wolfram needs to do is publish on the arXiv, but even if he does, the criticisms don’t stop. Suppose he does; then they’ll say, “Well, it needs to be in a peer‑reviewed journal.” Suppose he does; then they’ll say, “Well, it’s not in a respectable peer‑reviewed journal.” Suppose he does, then they’ll say, “Well, the citation count is trifling.” Suppose it’s substantive, then they’ll say, “Well, it’s only cited by people who actually don’t matter.” And on and on, until at some point, they’re implicitly admitting that unless they get the go‑ahead from those at the top of the hierarchy (effectively knighting it), they themselves won’t publicly suggest legitimate new work.

Understandably, it’s easier to catch a late train going to a socially acceptable place and say “sorry,” than it is to buy a ticket early for a train which hinders one’s career prospects.

The motto is to always put something forward as a series of tentative results, and it will be better received, even if it’s the exact same content. Thus, what’s being objected to isn’t always the inside (merit‑worthy or otherwise), but the wrapper. In other words, we think, “Don’t judge a book by its cover, but please do judge a theory by the pride of its proposer.”

Those That Impinge also tend to be on the older side. It may have something to do with being publicly grouped here as an Impinger not being super‑fantastic for their career prospects; thus they already have income elsewhere outside a tenured position and aren’t actively seeking one. If they were actively seeking a position, they’d have to be much more careful about the aforementioned “wrapping” of their ideas than about the ideas themselves.

Something I didn’t know until recently was that collaborating publicly with a controversial figure lowers your own perceived credibility (a sort of “contagion” effect measured in lab studies of reputational risk; see Mongeon & Larivière (2016), Costly Collaborations).

Now, it’s worth disclaiming explicitly here once more: observations on culture, incentives, and dispositions are an entirely separate matter from the objective scientific merit of any given proposal. The former should in no way be mistaken for an endorsement of the latter.

With that out of the way, let’s consider the dispositional gulf…

The Epistemic Divide…

Throughout the above, I have focused on the differences between the three groups, but for now I’d like to focus on the difference between the third and the fourth—namely, between those hard working on the established theories (The Hinge) versus those that aren’t (Those That Impinge). Yes, they differ in terms of research direction, but they also differ dispositionally.

Those That Impinge tend to have near forceful conviction in their ideas, whereas, for the most part, those who aren’t (The Hinge) view themselves as participants in a process of accumulative knowledge‑building, where that knowledge may or may not ultimately relate to the real physical world. This process is thought of like a roulette wheel.

I know this first‑hand: if you were to ask them, “Would you bet money that your research is actually going to lead to a breakthrough / be proven to be on the correct track?” what do you think they would say? My experience is that they wouldn’t be willing to bet money on it, at least not large sums proportionate to the odds even if it’s according to their own stated odds.

The logic is understandable, of course. It’s something approximating “No one knows the future, let alone the future in fundamental physics, so let’s each research what we each think is promising and have the entire enterprise of the academy be akin to an investor who holds a diversified portfolio of different bets (most of which will go nowhere, but some of which will, hopefully, pay off large at some undetermined point in the future).”

This distributed approach (thousands of researchers making additive contributions without the strong individual conviction to bet large sums of their own cash) produced quantum electrodynamics, then the standard model, gravitational‑wave detection, and virtually every major physics breakthrough since 1950! This means that this portfolio model, and peer-review with its error-correcting mechanisms, serve major functions that the lone Impinger approach can’t.

Yet this feels like an unsatisfying answer, not just to you reading this… but to them as well. Something is off. It seems like the soul is lost in the transition from being K‑selected to R‑selected. This is true even in companies. In the beginning, what matters most is who your co‑founder is. That’s when you have a small family in your group—maybe two or three people. What matters after that is who your first employee is, and then, as your company grows, who your first investors are, etc. However, once the company reaches the level where you have hundreds or even thousands of employees, you become R‑selected and you’ve automated away your soul. This innate soul / heart that we sense from the figures who drew us to this field in the first place (people like Einstein, Schrödinger, etc.) is what gets automated away once the enterprise becomes R‑selected in that particular subfield. This is likely a major contributor behind why AI “art” (or AI output in general) isn’t considered to have heart. It may just be that automation devours spirit.

Of course, all of the above observations should be caveated with addenda like “for the most part,” because there are exceptions everywhere. (I think this is my first “should” in this essay.)

An interesting consideration is that those with little certainty that what they are pursuing is correct are generally takers of money. They get money in order to make their contributions. That’s good! People should be paid to follow their flame! (I think this is my second “should” in this essay!) On the other hand, for Those That Impinge, it’s the opposite. They believe in their theories with perhaps a standard deviation or more higher conviction than a generic Hinger, so much so that they themselves pay to do their research! Garrett Lisi, for instance, pays. He does not get paid. Garrett had to get his money independently. Stephen Wolfram pays to do his research. One may say he “puts his money where his mouth is.” Those That Impinge also pay with their intellectual credibility.

Something that is considerably difficult for people outside the academy to appreciate is that there’s “alternate theory latitude” and then there’s “academic cred.” In order to get that latitude, you have to spend your academic cred. To spend that cred, you have to earn that academic cred. A PhD in the relevant field is the minimum way to do so, but even that is just nickels and dimes. A tenured position is an honest way to earn such academic cred, and it’s of course better if it’s tenured at a “respectable” university, or even better, the IAS, etc. There’s an unspoken hierarchy.

Yes, this can be “polluted,” as David Deutsch pointed out yesterday, but perhaps that's the exception. One wants to omit as much foolish work as possible and produce as much fruitful work as possible. Academic cred tends to be incentive‑aligned in this admirable direction.

Every approach has failure modes. For instance, with the self‑funded Impingers, if you’ve made a panoply of money, you can just spend your way to research rather than having to “earn it” through traditional means such as peer validation. The wealthy person can continue to put out nonsensical research without the same fear of reputational stakes. There are problems all around.

Who Cares About The Public? They’re Mostly Idiots, Right?…

Interestingly, even though science as a whole serves the public, there are zero “public engagement” requirements for scientists. This is beneficial in a sense because public engagement is its own separate skill that would otherwise detract from the difficult, deep work of diligently pursuing your subject in the lab, at the blackboard, collaborating, networking, interrogating yourself and other fields, conducting studies, etc. And that’s where the bulk of scientific work is birthed. That’s not the interesting part. The interesting part is that academics who succeed publicly—say, Brian Cox, Neil deGrasse Tyson, or anyone else who becomes popular—are spending their academic cred on public engagement. They’re not earning it. This is supported by the literature (see Watermeyer (2015)).

In other words, you’ll often hear, “Yeah, but so‑and‑so isn’t a ‘true’ scientist. They’re not ‘highly respected’ in the field.” Those sentiments aren’t confined to comment sections or Reddit threads; I’ve heard working researchers voice them about colleagues who receive public attention. Not that what science communicators do is of little value—indeed, it’s of tremendous value! Indeed, even the scientists who consider themselves the true contributors were inspired by the more public‑facing people; the popularizers are, at minimum, the soil from which the scientific academy grows. But something you’ve probably noticed, especially if you’re an academic, is that many scholars are blinded to what isn’t academically valued or “prestigious.” Many tie much of their personal worth to prestige, and anything that reduces that prestige (such as becoming popular or not producing work respected by peers) is not only avoided but generally looked down upon. I’ve heard that accusation of “yeah, he’s great with the public but he’s not highly respected in the field,” thrown at Brian Greene, and Brian, in my opinion (not that he needs my opinion), is a fantastic, formidable physicist! He’s highly respected by me for the twin prongs of his work with Plesser and his wonderfully articulate and his charitably warm cordiality. There’s basically no one who possesses all these qualities simultaneously except him.

This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.


Subscribe
This pattern appears across many fields. Last week I watched the OJ Simpson’s Netflix documentary, and one of the lawyers lamented another lawyer for being a “celebrity lawyer.” They noted that lawyers who receive ample media attention tend to be looked down upon, not because of the quality of their work or whether they uphold justice, but simply because the more spotlight falls on them, the more they’re resented by others who feel they deserve less attention.

You can see this even with the term “public intellectual.” It’s a dirty word in The Hinge. You’ll encounter it even when the public intellectual in question was revered by peers and students prior to fame. The only public intellectuals we can laud as being of quality are those no longer practicing, such as Chomsky or Russell.

Hobbes wrote about this phenomenon succinctly several centuries ago: “Competition of praise inclineth men to a reverence of antiquity. For men contend with the living, not with the dead; hoping the glory of the latter obscures the former.”

Then there’s Kane Baker, who said in 2023:

There are certainly philosophers doing public‑engagement work, especially since COVID, with more online presence, YouTube channels, and podcasts. That’s wonderful, but none of this work is rewarded with better career prospects. We’re encouraged to do it, yet it’s seen as altruistic. To be clear, this YouTube channel has been harmful to my academic career. If I had spent my time creating scholarly articles instead of this content, I’d be in a far stronger position. The time I spend on this channel is completely useless for furthering an academic career, and I’m not special—any philosopher producing public‑facing content is, from a career standpoint, wasting time.

Science, like philosophy, values publication of articles that expand the discipline’s frontiers and are accessible only to highly trained specialists. It’s “publish or perish,” but in a very narrow sense—only a specific kind of publication matters, and that’s the case in science as well.

Scientists value this exclusively because their work has direct practical applications that interest the public. Discovering new mechanisms for DNA methylation could lead to medical therapies; a new technique for analyzing cosmic‑ray data can produce striking Milky Way images for books or TV, engaging the public. By compelling scientists to focus exclusively on expanding the discipline’s boundaries, we also achieve public engagement—public interest follows when theories have direct practical applications.

That’s not the case for philosophy. Expanding philosophy’s frontiers with specialist journal articles has no direct practical utility. Nobody outside academia has a reason to care. Philosophers won’t cure cancer or build particle accelerators, nor will they achieve convergence on theories that other disciplines can readily build upon, as computer engineers have done with quantum mechanics. Science embeds a public‑facing aspect that philosophy lacks.

The suggestion, then, is to change incentives so that public‑engagement work becomes relevant to career success. Journal publications should still matter, but criteria should expand to count projects like this channel. Obviously, this is a very self‑serving position—or maybe it isn’t, because I don’t know. I may not pursue academia, and I’m not that bothered; there are other things I can do with my life. But I care about philosophy as a discipline. I want people to be more interested in it, and I think the way to achieve that is to change the criteria for success.

There’s no need to change philosophy’s content. Philosophers can continue doing what they’ve always done. I’ve found that topics expected to interest only specialists can engage laypersons when presented accessibly.

Much of what Kane said I’ve also found to be the case. Consider feeding into an LLM one of the transcripts from one of the most popular videos on the Theories of Everything channel, say with Claudia de Rham or Ted Jackobson, etc., and ask it, “At what level is this aimed at, given the material? Is it high schoolers? Is it a general undergrad?” You’ll find that most often it’s for a PhD‑level audience in the same relevant field, yet they have 100,000s of views. This is the specialty of the channel, and it’s toward this that I aim.

To close the loop, it may be that these differing epistemic stances (portfolio diversification versus concentrated conviction) are distinct, yes, but are potentially complementary in fundamental physics. It’s not about “which is correct.”

It also may very well be that if you start thinking of yourself as a lottery ticket, then you view your colleagues as a lottery ticket. If that happens, your accountability is minimized, because who cares if what you’re personally pursuing is likely of little value? After all, the same applies to everyone else, and besides, this is just the “natural process.”… But perhaps in fundamental physics it’s not the natural process; perhaps it never was; perhaps it never should be. Perhaps when you view yourself as an unlikely barcode, you view the general public as that as well. And perhaps that’s a horrible, unproductive, deleterious view of your brothers and sisters.

The Climbing Rules and Field Extension Closure…

Defenders of the university system portray science (and, in particular, the quest for a TOE) as the quest to scale a mountaintop. There’s an objective, singular peak that represents ultimate scientific truth. Publicly, there’s an emphasis on collective progress toward the apex, with the scientific community portrayed as cooperative climbers equipped with the necessary tools and knowledge to ascend.

The problem is that the tools of science are not necessarily the same as the tools of the academy. Science is concerned with being objectively correct, and the academy is concerned with that, yes, but also with ensuring you don’t step on the wrong toes, have grant acquisitions, that you achieve a certain citation count, that you’re invited to certain conferences, etc.

Just yesterday, Deutsch recounted meeting the committee member who approved his quantum‑computing grant: “I said if ‘I were to apply today under today's criteria would you have been able to give me the grant?’ The committee member replied, ‘No chance. No chance because you wouldn't have been able to fill out none of the boxes. Literally none.’”

To Deutsch and other Impingers, the community isn’t about scaling the mountain; it’s more akin to a regulated sport, imposing strict norms and methodologies (akin to climbers using regulated equipment and adhering to safety protocols).

On the other hand, there are people outside this established framework who employ unconventional methods, perhaps seen as irrational. Those That Impinge aren't tied to the same incentive structure. These outsiders are seen by the defenders as disregarding the communal rules and are portrayed as undermining the integrity of the scientific pursuit, but actually, these Impingers are undermining the integrity of the academic pursuit (and that's different). We resist integrating mavericks who can scale higher more quickly, dangerously. Free soloing isn't allowed.

The idea is that relaxing academic standards for one outsider risks a floodgate effect.

I think what else is happening is that when you have a finite field extension, you don’t just let in a single irrational root. If you append the square root of two to the rationals, it’s not just about appending the square root of two. You also have to append one plus the square root of two, three halves minus the square root of two, etc. To keep closure and consistency, you have to let in a slew of poppycock elements. When you let in one outsider, you open the floodgates.

Those That Impinge don’t (necessarily) play by the same rules. Why would The Hinge play chess with you if you’re allowed to move your pawn more than one space after the first move? Why would they play in the field extension when they can form a Galois group, keep their academic rational field fixed, and allow all those irrational people to merrily mix about themselves instead?

Another useful distinction is the philosophical difference between vehicle and object. A vehicle is the means by which something is achieved. The object is what’s being achieved (or the “referent”). I think what’s going on is that someone like Gregory Chaitin views the academy as a vehicle with the object being “science”. He may say that those that defend The Hinge may implicitly view it oppositely, with the academy as the object and science as the vehicle. That is, your answer to the following question determines if you lie in Those That Impinge or The Hinge:

Is science the goal, with academic employment / prestige serving as the vehicle toward it? Or is academic employment / prestige the goal, with science being the instrument toward it?




People Over Projects and Some Unhinged Notes…

David Deutsch recommends funding people (rather than projects) and doing so without conditions. I don’t know if this is the correct approach, and hopefully sometime soon I can speak with David Deutsch on the podcast about it.

His view does seem to be supported by a large‑scale study by Wu, Wang & Evans (2019), who analyzed 65+ million papers, patents, and software products from the 50s to the 2010s. They found that smaller teams tended to disrupt science and technology with new ideas, while larger teams tended to develop existing ones. Turns out even Nobel‑Prize‑winning papers had nearly three times as high a probability of being from small teams compared to the control group.

Y Combinator also runs on this “fund founders, not companies” mentality, so it’s not entirely foreign.

Deutsch caveats this with, “But I guess it’s not going to be feasible for all kinds of research because some kinds of research involve the collaboration of five people or 50 people, and then it’s extremely disadvantageous to have a hierarchy.” Again, the interview just launched yesterday, and the link is here.

I'd like to end with some more from Kane Baker on his views on if journals should be the sole method of furthering philosophy:

Journal publication is not the only way to develop new ideas. Indeed, the weight that’s given to such publications, the fact that we take this to be the only way of legitimately contributing new ideas, I think that might actually stifle creativity in some ways because journals can be quite conservative. There are several features, I think, of academic journals that might tend to stifle the development of new ideas. Here are some of them.

First of all, if you try to publish in a journal, you’re going to be required to address topics that are considered important or relevant, which is to say topics that professional philosophers happen to find interesting at the moment. You’re going to be limited, probably, by whatever the current philosophical fads are. You’re going to be forced to frame issues in terms of the tradition that has prevailed beforehand. I mean, just consider how, for decades, many philosophers in Western universities were very dismissive of work that was seen as continental. No doubt there are plenty of reasonable criticisms of continental philosophy, but it seems like it wasn’t really given a fair hearing. By placing a bit more emphasis on non‑peer‑reviewed work, we may make it easier for philosophers to overcome these kinds of biases and bring new ideas into the discourse.

Second, when you publish in journals, there’s a requirement that you demonstrate familiarity with the literature. In many ways, that’s a good thing. But what this means is that in practice, if you come up with a new idea, you have to respond to all of the major alternatives. This can take a lot of time. Maybe you don’t want to devote that much time to it. It would be a lot easier to just throw out the idea in a blog post, for instance. It could still be a genuinely new contribution, right? Even if you’re not in the mood for shaping something into the sort of article that could be published in a journal, you can still make a new contribution by putting the idea out there in some other way.

Finally, there is some interesting evidence that progress slows in large fields. I will link this in the description. It’s the study “Slowed Canonical Progress in Large Fields of Science” by Chu and Evans. They focus on the sciences, but the results may generalize to other fields as well. One of their findings is, and I quote, “When the number of papers published per year in a scientific field grows large, citations flow disproportionately to already well‑cited papers. The list of most‑cited papers ossifies, new papers are unlikely ever to become highly cited, and when they do, it is not through a gradual, cumulative process of attention gathering, and newly published papers become unlikely to disrupt existing work.” These findings suggest that the progress of large scientific fields may be slowed, trapped in existing canon.

Now, if that’s right, and if that does generalize to philosophy as well, then we have the somewhat surprising result that by incentivizing philosophers to produce work beyond journal publications—and so by reducing the amount of time spent on journal publication—we might actually promote progress within journal publication. Fewer people publishing articles might be the best way to promote progress within that area. That’s just a suggestion. Again, that evidence is very unclear at the moment, I believe.

Anyway, the general point is that methods of public engagement do provide avenues for exploring genuinely novel ideas. Here are a couple of examples. One is from Oxford’s The Practical Ethics Blog, the post “Why Philosophers Should Write More Accessibly.” This post introduced a new concept of epistemic injustice called “respondent injustice.” That concept could have been worked into an academic article, but it was presented on a blog, and it’s still a new idea and a new argument. Other examples, taken from my own channel, include a video on the philosophy of rainbows in which I give an empiricist account of rainbows, serving as a response to Bas van Fraassen, and a video on the incoherence of morality, the first part of which presents my own moral incoherence argument. I don’t think either of these ideas is publishable in their current form, and I don’t think I’ll ever bother to shape them up to make them publishable. Still, I think these are contributions that expand the frontier; they present new ideas in the same way journal articles are supposed to.

From my interview with economist and physicist Prof. Robin Hanson: “Academia’s main social role is credentialing impressive associations. Academia talks as if its main product were intellectual progress or insight, but plausibly its main actual product is prestige. There’s a huge demand for prestige, and they seem to be successfully supplying that demand.”

Prof. Robin Hanson believes one should replace narrative peer judgment with long‑horizon prediction markets (or other “information prizes”) that pay out if work is still judged valuable in 50–200 years. This is an interesting proposal, but I can see issues such as hyperbolic discounting and the fact that “valuable” is operationally undefined. He may have responses to these, though, as he’s incredibly sharp and well‑read.

Thomas Gieryn (1983) has a term called boundary‑work. This is something I’ve only come across recently. Boundary-work is where one emphasizes that “real” science is what they do, and casts the dissenters as “pseudo” or “deviant” practitioners to be excluded from legitimate science. It’s not enough to dispassionately find faults / no-go theorems being violated / contradiction with experiment. Instead, connotations of debasement and degradation accompany the denunciative denotations.

Essentially, Gieryn found that it consists of the so‑called in‑group (“we are serious scientists with standards”) and denigrates the out‑group (those who flout our norms). Of course, I’m aware that even my own delineation here of The Fringe vs. The Cringe vs. etc. is itself a boundary! Such bounds seem to be inevitable. The issue is the function of each, and whether the attitudes some of these clusters have for one another are productive / counterproductive. What Phillips & Zuckerman (2001) found is the interesting observation is that the “boundary policing” tends to not be generated from people who are existing tenured professors. This is decidedly unexpected because you would think the most push back would be from the most credentialed people. The reason that readily comes to mind is that those who are tenured are concerned with more important matters than commenting on speculative theories; this is true. However, this isn’t the sole reason. The other reason is that it’s actually in the incentives for people who are not tenured academics to perform the boundary policing in order to signal that they are a part of what is within whatever boundary. To put it simply, an alternative method of accumulating academic cred is to formulate a crackpot index and to designate others as being it.

Thus, The Hinge isn’t causing any of these boundary issues at all! It’s more like a certain cluster, let’s say The Unhinged, who want to be seen as a part of The Hinge do the boundary work to pronounce that they’re defenders. It’s also understandable as the immune system of not wanting that contagion effect referenced earlier, of course.

Those perceived as outsiders have the boundary enforced on them (“you’re not one of us, so your opinions don’t count”), whereas insiders or allies are given leeway to roam intellectually. Again, these don’t just seem to be mere dispassionate, rational assessments of theories / propositions. I’ve observed that perceived political alignment also matters for how much someone is shot down. It’s positioned as if it’s theory obliteration, but it seems more like the theory is collateral damage, with the intended target being something else.

Subscribe
I offer the above observations for what I believe to be a more fruitful and accurate classification than the traditional “in = good” and “out = crank”. Of course, reasonable people disagree about these characterizations, culpability, causes, and consequences.

TLDR: I don’t like short tweetable chunks, so you should read the entire essay above but if I had to truncate it into something fashionable it would be: Fundamental physics research is like a manifold with boundary, but some want to think it’s a closed manifold. ∂M impinges. The tangent space is fringe. The disconnected component is cringe. What unhinges isn’t ∈ M but wants to be, and indicates by being some function which takes {M} → {M - ∂M}.

I want to hear from you in the Substack comment section below. I read each and every response.

A great effort, Curt. I just read the whole thing, and congratulation you on keeping a solid thread focused on being clear and comprehensive… certainly two of your practiced strengths.

I’ll limit my reactions here to one point, as someone who aspires to impinge… there was a time when the only way to have access to the prerequisites for any academically established field was to spend hours searching through journals in libraries, attending graduate level classes, being mentored by a handful of pillars in the field, participating in post-doc research and hypothesizing boundaries of the field which could be pushed in specific incremental ways.

Now that I’m retired, I can spend my time watching MIT online courses, fill in gaps in my number theory (or whatever) with Brilliant, and yes, have LLMs explain details where the vocabulary is over my head… and from there start to first make sense of what is established, and start speculating on what may come next.

But on your scale, I can never reasonably qualify for anything but cringe, or waiting outside the fringe cafe to get a sentence or two out before the person ignoring me turns a corner. But mostly I learn so that I can understand for myself … and for the record listen to many of your interviews all the way through.
