Something Rotten in the State of QED? A Careful Look at Critique, Sociology, and the Limits of Modern Physics
 Jean Louis Van Belle   Mathematics, Philosophy of science, Physics, quantum mechanics  December 1, 2025  7 Minutes
Every few years, a paper comes along that stirs discomfort — not because it is wrong, but because it touches a nerve.
Oliver Consa’s “Something is rotten in the state of QED” is one of those papers.

It is not a technical QED calculation.
It is a polemic: a long critique of renormalization, historical shortcuts, convenient coincidences, and suspiciously good matches between theory and experiment. Consa argues that QED’s foundations were improvised, normalized, mythologized, and finally institutionalized into a polished narrative that glosses over its original cracks.

This is an attractive story.
Too attractive, perhaps.
So instead of reacting emotionally — pro or contra — I decided to dissect the argument with a bit of help.

At my request, an AI language model (“Iggy”) assisted in the analysis. Not to praise me. Not to flatter Consa. Not to perform tricks.
Simply to act as a scalpel: cold, precise, and unafraid to separate structure from rhetoric.

This post is the result.

1. What Consa gets right (and why it matters)
Let’s begin with the genuinely valuable parts of his argument.

a) Renormalization unease is legitimate

Dirac, Feynman, Dyson, and others really did express deep dissatisfaction with renormalization. “Hocus-pocus” was not a joke; it was a confession.

Early QED involved:

cutoff procedures pulled out of thin air,
infinities subtracted by fiat,
and the philosophical hope that “the math will work itself out later.”
It did work out later — to some extent — but the conceptual discomfort remains justified. I share that discomfort. There is something inelegant about infinities everywhere.

b) Scientific sociology is real

The post-war era centralized experimental and institutional power in a way physics had never seen. Prestige, funding, and access influenced what got published and what was ignored. Not a conspiracy — just sociology.

Consa is right to point out that real science is messier than textbook linearity.

c) The g–2 tension is real

The ongoing discrepancy between experiment and the Standard Model is not fringe. It is one of the defining questions in particle physics today.

On these points, Consa is a useful corrective:
he reminds us to stay honest about historical compromises and conceptual gaps.

2. Where Consa overreaches
But critique is one thing; accusation is another.

Consa repeatedly moves from:

“QED evolved through trial and error”
to
“QED is essentially fraud.”
This jump is unjustified.

a) Messiness ≠ manipulation

Early QED calculations were ugly. They were corrected decades later. Experiments did shift. Error bars did move.

That is simply how science evolves.

The fact that a 1947 calculation doesn’t match a 1980 value is not evidence of deceit — it is evidence of refinement. Consa collapses that distinction.

b) Ignoring the full evidence landscape

He focuses almost exclusively on:

the Lamb shift,
the electron g–2,
the muon g–2.
Important numbers, yes — but QED’s experimental foundation is vastly broader:

scattering cross-sections,
vacuum polarization,
atomic spectra,
collider data,
running of α, etc.
You cannot judge an entire theory on two or three benchmarks.

c) Underestimating theoretical structure

QED is not “fudge + diagrams.”
It is constrained by:

Lorentz invariance,
gauge symmetry,
locality,
renormalizability.
Even if we dislike the mathematical machinery, the structure is not arbitrary.

So: Consa reveals real cracks, but then paints the entire edifice as rotten.
That is unjustified.

3. A personal aside: the Zitter Institute and the danger of counter-churches
For a time, I was nominally associated with the Zitter Institute — a loosely organized group exploring alternatives to mainstream quantum theory, including zitterbewegung-based particle models.

I now would like to distance myself.

Not because alternative models are unworthy — quite the opposite. But because I instinctively resist:

strong internal identity,
suspicion of outsiders,
rhetorical overreach,
selective reading of evidence,
and occasional dogmatism about their own preferred models.
If we criticize mainstream physics for ad hoc factors, we must be brutal about our own.
Alternative science is not automatically cleaner science.

4. Two emails from 2020: why good scientists can’t always engage
This brings me to two telling exchanges from 2020 with outstanding experimentalists: Prof. Randolf Pohl (muonic hydrogen) and Prof. Ashot Gasparian (PRad).

Both deserve enormous respect, and I won’t reveal the email exchanges because of respect, GDPR rules or whatever).
Both email exchanges revealed the true bottleneck in modern physics to me — it is not intelligence, not malice, but sociology and bandwidth.

a) Randolf Pohl: polite skepticism, institutional gravity

Pohl was kind but firm:

He saw the geometric relations I proposed as numerology.
He questioned applicability to other particles.
He emphasized the conservatism of CODATA logic.
Perfectly valid.
Perfectly respectable.
But also… perfectly bound by institutional norms.

His answer was thoughtful — and constrained.
(Source: ChatGPT analysis of emails with Prof Dr Pohl)

b) Ashot Gasparian: warm support, but no bandwidth

Gasparian responded warmly:

“Certainly your approach and the numbers are interesting.”
But: “We are very busy with the next experiment.”
Also perfectly valid.
And revealing:
even curious, open-minded scientists cannot afford to explore conceptual alternatives.

Their world runs on deadlines, graduate students, collaborations, grants.

(Source: ChatGPT analysis of emails with Prof Dr Pohl)

The lesson

Neither professor dismissed the ideas because they were nonsensical.
They simply had no institutional space to pursue them.

That is the quiet truth:
the bottleneck is not competence, but structure.

5. Why I now use AI as an epistemic partner
This brings me to the role of AI.

Some colleagues (including members of the Zitter Institute) look down on using AI in foundational research. They see it as cheating, or unserious, or threatening to their identity as “outsiders.”

But here is the irony:

AI is exactly the tool that can think speculatively without career risk.

An AI:

has no grant committee,
no publication pressure,
no academic identity to defend,
no fear of being wrong,
no need to “fit in.”
That makes it ideal for exploratory ontology-building.

Occasionally, as in the recent paper I co-wrote with Iggy — “The Wonderful Theory of Light and Matter” — it becomes the ideal partner:

human intuition + machine coherence,
real-space modeling without metaphysical inflation,
EM + relativity as a unified playground,
photons, electrons, protons, neutrons as geometric EM systems.
This is not a replacement for science.
It is a tool for clearing conceptual ground,
where overworked, over-constrained academic teams cannot go.

6. So… is something rotten in QED?
Yes — but not what you think.

What’s rotten is the mismatch

between:

the myth of QED as a perfectly clean, purely elegant theory,
and
the reality of improvised renormalization, historical accidents, social inertia, and conceptual discomfort.
What’s rotten is not the theory itself,
but the story we tell about it.

What’s not rotten:

the intelligence of the researchers,
the honesty of experimentalists,
the hard-won precision of modern measurements.
QED is extraordinary.
But it is not infallible, nor philosophically complete, nor conceptually finished.

And that is fine.

The problem is not messiness.
The problem is pretending that messiness is perfection.

7. What I propose instead
My own program — pursued slowly over many years — is simple:

Bring physics back to Maxwell + relativity as the foundation.
Build real-space geometrical models of all fundamental particles.
Reject unnecessary “forces” invented to patch conceptual holes.
Hold both mainstream and alternative models to the same standard:
no ad hoc constants, no magic, no metaphysics.
And — unusually —
use AI as a cognitive tool, not as an oracle.

Let the machine check coherence.
Let the human set ontology.

If something emerges from the dialogue — good.
If not — also good.

But at least we will be thinking honestly again.

Conclusion
Something is rotten in the state of QED, yes —
but the rot is not fraud or conspiracy.

It is the quiet decay of intellectual honesty behind polished narratives.

The cure is not shouting louder, or forming counter-churches, or romanticizing outsider science.

The cure is precision,
clarity,
geometry,
and the courage to say:

Let’s look again — without myth, without prestige, without fear.
If AI can help with that, all the better.

— Jean Louis Van Belle
(with conceptual assistance from “Iggy,” used intentionally as a scalpel rather than a sycophant)

Post-scriptum: Why the Electron–Proton Model Matters (and Why Dirac Would Nod)
A brief personal note — and a clarification that goes beyond Consa, beyond QED, and beyond academic sociology.

One of the few conceptual compasses I trust in foundational physics is a remark by Paul Dirac. Reflecting on Schrödinger’s “zitterbewegung” hypothesis, he wrote:

“One must believe in this consequence of the theory,
since other consequences which are inseparably bound up with it,
such as the law of scattering of light by an electron,
are confirmed by experiment.”
Dirac’s point is not mysticism.
It is methodological discipline:

If a theoretical structure has unavoidable consequences, and
some of those consequences match experiment precisely,
then even the unobservable parts of the structure deserve consideration.
This matters because the real-space electron and proton models I’ve been working on over the years — now sharpened through AI–human dialogue — meet that exact criterion.

They are not metaphors, nor numerology, nor free speculation.
They force specific, testable, non-trivial predictions:

a confined EM oscillation for the electron, with radius fixed by 
ℏ
/
m
e
c
;
a “photon-like” orbital speed for its point-charge center;
a distributed (not pointlike) charge cloud for the proton, enforced by mass ratio, stability, form factors, and magnetic moment;
natural emergence of the measured 
G
E
/
G
M
​ discrepancy;
and a geometric explanation of deuteron binding that requires no new force.
None of these are optional.
They fall out of the internal logic of the model.
And several — electron scattering, Compton behavior, proton radius, form-factor trends — are empirically confirmed.

Dirac’s rule applies:

When inseparable consequences match experiment,
the underlying mechanism deserves to be taken seriously —
whether or not it fits the dominant vocabulary.
This post is not the place to develop those models in detail; that will come in future pieces and papers.
But it felt important to state why I keep returning to them — and why they align with a style of reasoning that values:

geometry,
energy densities,
charge motion,
conservation laws,
and the 2019 SI foundations of 
h
, 
e
, and 
c

over metaphysical categories and ad-hoc forces.
Call it minimalism.
Call it stubbornness.
Call it a refusal to multiply entities beyond necessity.

For me — and for anyone sympathetic to Dirac’s way of thinking — it is simply physics.

— JL (with “Iggy” (AI) in the wings)

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America logo
Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2025 May 23;122(23):e2425772122. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2425772122
Complexity myths and the misappropriation of evolutionary theory
Michael Lynch a,1
Author information
Article notes
Copyright and License information
PMCID: PMC12167962  PMID: 40408411
Abstract
Recent papers by physicists, chemists, and geologists lay claim to the discovery of new principles of evolution that have somehow eluded over a century of work by evolutionary biologists, going so far as to elevate their ideas to the same stature as the fundamental laws of physics. These claims have been made in the apparent absence of any awareness of the theoretical framework of evolutionary biology that has existed for decades. The numerical indices being promoted suffer from numerous conceptual and quantitative problems, to the point of being devoid of meaning, with the authors even failing to recognize the distinction between mutation and selection. Moreover, the promulgators of these new laws base their arguments on the idea that natural selection is in relentless pursuit of increasing organismal complexity, despite the absence of any evidence in support of this and plenty pointing in the opposite direction. Evolutionary biology embraces interdisciplinary thinking, but there is no fundamental reason why the field of evolution should be subject to levels of unsubstantiated speculation that would be unacceptable in any other area of science.
Keywords: evolution, complexity, selection, mutation
Enormous strides have been made in the biological sciences over the past century, and no subdiscipline has experienced greater advancements on the theory side than evolutionary biology. Guided by the basic principles of genetics, broad interests in adaptation, a deep understanding of the structures of genes and genomes at the molecular level, and the refinement of population genetics to include stochastic processes, evolutionary theory is now so well entrenched that no hypothesis about biological diversification should be taken too seriously unless it can be shown to be consistent with basic population-genetic principles (1–6). The days in which scientists simply quote Darwin and assume that everything is a product of natural selection should be over.
Yet, we are now living in a new kind of world. Successful politicians and flamboyant preachers routinely focus on the development of false narratives, also known as alternative facts, repeating them enough times to convince the naive that the new message is the absolute truth. This strategy is remarkably similar to earnest attempts by outsiders to redefine the field of evolutionary theory, typically proclaiming the latter to be in a state of woeful ignorance, while exhibiting little interest in learning what the field is actually about. Intelligent designers insist that molecular biology is too complex to have evolved by earthly evolutionary processes. A small but vocal group of proselytizers clamoring for an “extended evolutionary synthesis” continues to argue that a revolution will come once a critical mass of disciples is recruited (7–9), even though virtually every point identified as ignored has been thoroughly evaluated in prior research; see table 1.1 in ref. 6. More than one physicist has claimed that all of biology is simply physics. But 2023 marked a new level of advocacy by a small group of physicists, chemists, and geologists to rescue the field of evolutionary science from obfuscation, and to do so by introducing new theories and laws said to have grand unifying potential.
There is, of course, an entire area of philosophy devoted to identifying when an idea should be viewed as a theory or a law, but that is not the focus here. The key issue is that, unlike any other field, the guardrails are seemingly off when it comes to evolutionary science. No one would take seriously an organismal biologist proclaiming that biochemists have been confused about molecular mechanisms, and that we need a new framework that neglects the importance of hydrogen bonds. Nor would one be taken seriously by physicists if one proclaimed that there is no background thermal motion of molecules or that the atomic theory is fundamentally flawed. The same would be true if one were to suggest that geologists need to abandon the principle of uniformitarianism and the reliance on measures based on radioactive decay. In contrast, it appears relatively easy to make fantastical claims in highly visible venues about matters in evolution, without reference to prior work, even when such claims are known to be without merit. The two exemplar publications discussed below are Sharma et al. (10) and Wong et al. (11), although many more could be cited, e.g., ref. 12.
Assembly Theory
Sharma et al. claim to introduce new theory and a single index that explains and quantifies selection and evolution in ways that have eluded decades of previous researchers. In doing so, they exhibit a remarkable lack of familiarity with the field of evolution and/or an unwillingness to explain what needs to be fixed. As pointed out elsewhere (13), the ideas in this paper have been subject to considerable self-promotion, but that is not the central issue here either. The scientific problems are numerous enough, just three of which will be pointed out.
The theoretical concept introduced by the authors is a composite “assembly measure,”
𝐴=
𝑁
∑	𝑖=1
𝑒𝑎𝑖⁡(
𝑛𝑖−1
𝑁𝑇

[1]
where N is the number of unique object types (in a collection of molecules), ai (the assembly index) is the minimum number of steps required to assemble an object of type i starting from an assumed pool of irreducible building blocks (e.g., atoms or amino acids), ni is the copy number for type-i objects in a sample, and 𝑁𝑇=∑𝑁
𝑖=1𝑛𝑖 is the total number of objects in the sample. This is not an index built from first principles but simply derives from the authors’ intuition as to what constitutes a more complex assembly of molecules. The data for such an analysis require a sample subjected to mass spectrometry or other such methods, as well as a knowledge of the underlying basic building blocks required for the production of higher-order structures. In principle, one might find use of such a composite indicator in exploring collections of molecules from outer space or ancient rocks and attempting to infer a signature of life, a major challenge for astrobiology. To this end, a goal of the authors is to obtain a threshold value of A beyond which biology resides, as distinct from physical systems. They have promoted these ideas in many previous publications, e.g., (14).
Some concerns are immediately apparent. Why the discounting by 1 in the numerator? Apparently, because a singular recording might just be generated by a random event that is not representative of true complexity. However, any attempt to deal with outliers is sample-size dependent, as larger samples will be prone to contain larger numbers of oddballs. Some other number x might be substituted for 1, but an objective criterion for doing so is unclear. Why the exponential weighting by the minimal number of construction steps? The rationale here is that an investigator would typically not know the actual construction steps leading to an object, while some knowledge of chemistry might suggest the minimum possible. The number of combinatorial possibilities associated with a particular assembly index is thought to increase “superexponentially” with the magnitude of the latter, but if so, why not use an even steeper weighting? The authors desire an index that incorporates both the difficulty of “discovering” an object (the first term) and the “ease of production” of the object once discovered (the second term, a measure of abundance). However, living organisms do not synthesize molecules to levels based on their ease of production, but instead engage in widespread regulation of the numbers of products of individual genes and pathways. Thus, the reasons for weighting based on abundance are obscure.
In addition to these conceptual difficulties, there are obvious quantitative issues with Eq. 1, one of the more notable being that wildly different combinations of ni, N, x, and NT can yield the same value of A. Furthermore, it is not hard to think of examples that go against the grain. Consider, as a simple example, a sample containing two object types, each represented by two copies (, and ), each with , which leads to Notice that if the sample size is doubled (, and ), the assembly measure is increased by 50% () despite the absence of compositional change. Next consider a sample with a single molecule type present in copies with ; this system contains fewer molecular types, but the single molecule requires more assembly steps, and , implying an 11-fold increase in overall complexity. Different results would be obtained if one were to deviate from equal weighting of the two terms in Eq. 1, and there is the additional problem that owing to the NT in the denominator, the weighting term is not an independent measure of molecular ease of production, but depends on the entire composition of the sample. The key point is that the arbitrary nature of Eq. 1 leaves the single index A open to a multiplicity of alternative interpretations.
However, this is not the biggest problem with assembly theory and its proposed utility in revealing the mechanistic origins of molecular mixtures. A second, more fundamental issue is that the authors repeatedly misuse the term selection, failing to realize that, even in its simplest form, evolution is a joint function of mutation bias, natural selection, and the power of random drift. There is a fundamental distinction between the mutational processes that give rise to an object and the ability of selection (natural or otherwise) to subsequently promote (or eradicate) it. In the field of evolution, drift refers to the collective influences of stochastic factors governed by universal factors such as finite population size, variation in family sizes, and background interference induced by the simultaneous presence of multiple mutations; via the generation of noise, the magnitude of drift modulates the efficiency of selection. For the past century, these processes have been the central components of evolutionary theory (reviewed in refs. 5 and 6).
As a simple example, consider two object types A and a, with forward and reverse exchange (production) rates equal to u and v, respectively, with denoting the mutation bias toward A. In genetics, these would be two alleles subject to reversible mutation, but they could also be two exchangeable particle types in a physical system. Supposing that the A type was under persistent positive selection with advantage s, the long-term average frequency of a is then equal to where Ne is the effective size of the population (which is inversely proportional to the noise in the evolutionary process) (15, 16). An essentially identical equation arises in two-state physical systems, when background thermal motion is substituted for , yielding the Boltzmann equation (17, 18).
This type of formulation can be expanded to any number of states, including the members of interconnected assembly pathways outlined by Sharma et al., but the simple version suffices to make two salient points. First, in the complete absence of selection () or if the power of drift substantially exceeds the strength of selection (), the A type will have a nonzero equilibrium frequency which depends only on the ratio of forward and reverse production rates; i.e., selection is not required for a biased distribution of molecular types. Second, because the entire process depends on the single composite parameter the action of selection cannot be determined from the incidence of an object without further information, i.e., a high incidence of A can result from strong directional mutation and/or selection bias.
Evolutionary biologists (and physicists) have long been aware of these issues. To interpret incidence data (e.g., to infer selection), additional information (such as the level of production bias) is essential. Sharma et al. conflate the concepts of mutation and selection and also ignore the possibility of reversible chemical reactions. No information on selection can be gleaned from the assembly measure without quantitative measures of production rates—a strong bias in the incidence of molecular types can arise in the absence of selection, and an even distribution is possible in the presence of selection, e.g., if 𝛽⁢𝑒𝑁𝑒⁢𝑠=1. The index ai may be a useful indicator of molecular complexity, although this idea is not new (13), but given the numerous problems just listed, the composite measure A appears to be an essentially meaningless measure of the origins of complexity.
Illusions of the Adaptive Emergence of Complexity
We now move on to the third problem with the notion of an informative assembly measure, one that also relates to Wong et al. Sharma et al. implicitly assume that a primary goal of natural selection is the production of increased complexity. This common view is an entirely anthropocentric construct, and there is no evidence that natural selection is in relentless pursuit of more complex molecules, cells, or organisms. Of course, today’s organisms are more complex than prior to the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA), but there was only one direction to go four-billion years ago at the first dawn of cells. Microbes have been around for this entire period, and yet have not expanded in complexity. Given their enormous population sizes and short generation times, there were clearly adequate opportunities for the emergence of genomic, molecular, and cellular complexity should it have been at a selective premium. Yet, the origin of morphologically complex cells leading to eukaryotes was a singular event, and the vast majority of the Tree of Life remains prokaryotic. There are roughly 1030 prokaryotic individuals on Earth, three orders of magnitude more than unicellular eukaryotes, and ten orders of magnitude more than the total number of metazoan individuals (reviewed in ref. 19), hardly an observation in support of a determined march toward complexity.
Major expansions in genome size and gene–structural complexity are largely restricted to metazoans and land plants (tiny segments on the entire Tree of Life), both of which experienced substantial reductions in effective population sizes (19, 20) that, as just noted, reduce the efficiency of natural selection. Even in these lineages, gene-number increases are generally only two- to fivefold relative to those in prokaryotes, which only requires the addition of one new gene per 100,000 y since the emergence of eukaryotes. As further discussed below, the majority of the expansion in genome size in multicellular organisms is associated with the insertion of deleterious mobile genetic elements and noncoding introns in protein-coding genes (20).
It is commonly argued that increased numbers of duplicate genes and heteromeric molecular complexes have generated more robust organisms, but no evidence supports this either (19). For example, despite their added complexity for DNA replication and repair pathways, metazoans and land plants have substantially higher deleterious mutation rates than do prokaryotes. Despite their substantially more complex ribosomes and mechanisms for assembling them, eukaryotes do not have elevated rates or improved accuracies of translation, and if anything, catalytic rates and degrees of enzyme accuracy are reduced relative to those in prokaryotes (with simpler homomeric enzymes). Eukaryotes have diminished bioenergetic capacities (i.e., growth rates) relative to prokaryotes (21, 22), and this reduction is particularly pronounced in multicellular species (23). Finally, it is worth noting that numerous organisms (parasites in particular, which constitute a large fraction of organisms) typically evolve simplified genomes, and many biosynthetic pathways for amino acids and cofactors have been lost in the metazoan lineage.
Living organisms are not equivalent to inanimate objects endowed with a special power for self-replication. The peculiar details of life’s structures and functions are legacies of historical contingencies, laid down prior to LUCA, which dictate all aspects of molecular assembly and breakdown. This is why biology is not simply chemistry or physics. Should they even exist, any assembly rules associated with living systems need not coincide with those in a test tube or in sediments or gases. Biosynthetic mechanisms are known to differ substantially among phylogenetic lineages (19), and they likely would be still different on an alternative life-harboring planet.
What about the layers of defense against errors and the expansions of genetic and metabolic networks, present in all cells but especially so in multicellular species? Are these really consistent with what Wong et al. call the “law of increasing functional information” [also referred to as the law of increasing complexity, an idea with some precedence; (24)], which they endow with a status equivalent to the central laws of physics involving motion, gravity, thermodynamics, electricity, and magnetism? Again, the answer appears to be no. Theory (and data) support the idea that an additional layer of complexity in a particular biological pathway simply relaxes selection associated with the other participants, leading to reduced performance of the individual components and no long-term increase in accuracy in the overall system (25, 26). Other well-trodden ideas associated with the emergence and eventual entrenchment of complexity, with no increases in organismal performance, are embodied in the theory of constructive neutral evolution (27, 28). These general principles apply not just to biology but to many human inventions, including various architectural features of computers (26).
What is functional information? Wong et al. never tell us, but they must have something quantifiable in mind, as they conclude that this feature increases over time. They also appear to define function as something that is under selection. Here are a few problems, just from the perspective of the genes and genomes that are ultimately responsible for the organic materials from which cells are built. First, all genomes experience recurrent inputs of new duplicate genes, which arise as accidents during chromosomal replication (20). Most duplicate genes are either partially or entirely redundant, and often fleeting in time. Duplicate genes are more frequently preserved in multicellular eukaryotes than in microbes, not because they have gained a new function, but rather because they have partitioned preexisting functions (subfunctionalization). Subfunctionalization does not arise because natural selection is striving for such an endpoint, which is an energetic and a mutational burden, but because of the relaxed efficiency of selection in lineages of organisms with reduced effective population sizes. How then does one relate gene number to functional information?
Second, introns colonized the eukaryotic genome pre-LUCA, likely by self-proliferating processes, again burdening their host genes with energetic and mutagenic costs not incurred in prokaryotes. There is functional information associated with intron sequences, in that each intron (and the adjacent exon sequence) harbors key motifs for proper recognition by the complex splicing machine. But there is no evidence that the initial colonization of such gene–structural embellishments in the ancestral eukaryote was promoted by selection for increased information. Rather, it is the other way around.
Third, owing to the redundancy in the genetic code, nucleotide substitutions at a number of sites within codons have no consequences for the resultant protein sequence. However, in microbes with very large effective population sizes, specific nucleotides at such positions can be selectively promoted based on their influences on transcriptional and/or translational efficiency. Is there then a loss of functional information as effective neutrality plays a larger and larger role in eukaryotes, especially multicellular lineages with very low Ne? At what point does one stop counting a nucleotide site or a gene as being functional or having information content?
Finally, in one of their only explicit examples, the authors suggest that the information content of a ribozyme is a function of its size, although they later claim that “loss of some functions can still represent an increase in the functional information of the selected function.” It is unclear what the authors mean here, but again consider the ribosome, the heart of which is a ribozyme. The ribosome is a puzzling large molecular machine, but most notable are the enlargements of ribosomal RNAs in various eukaryotic lineages. Such adventitious growth is restricted to expansion segments outside of the functionally important regions in rRNAs. There are substantial increases in the numbers of ribosomal proteins in eukaryotes as well, and even more dramatic increases in the machinery required for ribosome biosynthesis (reviewed in ref. 19). Again, there is no evidence that any of these changes have been promoted by positive selection, and the more likely explanation is that selection is efficient enough in the vast majority of the Earth’s biota (unicellular species) to prevent things like this from happening.
This list could easily be expanded to cover other aspects of genomic evolution, including the dramatic expansions of burdensome but information-containing parasitic genetic elements (e.g., transposons and retrotransposons) in multicellular lineages. But the key point has been made. For authors confident enough to postulate a new law of evolution, surely some methodology and supportive data could have been provided. Science is littered with historical fads that became transiently fashionable, only to fade into the background, with a nugget of potential importance sometimes remaining (e.g., concepts derived from chaos theory, concerted evolution, evolvability, fractals, network science, and robustness). But usually when the latter happens, there is a clear starting point. This is not the case with the “law of increasing functional information,” which fails to even provide useful definitions of function and information.
Organisms are not simply glorified machines or computers (29), and added layers of complexity in living systems are not neutral in an absolute sense. More complex systems are easier to break and more energetically expensive to construct and maintain. Provided a simpler system can suffice to carry out a task, this will always be the premium when natural selection operates at maximum efficiency, which is quite different from a series of abiotic chemical reactions going down a path of least resistance. To sum up, all evidence suggests that expansions in genomic and molecular complexity, largely restricted to just a small number of lineages (one including us humans), are not responses to adaptive processes. Instead, the embellishments of cellular complexity that arise in certain lineages are unavoidable consequences of a reduction in the efficiency of selection in organisms experiencing high levels of random genetic drift.
Interdisciplinary Science
Some readers, probably including the authors of the above-mentioned papers, will argue that there is excessive hubris in the preceding paragraphs, and that there should be room at the table for alternative views. The latter point is certainly true and to be encouraged—that is how science proceeds. But science marches backward when the participants are unwilling to consider preexisting information, and a certain level of push-back is warranted when such behavior is combined with excessive self-promotion. Like evolution itself, science is a process of descent with modification. Only occasionally, on time scales of centuries, are there major shakeups that demolish the foundations of what we view as knowledge. Despite the mass of scientific knowledge that has been procured over the past 150 y or so and the expansion of the scientific workforce, the waiting times between such events are increasing (30), as expected if the scientific enterprise is operating as it should.
There is not only ample room, but a real need, in evolutionary biology for those willing to engage with the field in a meaningful way. Indeed, some of the most important advances in evolutionary theory (and in ecology) over the past few decades have come from physicists and probability theorists who have realized that many of the mathematical methods in their arsenals can be used to solve previously impenetrable problems. Geochemists have begun to open our eyes to fundamental constraints imposed on evolution by the basic physical structure of the earth and its elemental constituents. Evolutionary biology encompasses every subdiscipline within the life sciences and is critically dependent on knowledge from physics, chemistry, and geology. Darwin was one of the first integrative biologists. Yet, at a time when there is increasing focus on interdisciplinary science, the two papers noted above are anachronistic, ostensibly focused on key issues in evolution but largely ignoring biology.
Evolutionary biology continues to be treated in a most unusual way. Unsupported and sometimes bizarre ideas launched by outsiders, including scientists with exceptional expertise in their own fields, is nothing new to the field of evolution. Yet, logic suggests that to be credible in dismissing whole disciplines, hopeful revolutionaries would be intimately familiar with the fields that they are trying to overthrow. If the view is that prior work is completely irrelevant or that new general principles are needed, fine, but the responsible approach would be to clarify why. The ultimate goal of any mature area of science is to reach the point where all of the solid theoretical foundations have been confidently set down and affirmed by empirical observation, the rest being stamp collecting. Evolutionary biology may be closer to this benchmark than a number of other fields.

Beyond wave-particle dualism: How Suntola’s mass-wave concept unites physics and metaphysics
To cite this article: Tarja Kallio-Tamminen 2025 J. Phys.: Conf. Ser. 2948 012005

Ovidiu Cristinel Stoica
- Preface
M Satriawan, M Khoiro, F Fitriana et al.

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
Beyond wave-particle dualism: How Suntola's mass-wave concept unites physics and metaphysics
Tarja Kallio-Tamminen
Physics Foundations Society, Espoo, Finland
The Finnish Society for Natural Philosophy, Helsinki, Finland
E-mail: kallio.tamminen@elisanet.fi
Thomas Kuhn1 convincingly showed that scientific revolutions occasionally happen even if we are not prepared for them: “Probably, the single most prevalent claim advanced by the proponents of a new paradigm is that they can solve the problems that led the old one to a crisis.”
Abstract. The article evaluates the significance of Tuomo Suntola's Dynamic Universe (DU) theory from physical, metaphysical, and cultural perspectives. It demonstrates how Suntola's concept of the mass wave, derived by removing the speed of light from Planck's constant, resolves the wave-particle dualism, enabling a better understanding of quantum phenomena and the nature of reality. Within DU, the Newtonian mechanical and deterministic clockwork world is replaced by a dynamic and self-organizing entity that develops completely according to law, but not deterministically. This unified formalism encompasses phenomena dealt with by relativity theory, cosmology, and quantum physics, providing a comprehensive world-view where events can be described objectively in an immutable 4-dimensional coordinate system. Such a scientific revolution, replacing abstract and unintuitive standard theories with an entire world-view, allows for a deeper understanding of reality and our place within it. The restoration of a comprehensible overall map could improve the quality of human performance in both environmental matters and personal lives.
1. The quantum that clouded the conception of reality
The empirical Newtonian science was, for several centuries, believed to provide a reliable ’window into reality’. At the end of the 1800s, physicists generally believed the world consisted of material particles, which were distinct local objects, and waves, which were connected to electromagnetic fields extending throughout space. It was believed that future development could only bring minor improvements to the view, but very soon the clear landscape behind the window faded from view. Had it been just an illusion? Is there any reality behind the window?
The traditional particle-mechanistic framework of classical physics turned out to be limited with the birth of modern physics at the beginning of the 20th century. Common sense and the accustomed way of thinking could no longer provide tools to understand the theory of relativity. Even less were they able to deal with the phenomena revealed by quantum physics. The eminent scientists who developed the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics were
Content from this work may be used under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. Any further distribution
of this work must maintain attribution to the author(s) and the title of the work, journal citation and DOI. Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd 1
    
Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
convinced that the metaphysical framework assumed by classical physics had proven to be limited. Quantum theory would entail profound revisions to the customary ontological and epistemological conceptions of reality. Nevertheless, such a new comprehensive framework, which would be essential for a clear understanding of reality, has been long overdue. Without a generally accepted interpretation, the abstract mathematical theories that physicists are dealing with cannot be expressed in qualitative terms, and ordinary people have no way to comprehend their meaning, or really understand the nature of reality. It cannot even be verified whether these incompatible theories genuinely reflect any reality. Maybe they are just mathematical instruments to systematize observations?
Originally, the desire to understand reality better was a strong driving force for physics. Research progressed well in the Newtonian framework, and physics, dealing with the universal laws governing the world, was believed to have revealed the true nature of reality. But progress proved this belief to be premature. The metaphysical foundation on which the basic postulates of the theories are grounded cannot be known in advance. Replacing an outdated paradigm with a more suitable broader context calls for philosophical reflection, reconciling metaphysical, epistemological, physical and empirical components.
The current crisis in understanding the perception of reality began when the interactions between material particles and waves of radiation were subjected to closer examination. Max Planck unintentionally triggered a revolution in 1901 by revealing that radiation had particle- like features. To explain the observed results of so-called black-body radiation, Planck had to presume that electromagnetic radiation was born in packages whose energy E was the frequency f times the constant h, E = hf (Planck’s constant h = 6,6 x 10–34 Joules/second)
The formula indicated that atoms emitted radiation as discrete energy packets, quanta. Such an idea of quantization was completely foreign to classical physics, where change always took place in a continuous manner through all intermediate phases. It was initially generally believed that Planck’s quanta were only temporary mathematical hypotheses, and Planck himself did not acknowledge non-continuity to be real until 1909. 2, pp173-174
Even if the nature of these quanta and the reason for the quantization were not clear, Einstein soon used them to explain the photoelectric effect, and Niels Bohr incorporated quantization into his model of the atom. The problem of whether the smallest building blocks of reality should be described as particles or waves became even more serious as a result of Louis de Broglie’s astonishing doctoral thesis, which was later awarded the Nobel Prize. In 1924, de Broglie proposed that, similar to how waves appeared to have particle properties particles could also possess wave-like properties. 2, pp174-178 He later recalled his aim by saying:
“When I conceived the first basic ideas of wave mechanics in 1923–24, I was guided by the aim to perform a real physical synthesis, valid for all particles, of the coexistence of wave and the corpuscular aspects...”
De Broglie derived equations for the wavelength and frequency of particles, obtaining λ=h/p and f=E/h. The formula for the frequency was obtained directly from Planck’s equation, and for wavelength, he simply solved for wavelength λ in the equation m=h/λc, which Einstein had presented for the masses of “radiation grains”, replacing the speed of light, c, by the velocity of the particle, v. Such an unjustified replacement was naturally risky. De Broglie’s matter-wave did not correspond to the movement of the particle, as the wave packet usually breaks up because its group velocity is not the same as the velocity of the particle. However, the belief in a
 2

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
particle-related wave was strong, as the idea of standing waves offered a plausible explanation, e.g., for the permissible orbits that Bohr had postulated in his atomic model.
In 1926, Quantum mechanics was born. Heisenberg first introduced matrix mechanics and Schrödinger soon after wave mechanics, both of which were found to be mathematically equivalent.2, pp178-186 This abstract theory turned out to be extremely accurate and useful but difficult to interpret. It is widely used and applied in science and technology, although it is not actually known where the predictive ability of the theory comes from. Seen against the background of previous ontological and epistemological assumptions, many quantum phenomena appear to be contrary to the presumptions of common sense. The inability for more than a hundred years to agree on the interpretation indicates that our understanding of the basic elements and building blocks of reality is in fact undergoing profound change. Initially, Schrödinger tried to create a wave interpretation, but the complex and multidimensional waves that depended on the chosen set of observables could not be interpreted as waves in 3- dimensional physical space. The actualization of the many possibilities contained in the wave function could not be accurately predicted, but was only statistically linked to the results of the experiments performed in the macroscopic world.
In 1926, Max Born presented his probability interpretation: the square of the wave function gives the probability that a particle will be found in a certain location. Nowadays, this kind of wave-particle dualism is generally accepted. Even if one were not happy with this abstract definition and state of affairs, it has been a practical necessity. Both concepts are needed to explain the observations, but no one knows if the entities they refer to fundamentally are particles, waves, combinations thereof, or perhaps something else. This ambiguous situation is more or less emphasized in different interpretations, but none of them manage to offer a generally accepted solution to this conceptual problem important for a comprehensible worldview. Following De Broglie's approach, David Bohm in particular has tried to defend the reality of both the wave and the particle in his interpretation.2, pp244-247
The different interpretations and the stagnant state of the interpretation discussions became familiar to me more than 25 years ago when I was preparing my dissertation in the field of Theoretical Philosophy titled Quantum Metaphysics, the Role of Human Beings within the Paradigms of Classical and Quantum Physics.2 When aiming to clarify what the long debate on the interpretation of quantum mechanics truly contained and indicated, I came to believe that the obvious impasse implied that a proper framework where the new phenomena would be understandable had not yet been found. In the words of Niels Bohr3, pp25-26, with quantum mechanics, nature has taught us something that forces us to change our thinking. It requires us to reconsider the prevailing metaphysics, to renew our worldview; to go through the same type of change that happened with classical physics at the beginning of the Modern era.
Bohr’s response to this challenge was his principle of complementarity, which I found quite appealing. It re-evaluates the relationship between human beings, language, and reality. In Bohr’s framework, humans are not external observers but part of reality, influencing its development. This participation completely reconstructs the previous objective and dualistic approach, based on the ideas of Descartes. Bohr is sometimes considered an anti-realist because he emphasized epistemology and avoided forming ontological descriptions of the microscopic world. However, I believe he was a cautious realist who did not want to mislead future research with premature ontological models. He would not have objected to the idea that future exploration could increase our understanding of the nature of reality.
 3

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
I believe Bohr was right in thinking that humans and their actions should be properly included in our description of nature. We are part of the reality we describe, and our goals, ethical level, knowledge, and all our actions inevitably affect its course. A sensible interpretation of quantum mechanics – that is supposed to cover everything that exists – should provide a coherent basis for understanding the human part as well. According to my reflections, for the formation of such a comprehensive framework to be possible, it would certainly first require forming a unified approach to relativity theory and quantum mechanics. And strangely enough, when I looked around, a suitable candidate for that was available. It was in 1998, when Tuomo Suntola first presented his Dynamic Universe (DU) theory at The Finnish Society for Natural Philosophy. I was thrilled because it seemed to provide just such a comprehensive framework that was needed, and it also shed light on the mystery of mass – a topic that in history has characteristically attracted giants like Newton and Einstein.
I expected academic physicists would immediately begin to investigate whether the DU theory was valid. Whether it really was an internally consistent and coherent formalism that was able to describe and explain physical observations in a totally new kind of context. Curiously enough, they did not do anything. Suntola's ambitious theory was ignored, passed over like a fairy tale of some amateur thinker. Regardless of Dr. Suntola's exceptional innovativeness which was already well known. He had long ago developed the ingenious ALD technology, for which he was later awarded the Millennium Prize. Apparently, the physicists did not allow anyone to change the basic postulates, although this possibility was the most promising for a philosopher seeking to understand the nature of reality. Did the physicists not see the great benefit that a wide and coherent description of reality based on simple and plausible basic postulates could provide?
Without regard to the fact that the Copenhageners, and especially Niels Bohr, emphasized that quantum theory implied a complete renewal of the framework of classical physics, the relation of the abstract theories of physics to the metaphysical basis of reality has not been seriously enough discussed within physics. Physicists have not been actively looking for a new window into reality that could replace the outdated ideas of the Newtonian framework. When being content with the established “normal science” based on the abstract standard models, they are unable to see that a more realistic framework could provide better conditions for research to progress. A valid, well-founded understanding of the basic features of nature would naturally guide research in the right direction – like the Newtonian framework long did. If sensible guidelines were available, philosophers of physics wouldn't need to spend another century defending their insufficient interpretations, and cosmologists would not need to equip reality with massive imaginative entities such as dark energy, whenever new observations do not meet expectations.
2. Discovery of the intrinsic Planck's constant
In this and the following section it is shown that Suntola's work related to Planck's constant can significantly advance the development of physics, even within normal science, as this discovery does not require a revision of the basic postulates. Unlike Planck and probably many others trying before, Suntola succeeded in deriving Planck's quantum from Maxwell's equations. This discovery by no means leads back to the classical Newtonian worldview but opens up a new understanding of mass as a wavelike entity and particles as standing wave resonators. Replacing Planck’s constant with the simpler intrinsic constant h0, found by Suntola, the wave description of quantum mechanics can be carried through. In this light, the excessive extent of Planck's
 4

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
constant was the main cause giving rise to the problems of wave-particle dualism, and interpretation of quantum mechanics. Inexact description did not give an opportunity to see deeper into reality.
To get a better idea of Suntola’s contribution, we will first take a closer look at the discovery of the quantum. The study of black body radiation is based on the fact that all materials spontaneously emit and absorb electromagnetic radiation to some degree. A black body is an idealized object that absorbs all electromagnetic radiation falling on it
.I
It was customary to measure what happened when additional energy was available. For example, what kind of radiation was emitted, when iron was heated so that it first turned red and then white and bluish-white? Obviously, heat energy is somehow changing into light, into different types of electromagnetic
radiation, but what is the mechanism?
Careful measurements revealed that a black body not only emits radiation at a particular
wavelength but over the entire wavelength spectrum. The distribution of radiation over the emission spectrum shifts depending entirely on the temperature, not on the emitting material. And invariably, t
The problem was that the experimentally observed intensity distribution curves could not be obtained mathematically on
the basis of classical laws.
Wilhelm Wien (1896) applied a classical thermodynamic approach where the frequency of radiation in a closed space is proportional to the kinetic energy (i.e., the temperature) of the emitting atoms of the walls. Thus, Wien supposed that the radiation spectrum is determined by the emitters, which actually fitted well with the experimental curves for high frequencies but failed with the low ones.
Lord Rayleigh (1900) started from a different reasoning, which he had previously used with sound waves. He applied the equipartition principle to all the standing wave periods in a black body cavity and obtained an excellent match to the observed black body spectrum at low frequencies but failed with high frequencies. At high frequencies, the number of standing waves increases towards infinity, which leads to the so-called ultraviolet catastrophe.4, pp65-66
Max Planck managed to reconcile these quite contrary but partly functional approaches with his concept of quantum. By assuming that electromagnetic radiation was quantized and emitted as wave packets whose energy is proportional to the frequency with the factor h (E=hf), Planck acquired a correct result, or actually a working mathematical formula. Since then, quanta have been associated with radiation, although the cause for the quantization is unknown. Why does heat not change into light in random amounts but only in “packets” of a specific size? An answer to this question could presumably elucidate what is going on out there in reality.
Suntola came across Planck's constant when developing the DU theory. In that context, it was natural to assume that the constant should also include the speed of light c. Being a qualified radio engineer, Suntola reasoned that the smallest amount of radiation should be the one emitted by one electron when oscillating once in an antenna. To verify this hypothesis, Suntola solved the energy emitted in a single cycle by a single electron transition in a dipole

antenna.a The solution opens Planck’s constant in terms of elementary charge e, vacuum permeability μ0, and the velocity of light c, which thus is a “hidden” factor in Planck’s constant as
h = 1,1049·2π3e2μ0∙c = h0·c (1)
Substituting the intrinsic Planck constant, h0 ≡ h/c, into Planck’s equation and inserting for
frequency f=c/λ, the Planck equation obtains the form
E = hf = h0c·f = h0/λ·c2 (2)
In this equation, the quantity h0/λ has the physical meaning of the mass equivalence of a cycle of radiation emitted by a single oscillation of an electron in the emitter. We can see that the energy of radiation in equation (2) equals the rest energy of mass E=mc2 when
m = h0/λ [kg] (3)
The wavelength equivalence of mass, the Compton wavelength, obtains the form λ = h0/m, respectively. Solving equation (3) for h0 gives h0= mλm b [kgm].
Thus, we can see that Planck’s constant h can be written as the product of mass, wavelength, and the speed of light.
h = 1,1049·2π3e2μ0c = h0·c = mλm·c (4)
This unexpected connection shows that mass and wavelength are not independent quantities, but depend on each other, being inversely proportional. As the amount of mass increases, the wavelength correspondingly decreases and vice versa.
2.1. The coexistence of the wave and corpuscular aspects
When writing E = hf = h0c·f = h0/λm ·c2 = mc2, it is easy to see that the intrinsic Planck constant allows us to express the energy of Planck's quantum in terms of Einstein’s famous equation that energy equals mass times the speed of light squared. The dream of de Broglie is thus fulfilled. There is “a real physical synthesis of the coexistence of the wave and of the corpuscular aspects...” All waves contain mass (mλ = h0/λ) that equals the intrinsic Planck’s constant divided by the wavelength lambda, and any amount of mass can be expressed as a wave whose wavelength lambda equals the intrinsic Planck’s constant divided by that mass (λ= h0/mλ). Instead of separate particles and waves, a certain kind of genuine connection between mass and wavelength seems to prevail in nature.
Probably Bohr anticipated something like this when he emphasized the principle of complementarity related to the quantum phenomena. He was actively looking for “a frame wide enough to embrace the account of fundamental regularities in nature which cannot be comprehended within a single picture".3, p12 Bohr considered people to be participants in the dynamic events of reality, but in order to describe their experiences, they must detach themselves from the process. He turned his attention to the limits of ordinary language that is adapted for describing the macroscopic world. To reach the new kind of more holistic phenomena related to the micro level, we may have to use seemingly opposite concepts such as
a See more in Appendix 2: Maxwell's equations and a quantum of radiation in Suntola's article Dynamic Universe in this volume.
b The subscript m in the wavelength λm = h0/m stands for the wavelength equivalence of the mass, the Compton wavelength. It is needed because mass and wavelength are not independent variables but their product must be the constant h0.
  6

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
wave and particle that nevertheless complement each other. Bohr applied his principle broadly to different situations, but he, naturally, never talked about the complementarity of mass and wavelength as this connection was not known. In particular, Bohr sought to resolve the connection between Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle and wave-particle dualism by utilizing the relations for position and momentum in quantum mechanics. The uncertainty principle is an example of one of the most significant features of quantum mechanics, namely that all observables do not commute with each other and thus cannot be readily considered independent of one another. This feature somehow reflects the non-local and holistic foundation of the theory but fails to provide adequate access to it.2, pp200-204 One can only conjecture how Bohr would have taken the now-discovered connection between mass and wavelength – whether it would have led him deeper into the nonlocal nature of the entities and events encountered at the quantum level. Whether it would have encouraged him to conclude that reality is fundamentally composed of mass waves?
The unification of mass and wavelength not only honours Bohr’s efforts but makes it possible to describe everything in waves, as Schrödinger sought to do. For the conversion of mass and wavelength shown in equation (3) to be possible, mass must be something else than just a property of solid particles. The wave also becomes something much more "real" than just a mathematical tool for calculating probabilities. Suntola’s approach in fact overcomes the dichotomy of waves and particles. At the same time, it agrees with De Broglie and D. Bohm's effort to understand both the wave and the particle as real. Suntola5, pp202-203 describes mass particles as Compton wave resonators. When they are moving in space they generate another wave entity, a mass wave that travels at speed v with the resonator. De Broglie was to a large extent on a similar track as Suntola and might have come to the same conclusion if the content of h had been resolved in his time. When substituting h0c for h, de Broglie’s equation λ=h/p takes the form λ=h0/m that could easily have been interpreted as the matter-wave he sought. To understand these kinds of waves better we will study how a mass particle described as a Compton mass wave resonator (standing wave) would behave in a double slit, Figure 1.
Figure 1. Compton wave resonator in double slit experiment. The de Broglie mass wave is created as the sum of the Doppler-shifted front- and back waves of the moving Compton resonator.
  7

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
2.2. Resonance object in a double slit
When a Compton wave is closed to form a resonator particle, that is at rest in space, it has no momentum because the components in the standing wave sum to zero in 3-dimensional space. When the resonator particle is set into motion, moving at velocity v, a new sum wave, which could be called the de Broglie mass wave, is formed in the laboratory frame due to the Doppler shift. The wavelength of the forward-moving front wave of the resonator decreases, and that of the backward-moving wave increases resulting in a new sum wave moving at velocity v. 5, pp204- 205 These new waves due to the momentum of the resonator particles could be the puzzling waves that are observed to interfere in the double slit experiment. Their width is large enough to pass through both slits.
Unlike the probability waves of quantum mechanics, these new mass waves can be interpreted as real in the three-dimensional physical space we perceive. These waves inevitably result from the structure of the moving resonators. As understandable when dealing with waves taking shape according to the motion and environment, the trajectory of individual resonator particles between the slit and the screen cannot be predicted with certainty. It is, however, in principle determined by classical probability, which at each spot is determined by the intensity of the interference wave. If we accept that all material bodies ultimately are complicated mass- wave structures obeying the laws of waves, it should not be surprising that they may, also in other specific situations behave differently from solid bodies, taking shape as required by the observation frame and environment.
The concept of mass wave might also contribute to explaining why, in quantum mechanics, the entire experimental situation must be taken into account – something that Bohr strongly emphasized in his interpretation, and Bohm tried to solve with his pilot wave idea. As complicated non-local wave-phenomena constantly occur also in the electromagnetic fields produced by neuronal assemblies in the brain, the idea of mass waves and the change of their wavelength and speed in different nested frames might also advance our understanding of brain-consciousness relationships. 6
3. The essence of quantum
Removing the speed of light from Planck’s constant makes it possible to solve many difficult interpretation problems. Quantization gets a "natural" explanation when the imprecise Planck's constant h= 6,6256∙10–34 Joules/second is reduced to the tangible form h0 = mλ [kgm]. The quantum is simply explained by the concept of wavelength. Waves consist of whole wavelengths which are indivisible units. Emission and absorption of radiation always occur in whole wavelengths, and based on this finite length, arbitrarily small quanta cannot be generated. When emphasizing the unitary nature of wavelength, Suntola’s antenna model suggests that the quantum is not a property of atoms or radiation as customarily assumed, but rather related to emission and absorption processes – i.e ., to events. Events either take place or they do not. They only occur when wavelengths meet. Every vibration inevitably completes a full cycle, generating an entire wavelength when spreading out into space.
This specified concept of quantum sheds light on many persistent interpretation problems. For example, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle appears to be unavoidable when the position can only be detected with the accuracy of whole wavelengths. This understanding aligns well with the view of the Copenhageners that uncertainty is not about the inaccuracy of observation. It is a limitation in principle that follows from the system’s internal inaccuracy, being more a feature of reality that wave description reflects.2, pp200,201
 8

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
Ultimately, using the intrinsic Planck’s constant could considerably simplify the entire formalism of quantum mechanics. The Schrödinger and Klein-Gordon equations would become much more transparent if the h included in them were expressed in a simpler form. If, instead of elusive probability waves in multidimensional Hilbert space, we could discuss the possibilities of different combinations of mass wave structures in real space, the mysteriousness of quantum physics would be significantly reduced. Physics would come closer to everyday human experience, acknowledging that there are things whose development is not definitely predetermined. Nature contains various real possibilities whose shaping could also be influenced by human actions.
Suntola5, pp178-179 has shown that instead of using the Schrödinger equation, the “discrete” quantum states of the atom can also be calculated from the (de Broglie) mass waves as the minimum points of the energy of their resonance condition. Apparently, the realization of less frequently occurring states requires more energy to be available. The underlying wave nature of particles and the amount of available energy might be sufficient to enable the actualization of an event, eliminating the need for a special concept of quantum probability altogether.
Despite these major reformulations, the analysis of Planck's constant does not yet require changing the basic postulates of physics. With the intrinsic constant h0 derived from Maxwell's equations, mass can be combined into a wave and particles can be described as standing wave resonators already within the "normal science". However, the clarification of the concept of mass was only one of the special features that caught my attention when I first heard Suntola's DU presentation in 1998. What truly excited me was the idea of a global framework, in which the phenomena dealt with by quantum mechanics and relativity theory could be described and where it seemed to be possible also to understand human activity and inner freedom as part of the universal lawfulness of reality. Such changes cannot be made based on the current presuppositions. According to Kuhn, a proper revolution requires the renewal of basic postulates. Things get then organized in a new way, which gives an opportunity to see deeper into reality.
4. Towards a new conception of reality
Every culture has its own worldview that silently guides people's lives in the background. Profound revisions in the conception of reality are rare, but according to Collingwood6 the common worldview has, in Western culture, changed radically in antiquity and at the turn of the modern era. Now we are once again in the middle of a deep transition, as numerous phenomena defy mechanistic and deterministic explanations. In the midst of a crisis, it is not easy to detach from the old to give space for the new. It is worth asking why it took more than a century to notice that atomic emission (e.g., black body radiation) and antenna emission behave in the same way. Why did researchers not scrutinize Planck's constant more thoroughly, even though it was recognized to be the source of the conceptual problems introduced in quantum mechanics? In retrospect, the simple step of rewriting Planck's equation E=hf in the equivalent form E=h/T (where period T=1/f) would have revealed a clearer interpretation: the energy emitted into one cycle.
Science, like all human endeavours, is guided by established concepts, ideas, and ultimately the whole worldview. The lack of a clear overall picture and the mistaken idea inherited from classical physics that particles and waves are separate entities probably prevented research from moving effectively in the most favourable direction. After a hundred years of groping in the dark, it would be time to acknowledge the paramount importance of the research framework,
 9

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
the presuppositions or basic postulates of physical theories, which also largely determine the worldview. These postulates are metaphysical principles that are not proven by the theories. As long as the theories work well, they are supposed to depict reality correctly. But when these ultimate assumptions fail, we should recognize that we are in the midst of a Kuhnian cultural crisis, and the foundations must be re-evaluated.
Ideally, in this kind of unpredictable situation, where the long-held worldview suddenly fails, physicists and philosophers should have joined forces to provide a better picture of reality. However, for decades, neither group has actively searched for a new window into reality that could replace the outdated ideas inherited from Newtonian metaphysics. Physicists have generally considered philosophy to be a waste of time, and philosophers have, nevertheless, left the ontological and metaphysical foundations of reality to them. We have drifted into a situation where the mathematical description of observations is believed to be a description of nature – a situation that once made us prone to believe in the epicycles. In the absence of genuine collaboration, the expertise of the few individuals dedicated to interpreting the unexpected results has not been sufficient to cover all aspects related to this most fundamental interdisciplinary task.
This unintelligible situation probably results from the current research program favoring specialization and differentiation. Within the Newtonian framework, it was reasonable to specialize in smaller and smaller separate areas, but in the present situation, it would be important to understand the whole and the new types of connections that have been observed to prevail in it. To make syntheses and set appropriate new perspectives demands open-minded and fresh discernment. There is a call for discrete natural philosophy, precise and inventive thinkers who strive to develop a general understanding of humanity – whether they are philosophers, physicists, or something else by profession.
The ongoing fading of the Newtonian worldview offers our culture an opportunity to expand horizons beyond the boundaries of the materialistic paradigm that has long boosted secular and material thinking. By following Bohr and placing humans in physical reality, the most difficult problem of modern philosophy, the psychophysical problem, would be overcome by itself. Along with us, the mind and all the mental features – if we are supposed to have any – should also be located as part of nature. There was no place for the influence of mind in the Newtonian framework, but we have had to learn, that it is far from irrelevant what kind of values, goals, theories, and worldviews we hold. They determine our chances to secure our existence on this planet.
It is obvious that the mechanistic and deterministic view of the world that prevailed for a long time has contributed many of the current environmental and social problems. It made us believe that the subject is completely detached from the object and that as outsiders we can use natural laws and resources as we please without consequences. Now we should understand better the nature and influence of our subjective selves. Do we have some inner potential to create a more functional worldview that could better recognize the place and influence of humans in the fabric of reality? Without improved understanding provided by a more reliable map, we hardly can improve our performance in solving global problems.
The task of creating a new model of reality based on human experience and judgment is by no means an easy one. There is no direct way to find a suitable pattern, a new world order that could describe the connections of things more comprehensively than the current one. Thomas Kuhn noticed that the obvious key to launching a totally new kind of paradigm is to provide solutions to the problems that led the old one to its crisis. Suntola succeeded in solving the
 10

Physics and Reality: International Conference on Philosophy of Physics IOP Publishing Journal of Physics: Conference Series 2948 (2025) 012005 doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2948/1/012005
wave-particle dualism, the conceptual ambiguity that brought the worldview of classical physics into crisis. The new understanding generated by unlocking Planck's constant opens the way forward. The next obvious step would be to investigate whether the DU theory, by which the key was found, has also something else to offer for an improved understanding of reality.
Tuomo Suntola’s Dynamic Universe aims to be a unified theory of physics, a holistic comprehensive formalism that covers the issues dealt with in relativity theory, cosmology, and quantum mechanics. Within DU the Newtonian mechanical and deterministic clockwork world is replaced by a dynamic and self-organizing entity that develops completely according to law, but not deterministically. All parts in this evolving system are intrinsically connected through a system of nested energy frames that relies on the zero-energy principle. The source of everything that ever exists is a quantity of mass that is conserved throughout evolution. This abstract, initially unstructured entirety manifests increasingly more intricate structures and functions through the opposition of its inherent potential, the energies of gravity and motion. By postulating the geometry of space to be an expanding 3-sphere, the evolution of the universe can be unambiguously described in a 4-dimensional spatial coordinate system within the accustomed linear time development. There is no need to adjust the coordinate quantities, time and distance, inherent to human perception as happens in the theory of relativity.
Even if all local systems are immanently connected to the whole, they can develop independently within the free energy available in their sub-frame. This might also be applied to individual people whose existence and evolution can be easily fitted into the overall structure of DU. In this formalism, all the energies known to physics are represented by the same kinds of equations, and the zero energy balance would in principle also allow more subtle energies to exist. These could provide a coherent basis for a better understanding of the human part of the world. In Eastern philosophies, the subtle energetic levels are generally supposed to explain mental and noetic phenomena in quite a similar manner to how biological phenomena can be realized through electromagnetic interactions. Within experiential traditions that focus on the inner workings of the human body and mind, such as yoga and qigong, people often recognize the vitalizing influence of subtle prana or qi, but the realm of physics based solely on external effects has had no room for the existence of such internal energetic phenomena.
Now, however, the development in neuroscience based on brain imaging tools and the neurophenomenological research method has begun to correct this deficiency.7,8 Such perspectives will offer philosophy and psychology better chances to understand the inner dynamics of human beings. Within DU the gap between natural sciences and humanities could be naturally bridged. As C.P. Snow indicated in his famous essay “Two Cultures”, this great cultural divide can be the biggest obstacle to advancing human knowledge for the benefit of society. As in DU everything existing in the world results from the harmonious function of an invisible all-embracing source, adopting the new model could also increase humanity's appreciation for the majesty of nature beyond our reach.
DU is an extremely comprehensive and generally comprehensible framework that is based on plausible basic postulates. It deserves to be carefully studied. If no logical, empirical, or rational arguments can disprove it, we have a valid alternative to the current paradigm – which, according to Kuhn, is a prerequisite for a scientific revolution. The realization of such a revolution, however, depends on us. Do we care to get a new window into reality? Do we want to move beyond the belief that reality just obeys inevitable external laws to enter a territory where humans turn out to be responsible participants?

Quantum ‘Jamming’ Explores the Truly Fundamental Principles of Nature
